subQuestions.text: What are the segments of the affected lobe?
subQuestions.keyConcept: The middle lobe of the right lung has two bronchopulmonary segments: medial and lateral — the central fact needed for the segments of the affected lobe.
subQuestions.explanation: The decisive point is “The middle lobe of the right lung has two bronchopulmonary segments: medial and lateral.” This directly resolves the segments of the affected lobe and prevents confusion with nearby structures or related diagnoses.

questions.explanation: This vignette on lobar pneumonia tests the distinction between pain-insensitive visceral pleura and pain-sensitive parietal pleura, the combined nerve supply of the lung and pleura, and localizing the affected lobe/segments from the site of chest pain.
questions.keyConcept: Lobar pneumonia, pleural pain sensitivity, and lobar localization by nerve supply

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The endoderm lining the laryngeotracheal tube gives rise to all the following, EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The laryngeal cartilages develop from the surrounding splanchnic mesoderm, not from the endodermal lining of the laryngotracheal tube; the endoderm instead gives rise to all the epithelial linings of the respiratory tract (larynx, trachea, bronchi, and alveolar cells including Type I cells).
questions.keyConcept: Laryngeal cartilages are mesodermal, not endodermal, in origin

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding the respiratory system, all are true EXCEPT:
options: Type II alveolar cells produce surfactant
Its alveoli mature completely before birth
The supporting muscles and cartilages are mesodermal in origin
questions.explanation: Alveolar maturation is NOT complete before birth; new alveoli continue to develop and mature until about 8 years of postnatal life, making option d the false statement; the respiratory system is otherwise correctly endoderm-lined, foregut-derived, has surfactant-producing Type II alveolar cells, and mesodermal supporting muscles/cartilages.
questions.keyConcept: Alveolar maturation continues postnatally until age 8, not complete at birth

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards the larynx, all the following are true EXCEPT:
options: Its muscles develop from 4th and 6th arches
Its muscles are supplied by recurrent laryngeal and external laryngeal nerves
Its epithelium is derived from caudal part of laryngeotracheal tube
questions.explanation: The epithelium of the larynx is derived from the CRANIAL (not caudal) part of the laryngotracheal tube; the caudal part instead gives rise to the tracheal and bronchial epithelium. The larynx otherwise correctly originates from the foregut, has muscles from the 4th and 6th pharyngeal arches supplied by the corresponding laryngeal nerves, and undergoes temporary lumen obliteration during development (recanalizing later).
questions.keyConcept: Laryngeal epithelium derives from the cranial (not caudal) part of the laryngotracheal tube

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All are true regarding the bronchial tree EXCEPT:
options: Each lung bud forms a main bronchus
Each main bronchus gives three main bronchi (lobar bronchi)
Each lobar bronchus gives tertiary bronchi
Each tertiary bronchus with overlying mesoderm form a bronchopulmonary segment
Further division of bronchi continues after birth
questions.explanation: Only the RIGHT main bronchus gives three lobar (secondary) bronchi; the LEFT main bronchus gives only two lobar bronchi (corresponding to the left lung's two lobes), making the blanket statement in option b false; the other facts about bronchial tree development (main bronchus from lung bud, tertiary/segmental bronchi, bronchopulmonary segment formation, and postnatal continuation of bronchial division) are all correct.
questions.keyConcept: Right main bronchus gives 3 lobar bronchi; left main bronchus gives only 2

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards the frontonasal prominence, choose the INCORRECT statement:
options: It lies ventral to forebrain vesicle
It is formed due to migration of neural crest cells
Two olfactory placodes appear on each side of it
questions.explanation: The frontonasal prominence actually lies ABOVE (not below) the stomodeum (primitive mouth), making option b the false statement; it otherwise correctly appears in the 4th week, lies ventral to the forebrain vesicle, forms from migrating neural crest cells, and has olfactory placodes appearing on either side.
questions.keyConcept: Frontonasal prominence lies above the stomodeum, not below

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The nasal septum develops from:
questions.explanation: The nasal septum develops from the fused medial nasal prominences (which also contribute to the philtrum of the upper lip and the primary palate), distinguishing it from the lateral nasal prominences which instead form the alae of the nose.
questions.keyConcept: Nasal septum develops from the medial nasal prominences

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following develops around the 2nd year postnatally?
questions.explanation: The sphenoid air sinus develops around the 2nd year postnatally; the frontal air sinus develops later, around the 7th year postnatally, while the maxillary and ethmoidal air sinuses are already present (though small) at birth.
questions.keyConcept: Sphenoid sinus develops around age 2; frontal sinus around age 7; maxillary/ethmoidal present at birth

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards the development of the laryngeotracheal tube, choose the INCORRECT statement:
options: It begins to develop in the 4th week
It is formed by a laryngeotracheal groove which appears in the dorsal wall of the primitive pharynx
It has a dorsal part which gives the pharynx & the esophagus
It gives the lining epithelium of larynx & trachea
It is surrounded by splanchnic mesoderm which gives rise to the laryngeal cartilages
questions.explanation: The laryngotracheal groove actually appears in the VENTRAL (not dorsal) wall of the primitive pharynx; the laryngotracheal tube's dorsal part remains as the foregut, giving rise to the pharynx and oesophagus, while the ventral (laryngotracheal) part gives rise to the larynx/trachea/bronchi/lungs and their epithelial lining, surrounded by splanchnic mesoderm forming the cartilages, muscles, and connective tissue.
questions.keyConcept: Laryngotracheal groove appears in the ventral (not dorsal) wall of the primitive pharynx

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The splanchnic mesoderm gives rise to all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Terminal bronchioles develop by repeated branching/division of the endodermal lung buds, not from the splanchnic mesoderm; the mesoderm instead forms the laryngeal cartilages, tracheal/bronchial smooth muscle, connective tissue of the respiratory passages, and the bronchial and pulmonary blood capillaries (vasculature).
questions.keyConcept: Terminal bronchioles arise from endodermal lung bud branching, not splanchnic mesoderm

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All the following share in the formation of the diaphragm EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: There is no ventral mesentery of the oesophagus that contributes to diaphragm formation (the oesophagus has only a dorsal mesentery at that level); the diaphragm instead forms from four components: the septum transversum (central tendon), the pleuroperitoneal membranes, the dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus (crura), and muscular ingrowth from the lateral body walls.
questions.keyConcept: Diaphragm forms from septum transversum, pleuroperitoneal membranes, dorsal (not ventral) oesophageal mesentery, and lateral body walls

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The septum transversum lies opposite 3rd-5th cervical somites during:
questions.explanation: During the 4th week of development, the septum transversum (the primordium of the central tendon of the diaphragm) lies opposite the 3rd-5th cervical somites, which is why the phrenic nerve (derived from C3-C5 ventral rami) supplies the diaphragm after the septum transversum migrates caudally into the thorax, carrying its nerve supply with it.
questions.keyConcept: Septum transversum lies opposite C3-C5 somites during the 4th week, explaining the phrenic nerve's C3-C5 root value

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Tip of nose is sensory innervated by a branch of:
questions.explanation: The skin over the tip and ala of the nose is supplied by the external nasal nerve, a branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve, itself a branch of the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Tip of nose supplied by external nasal nerve (branch of trigeminal via anterior ethmoidal nerve)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Apex of arytenoid cartilage articulates with:
questions.explanation: The apex of each arytenoid cartilage articulates with the corresponding corniculate cartilage, which sits on top of it within the aryepiglottic fold, while the base of the arytenoid articulates with the cricoid cartilage (cricoarytenoid joint).
questions.keyConcept: Apex of arytenoid articulates with corniculate cartilage; base articulates with cricoid

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Thyrohyoid muscle is innervated by:
questions.explanation: The thyrohyoid muscle is supplied by C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve (not via the ansa cervicalis loop proper, which supplies the other infrahyoid muscles), making it and geniohyoid distinctive exceptions among the infrahyoid/strap muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Thyrohyoid is supplied by C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve, not the ansa cervicalis

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following muscles are attached to the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Stylopharyngeus inserts onto the posterior border/superior horn region of the thyroid cartilage and the pharyngeal wall, not the oblique line specifically; the oblique line on the outer surface of the thyroid cartilage's lamina is instead the attachment site for sternothyroid (upper part), thyrohyoid (lower part), and the inferior constrictor of the pharynx.
questions.keyConcept: Stylopharyngeus does not attach to the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Tracheal bifurcation lies at the level of:
questions.explanation: The tracheal bifurcation occurs at the level of the sternal angle, which corresponds anteriorly to the 2nd costal cartilage (and posteriorly to the T4/T5 intervertebral disc level).
questions.keyConcept: Tracheal bifurcation at sternal angle level = 2nd costal cartilage (T4/T5 vertebral level)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are anterior to the trachea EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve (particularly the left) ascends in the tracheo-oesophageal groove, related to the side/posterolateral aspect of the trachea rather than anterior to it; the thyroid isthmus, aortic arch (crossing near the tracheal bifurcation), and left brachiocephalic vein are all genuinely anterior to the trachea.
questions.keyConcept: Recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the tracheo-oesophageal groove, not anterior to the trachea

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Choose the correct statement regarding the left principal (main) bronchus:
options: It has a wider lumen than the right one
It makes a wider angle (~90°) with the trachea compared to the right bronchus
questions.explanation: The left main bronchus is longer (~5cm), narrower, and more oblique/horizontal than the right, making a comparatively wider angle with the tracheal axis; the right main bronchus is shorter (~2.5cm), wider, more vertical (in line with the trachea), and divides into 3 lobar bronchi (vs. 2 for the left).
questions.keyConcept: Left bronchus is longer, narrower, and more oblique (wider angle with trachea) than the right

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following lies on the right side of the trachea?
questions.explanation: The superior vena cava lies along the right side of the trachea in the superior mediastinum; the arch of the aorta instead relates to the left side of the trachea as it arches over the left main bronchus.
questions.keyConcept: SVC relates to the right side of the trachea; aortic arch relates to the left side

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding tracheal bifurcation, select the WRONG statement:
options: It lies at the level of the sternal angle
It is crossed by the aortic arch anteriorly
It occurs at the posterior mediastinum (border region)
The deep cardiac plexus lies just anterior to the bifurcation
questions.explanation: The arch of the aorta relates to the left side of the tracheal bifurcation/left main bronchus as it arches over it, rather than crossing directly anterior to the bifurcation itself; the bifurcation does lie at the sternal angle level (T4/T5), near the superior/posterior mediastinal boundary, with the deep cardiac plexus lying just anterior to it.
questions.keyConcept: Arch of aorta relates to the left side of the tracheal bifurcation, not directly anterior to it

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Structure that lies between the sternal & costal parts of the diaphragm is the:
questions.explanation: The superior epigastric artery, a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery, descends into the abdomen by passing between the sternal and costal muscular slips of origin of the diaphragm.
questions.keyConcept: Superior epigastric artery passes between the sternal and costal origins of the diaphragm

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Thoracic part of the trachea is separated posteriorly from the oesophagus by:
questions.explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends within the left tracheo-oesophageal groove, running directly between the trachea and oesophagus in the thorax and neck; the right recurrent laryngeal nerve instead loops around the right subclavian artery and runs more laterally/posteriorly.
questions.keyConcept: Left recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the tracheo-oesophageal groove, separating trachea from oesophagus

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding the trachea, select the TRUE statement:
options: It descends posterior to the oesophagus
It descends in the posterior mediastinum
It lies posterior and to the right of the arch of the aorta
It bifurcates at the level of the thoracic inlet
questions.explanation: At the level where the aortic arch passes over the left bronchus, the trachea lies posterior and to the right of the arch of the aorta. The trachea itself lies ANTERIOR (not posterior) to the oesophagus, is a superior mediastinal/neck structure (not confined to the posterior mediastinum), and bifurcates at the sternal angle (T4/T5) - well below the thoracic inlet.
questions.keyConcept: Trachea lies posterior and to the right of the aortic arch

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The innermost intercostal muscle:
options: Is present in the middle 2/4 of the intercostal space
questions.explanation: The innermost intercostal muscle is present only in the middle 2/4 (middle half) of the intercostal space; functionally and directionally it matches the internal intercostal muscle (expiratory, fibers downward-backward-laterally), not the statements in options b and c.
questions.keyConcept: Innermost intercostal muscle occupies only the middle half of the intercostal space

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The neurovascular plane of the thorax lies between:
questions.explanation: The intercostal neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve) runs in the plane between the internal intercostal muscle and the innermost intercostal muscle (with the innermost intercostal and internal intercostal separated by this neurovascular plane in the middle part of the space).
questions.keyConcept: Intercostal neurovascular bundle lies between internal and innermost intercostal muscles

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The costo-vertebral joint is between:
options: The head of the rib & the transverse process of the vertebra
The head of the rib & the body of the vertebra
The tubercle of the rib & the transverse process of the vertebra
The tubercle of the rib & the body of the vertebra
questions.explanation: The costovertebral joint is a synovial joint between the head of the rib and the body (and adjacent intervertebral disc) of the vertebra, distinct from the costotransverse joint between the tubercle of the rib and the transverse process.
questions.keyConcept: Costovertebral joint: head of rib + vertebral body; costotransverse joint: tubercle of rib + transverse process

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The costo-transverse joint is between:
options: The head of the rib & the transverse process of the vertebra
The head of the rib & the body of the vertebra
The tubercle of the rib & the transverse process of the vertebra
The tubercle of the rib & the body of the vertebra
questions.explanation: The costotransverse joint is a synovial joint between the tubercle of the rib and the transverse process of the corresponding vertebra, distinct from the costovertebral joint (head of rib with vertebral body).
questions.keyConcept: Costotransverse joint: tubercle of rib + transverse process

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The junction between the manubrium sterni & the body of the sternum lies at the:
questions.explanation: The manubriosternal joint (sternal angle) lies at the level of the 2nd costal cartilage, corresponding posteriorly to the T4/T5 intervertebral disc.
questions.keyConcept: Sternal angle (manubriosternal joint) is at the level of the 2nd costal cartilage

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are true as regards the posterior intercostal arteries EXCEPT:
options: They are paired arteries in each space
They are branches of the superior intercostal artery and the descending aorta
They anastomose with the anterior intercostal arteries at the middle of the intercostal space
questions.explanation: The posterior intercostal arteries anastomose with the anterior intercostal arteries near the anterior end of the intercostal space (close to the costal cartilages), not at the middle of the space; they are otherwise correctly described as paired, arising from the superior intercostal artery/descending aorta, and giving off collateral branches.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior and anterior intercostal arteries anastomose near the anterior end of the space, not the middle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are true as regards the anterior intercostal arteries EXCEPT:
options: They are single in each space
They are branches of the internal mammary (internal thoracic) artery & the musculophrenic artery
They run in the space between the internal and the innermost intercostal muscles
They anastomose with the posterior ones
questions.explanation: The anterior intercostal arteries are not uniformly single in each space: the upper 6 intercostal spaces typically each receive two anterior intercostal branches from the internal thoracic artery, while the lower spaces (7-9) receive only one from the musculophrenic artery.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior intercostal arteries: upper 6 spaces receive two branches each (not single) from internal thoracic artery

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The left 3rd anterior intercostal vein is drained into the:
questions.explanation: The anterior intercostal veins of the upper spaces drain into the venae comitantes accompanying the internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery, which then unite to form the internal thoracic vein.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior intercostal veins drain into the venae comitantes of the internal thoracic artery

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The bucket-handle movement is responsible for increasing which of the following diameters of the thorax:
questions.explanation: The bucket-handle movement of the middle and lower ribs (which rotate/swing outward and upward like a bucket handle) increases the transverse diameter of the thorax.
questions.keyConcept: Bucket-handle rib movement increases the transverse diameter of the thorax

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The pump-handle movement is responsible for increasing which of the following diameters of the thorax:
questions.explanation: The pump-handle movement of the upper ribs and sternum (which swing anteriorly and upward like a pump handle) increases the anteroposterior diameter of the thorax.
questions.keyConcept: Pump-handle rib/sternal movement increases the anteroposterior diameter of the thorax

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The diaphragmatic contraction is responsible for increasing which of the following diameters of the thorax:
questions.explanation: Contraction of the diaphragm flattens its dome and descends it, thereby increasing the vertical diameter of the thoracic cavity, the primary mechanism of quiet inspiration.
questions.keyConcept: Diaphragmatic contraction increases the vertical diameter of the thorax

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Fracture of the neck of the 1st rib may lead to injury to all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The 1st posterior intercostal vein is not closely related to the neck of the 1st rib; structures at risk with a fracture there include the T1 ventral ramus, superior intercostal vessels, and the cervicothoracic (stellate) ganglion, all of which lie in close proximity to the rib neck.
questions.keyConcept: 1st posterior intercostal vein is not a key relation of the neck of the 1st rib

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding the internal mammary (internal thoracic) artery, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
options: It provides the blood supply to the breast
It gives the superior intercostal artery
It gives the anterior intercostal arteries of the upper 6 spaces
Its vein is formed at the level of the 3rd costal cartilage
It is a branch of the 1st part of the subclavian artery
questions.explanation: The superior intercostal artery arises from the costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery, not from the internal thoracic artery; the internal thoracic artery does supply the breast, gives anterior intercostal arteries to the upper 6 spaces, has its accompanying vein formed near the 3rd costal cartilage, and arises from the first part of the subclavian artery.
questions.keyConcept: Superior intercostal artery arises from the costocervical trunk, not the internal thoracic artery

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: To avoid injury of the neurovascular bundle, a thoracocentesis needle is best placed:
options: Near the upper border of the rib
Near the lower border of the rib
Most anteriorly in the intercostal space
Most posteriorly in the intercostal space
questions.explanation: Since the intercostal neurovascular bundle runs along the costal groove at the lower border of the rib above each space, a thoracocentesis needle should be inserted close to the upper border of the rib below (i.e., away from the lower border of the rib above) to avoid injuring the vein, artery, and nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Thoracocentesis needle placed near upper border of rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The intercosto-brachial nerve is the lateral cutaneous branch of the:
questions.explanation: The intercostobrachial nerve is the lateral cutaneous branch of the 2nd intercostal (T2) nerve, supplying skin over the floor of the axilla and medial upper arm, often communicating with the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm.
questions.keyConcept: Intercostobrachial nerve = lateral cutaneous branch of T2

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The sympathetic chain descends from the thorax to the abdomen through:
options: By piercing the crura of the diaphragm
questions.explanation: The sympathetic trunk passes from thorax to abdomen behind the medial arcuate ligament (which arches over psoas major), distinct from the subcostal neurovascular bundle which passes behind the lateral arcuate ligament (over quadratus lumborum).
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic chain passes behind the medial arcuate ligament

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The left phrenic nerve passes through:
options: Piercing the left copula (dome) of the diaphragm
questions.explanation: Unlike the right phrenic nerve (which passes through the vena caval opening/central tendon with the IVC), the left phrenic nerve pierces the muscular left dome (copula) of the diaphragm independently to reach the abdominal surface.
questions.keyConcept: Left phrenic nerve pierces the left dome of the diaphragm directly (unlike the right, which uses the caval opening)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The nerve supply of the mediastinal pleura is provided by:
questions.explanation: The mediastinal pleura (and the central part of the diaphragmatic pleura) is supplied by the phrenic nerve, consistent with its embryological origin from the septum transversum region.
questions.keyConcept: Mediastinal pleura is supplied by the phrenic nerve

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The nerve supply of the costal pleura is derived from:
questions.explanation: The costal pleura (and the peripheral part of the diaphragmatic pleura) is supplied by the intercostal nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Costal pleura is supplied by the intercostal nerves

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following statements are true as regards the pleura EXCEPT:
options: The visceral pleura is insensitive to pain
The lungs are completely surrounded by the pleura
The parietal pleura is lining the thoracic cavity
The space between the 2 layers of the pleura contains no air
questions.explanation: The lung is not literally 'completely' surrounded by pleura: at the hilum, the pleura reflects off the lung (continuing below as the pulmonary ligament) to become continuous with the mediastinal parietal pleura, leaving the hilar structures themselves without a pleural covering; the visceral pleura being pain-insensitive, the parietal pleura lining the thoracic cavity, and the normal absence of air between the pleural layers are all true statements.
questions.keyConcept: The lung is not entirely enclosed by pleura at the hilum, where the pleura reflects to become parietal pleura

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The downward extension of the pleura at the hilum of the lung is:
questions.explanation: Below the hilum, the two layers of pleura (which reflect off the lung root) come together and hang down as a double-layered fold called the pulmonary ligament, which helps anchor the inferior part of the lung and accommodates its movement.
questions.keyConcept: Pulmonary ligament is the downward pleural extension below the hilum

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Introducing a needle in the midclavicular line at the level of the 10th rib on the right side will probably injure:
questions.explanation: Since the pleura's inferior margin in the midclavicular line lies at the 8th rib, a needle at the 10th rib in this line on the right side would pass below the pleura and lung, most likely injuring the liver, which lies immediately below the diaphragm on the right side.
questions.keyConcept: Needle at 10th rib, midclavicular line, right side risks injuring the liver (below pleura/lung level)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Fluids in the pleural cavity tend to be collected in:
questions.explanation: Pleural fluid, under the influence of gravity in the upright position, tends to accumulate first in the costodiaphragmatic recess, the most dependent part of the pleural cavity.
questions.keyConcept: Pleural effusion fluid collects first in the costodiaphragmatic recess

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The lower border of the parietal pleura at the level of the midaxillary line lies at the level of:
questions.explanation: The pleura's inferior margin crosses the midaxillary line at the level of the 10th rib (following the 8th rib at the midclavicular line and 12th rib/T12 spine posteriorly, per the classic 8-10-12 rule).
questions.keyConcept: Pleural inferior margin at midaxillary line: 10th rib

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The lower border of the lung at the level of the midaxillary line lies at the level of:
questions.explanation: The lung's inferior border crosses the midaxillary line at the level of the 8th rib (following the 6th rib at the midclavicular line and the 10th thoracic spine posteriorly, per the classic 6-8-10 rule).
questions.keyConcept: Lung inferior border at midaxillary line: 8th rib

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The horizontal fissure of the right lung begins anteriorly at the level of the:
questions.explanation: The horizontal fissure of the right lung begins anteriorly at the level of the 4th rib/costal cartilage and runs backward to meet the oblique fissure in the midclavicular line.
questions.keyConcept: Horizontal fissure of right lung begins anteriorly at the 4th rib level

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The left bronchial arteries are branches of the:
questions.explanation: The (usually two) left bronchial arteries arise directly from the descending thoracic aorta, distinct from the single right bronchial artery, which commonly arises from the right 3rd posterior intercostal artery or from the left superior bronchial artery.
questions.keyConcept: Left bronchial arteries arise directly from the descending thoracic aorta

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The right bronchial vein is drained into:
questions.explanation: The right bronchial vein drains into the azygos vein, while the left bronchial vein typically drains into the accessory hemiazygos vein or the left superior intercostal/brachiocephalic vein.
questions.keyConcept: Right bronchial vein drains into the azygos vein

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards the mediastinal surface of the right lung, it is related to all of the following structures EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The pulmonary trunk relates to the mediastinal surface of the LEFT lung (not the right), as it passes toward the left before its bifurcation; the right lung's mediastinal surface is genuinely related to the right atrium, ascending aorta, SVC, trachea, and oesophagus.
questions.keyConcept: Pulmonary trunk relates to the left lung's mediastinal surface, not the right

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The most anterior structure in the hilum of the lung is:
questions.explanation: Within the hilum, the superior pulmonary vein is the most anterior structure, followed by the pulmonary artery, then the bronchus (most posterior), with the inferior pulmonary vein being the most inferior structure.
questions.keyConcept: Superior pulmonary vein is the most anterior hilar structure

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The most posterior structure in the hilum of the lung is:
questions.explanation: The bronchus is the most posterior structure within the hilum of the lung on both sides, lying behind the pulmonary artery and veins.
questions.keyConcept: Bronchus is the most posterior structure in the lung hilum

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The anterior borders of both lungs are met (close together) in the midline at which of the following costal levels:
questions.explanation: Both lungs' anterior borders remain close to the midline from the sternoclavicular joint down to the level of the 4th costal cartilage, where the left border deviates laterally to form the cardiac notch while the right continues straight down.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior borders of both lungs stay close to midline until the 4th costal cartilage level

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The cardiac notch of the left lung extends between the:
questions.explanation: The cardiac notch of the left lung's anterior border extends between the 4th and 6th costal cartilages, where the border deviates laterally (about 3.5cm at the 4th costal cartilage) before returning medially to reach the 6th costal cartilage.
questions.keyConcept: Cardiac notch of left lung spans the 4th-6th costal cartilages

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The lower border of the lung reaches the posterior midline at the level of the:
questions.explanation: The lung's inferior border reaches the vertebral column posteriorly at the level of the T10 spine, following the 6-8-10 rule (6th rib midclavicular, 8th rib midaxillary, T10 spine posteriorly).
questions.keyConcept: Lung inferior border reaches posterior midline at T10 spine level

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The tracheal bifurcation is at the level of the:
questions.explanation: The tracheal bifurcation occurs at the level of the sternal angle, which corresponds both to the T4/T5 intervertebral disc posteriorly and the 2nd costal cartilage anteriorly - these being two descriptions of the same anatomical level.
questions.keyConcept: Tracheal bifurcation: T4/T5 disc posteriorly = 2nd costal cartilage anteriorly (same level)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The direct posterior relation of the trachea is:
questions.explanation: The oesophagus lies directly posterior to the trachea throughout its course in the neck and superior mediastinum, separated from it mainly by the left recurrent laryngeal nerve in the tracheo-oesophageal groove.
questions.keyConcept: Oesophagus is the direct posterior relation of the trachea

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The thoracic part of the trachea is separated from the esophagus by the:
questions.explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends within the left tracheo-oesophageal groove, running directly between the trachea and the oesophagus.
questions.keyConcept: Left recurrent laryngeal nerve separates trachea from oesophagus in the tracheo-oesophageal groove

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are true about the broncho-pulmonary segment EXCEPT:
options: The segments are pyramidal in shape with their bases directed toward the hilum
The segments could be surgically resected
questions.explanation: The bronchopulmonary segment is pyramidal/wedge-shaped with its APEX (not base) directed toward the hilum/root of the lung and its BASE directed toward the lung surface, making this option's description backwards and therefore false; the other statements (10 segments in the right lung, intersegmental veins, intrasegmental/segmental arteries, and surgical resectability) are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Bronchopulmonary segment: apex toward hilum, base toward lung surface (not the reverse)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: To pass a needle into the pleural space (cavity) in the midaxillary line, all of the following structures will have to be pierced EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Sternocostalis (transversus thoracis) is an anterior chest wall muscle located near the sternum and would not be encountered when introducing a needle laterally in the midaxillary line; the needle would instead pass through skin, fascia, external intercostal, internal intercostal, innermost intercostal muscles, endothoracic fascia, and parietal pleura.
questions.keyConcept: Sternocostalis muscle is not encountered in a midaxillary line pleural puncture

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following statements concerning the mediastinum are correct EXCEPT which:
options: The mediastinum forms a partition between the two pleural spaces (cavities)
The mediastinal pleura demarcates the lateral boundaries of the mediastinum
The heart occupies the middle mediastinum
Should air enter the left pleural cavity, the structures forming the mediastinum are deflected to the right
The anterior boundary of the mediastinum extends to a lower level than the posterior boundary
questions.explanation: The posterior boundary of the mediastinum (formed by the vertebral column) actually extends to a LOWER level than the anterior boundary (formed by the sternum), the reverse of what this option states; the mediastinum otherwise correctly partitions the two pleural cavities, is bounded laterally by mediastinal pleura, contains the heart in its middle compartment, and is deflected toward the unaffected (right) side by a left-sided pneumothorax.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior mediastinal boundary (vertebral column) extends lower than the anterior boundary (sternum)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All are true about the lungs EXCEPT:
options: Inhaled foreign bodies most frequently enter the right lung
The left lung is in direct contact with the arch of the aorta and the descending thoracic aorta
There are no lymph nodes within the lungs
The structure of the lungs receives its (nutritive) blood supply from the bronchial arteries
The costodiaphragmatic recesses are lined with parietal pleura
questions.explanation: There ARE lymph nodes within the substance of the lung (intrapulmonary/bronchopulmonary lymph nodes located along the bronchial tree), making this statement false; foreign bodies do preferentially enter the right lung, the left lung does contact the aortic arch and descending aorta, the lung tissue is nutritively supplied by bronchial arteries, and the costodiaphragmatic recesses are lined by parietal (costal and diaphragmatic) pleura.
questions.keyConcept: Lymph nodes ARE present within the lung substance (intrapulmonary/bronchopulmonary nodes)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The following statements concerning the right lung are true EXCEPT which:
options: It possesses a horizontal and an oblique fissure
Its covering of visceral pleura is sensitive to pain and temperature
The lymph from the substance of the lung reaches the hilum by the superficial and deep lymphatic plexuses
The pulmonary ligament permits the vessels and nerves of the lung root to move during the movements of respiration
The bronchial veins drain into the azygos vein
questions.explanation: The visceral pleura (covering the lung) is actually INSENSITIVE to pain and temperature, being supplied only by the autonomic pulmonary plexuses; the right lung otherwise correctly has both fissures, drains lymph via superficial and deep plexuses to the hilum, has a pulmonary ligament permitting root mobility, and its bronchial veins drain into the azygos vein.
questions.keyConcept: Visceral pleura is insensitive to pain and temperature (unlike parietal pleura)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All are true as regards the root of the right lung EXCEPT:
options: The right phrenic nerve passes anterior to the lung root
The azygos vein arches over the superior margin of the lung root
The right pulmonary artery lies posterior to the principal bronchus
The right vagus nerve passes posterior to the lung root
The vessels and nerves forming the lung root are enclosed by a cuff of pleura
questions.explanation: The right pulmonary artery actually lies ANTERIOR to (or above) the principal bronchus within the hilum (bronchus is the most posterior structure), making this statement's reversed relationship false; the right phrenic nerve does pass anterior to the root, the azygos vein arches over its superior margin, the right vagus passes posterior to the root, and a pleural cuff encloses the root's vessels and nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Pulmonary artery lies anterior to the bronchus in the hilum (bronchus is most posterior), not the reverse

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 31-year-old soldier received a shrapnel wound in the neck. During a physical examination, it was noticed that when he blew his nose or sneezed, the skin above the right clavicle bulged upward.

subQuestions.modelAnswer: Damage to the suprapleural membrane. This membrane normally spans and reinforces the thoracic inlet, resisting the piston-like upward protrusion of the underlying cervical (cupola of) pleura and lung apex during maneuvers that raise intrathoracic pressure (such as sneezing or blowing the nose). If it is damaged (e.g., by a penetrating shrapnel wound), the cervical pleura and apex of the lung can bulge upward through the defect, visibly lifting the skin above the clavicle during these maneuvers.
subQuestions.text: The upward bulging of the skin could be explained by which of the following: injury to the cervical pleura, damage to the suprapleural membrane, damage to the deep fascia in the root of the neck, or an ununited fracture of the first rib?
subQuestions.keyConcept: Damage to the suprapleural membrane — the central fact needed for The upward bulging of the skin could be explained by which of the following: injury to the cervical pleura, damage to the suprapleural membrane, damage to the deep fascia in the root of the neck, or an ununited fracture of the first rib.
subQuestions.explanation: The answer links “Damage to the suprapleural membrane” with “This membrane normally spans and reinforces the thoracic inlet, resisting the piston-like upward protrusion of the underlying cervical (cupola of) pleura and lung apex….” Together they supply the anatomical or clinical relationship the subquestion asks you to justify.

questions.explanation: This case tests knowledge of the suprapleural membrane (Sibson's fascia), which normally reinforces the thoracic inlet and prevents the cervical pleura/lung apex from bulging upward during raised intrathoracic pressure maneuvers like sneezing.
questions.keyConcept: Suprapleural membrane (Sibson's fascia) and thoracic inlet reinforcement

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital with a diagnosis of right-sided pleurisy with pneumonia. It was decided to remove a sample of pleural fluid from her pleural cavity. The resident inserted the needle close to the lower border of the eighth rib in the anterior axillary line. The next morning he was surprised to hear that the patient had complained of altered skin sensation extending from the point where the needle was inserted downward and forward to the midline of the abdominal wall above the umbilicus.

subQuestions.modelAnswer: The needle was inserted too close to the lower border of the eighth rib and damaged the eighth intercostal nerve. The intercostal neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve, from superior to inferior) runs in the costal groove along the lower border of the rib above each intercostal space; inserting the needle too close to this lower border risks lacerating or compressing the corresponding intercostal nerve, producing altered sensation along its dermatomal distribution, which for the lower thoracic nerves (e.g., T8) wraps obliquely forward and downward toward the anterior abdominal wall near/above the umbilicus.
subQuestions.text: The altered skin sensation in this patient after the needle thoracostomy could be explained by which of the following: the needle inserted too low, the needle inserted too close to the lower border of the eighth rib and damaging the eighth intercostal nerve, the needle impaling the eighth rib, or the needle penetrating too deeply and piercing the lung?
subQuestions.keyConcept: The needle was inserted too close to the lower border of the eighth rib and damaged the eighth intercostal nerve — the central fact needed for The altered skin sensation in this patient after the needle thoracostomy could be explained by which of the following: the needle inserted too low, the needle inserted too close to the lower border of the eighth rib and damaging the eighth intercostal nerve, the needle impaling the eighth rib, or the needle penetrating too deeply and piercing the lung.
subQuestions.explanation: The answer links “The needle was inserted too close to the lower border of the eighth rib and damaged the eighth intercostal nerve” with “The intercostal neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve, from superior to inferior) runs in the costal groove along the lower border of the rib above….” Together they supply the anatomical or clinical relationship the subquestion asks you to justify.

questions.explanation: This case tests the course of the intercostal neurovascular bundle in the costal groove along the lower border of each rib, and the consequence of nerve injury when a thoracocentesis needle is placed too close to the rib's lower border.
questions.keyConcept: Intercostal neurovascular bundle position and thoracocentesis nerve injury

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT true regarding the carina?
options: Its mucosa is the most sensitive area of the lower respiratory tract
It is located at the tracheal bifurcation
It is located at a distance of about 40 cm from the incisor teeth
questions.explanation: The carina lies at approximately 25-27 cm from the incisor teeth (not 40 cm) in an adult; it is otherwise correctly described as the most sensitive area of the tracheobronchial mucosa (triggering a strong cough reflex), located exactly at the tracheal bifurcation, and directly visible on bronchoscopy.
questions.keyConcept: Carina is located approximately 25-27cm from the incisor teeth, not 40cm

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The articular part of the tubercle of the rib articulates with the:
questions.explanation: The tubercle of a typical rib articulates with the transverse process of the corresponding vertebra, forming the costotransverse joint, distinct from the head of the rib which articulates with the vertebral body (costovertebral joint).
questions.keyConcept: Tubercle of rib articulates with the transverse process (costotransverse joint)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The musculophrenic artery gives rise to:
questions.explanation: The musculophrenic artery, a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery, gives rise to the anterior intercostal arteries of the lower spaces (7th-9th), while spaces 1-6 receive their anterior intercostal arteries directly from the internal thoracic artery.
questions.keyConcept: Musculophrenic artery supplies anterior intercostal arteries of spaces 7-9

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The level of the domes of the diaphragm varies according to all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The cardiac cycle (heart contractions) does not significantly alter the level of the diaphragmatic domes; the diaphragm's level does vary with the phase of respiration, posture, degree of abdominal visceral distention, and body build/habitus.
questions.keyConcept: Diaphragm level varies with respiration, posture, and abdominal distention, not the cardiac cycle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following does NOT pass through the esophageal hiatus?
options: Esophageal branches of the left gastric vessels
questions.explanation: The splanchnic nerves (greater, lesser, least) pierce the crura of the diaphragm directly and independently, rather than passing through the oesophageal hiatus, which instead transmits the oesophagus, vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels, and lymphatics.
questions.keyConcept: Splanchnic nerves pierce the diaphragmatic crura directly, not via the oesophageal hiatus

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following passes through the aortic hiatus?
questions.explanation: The aortic hiatus, lying behind the diaphragm between the two crura, transmits the aorta, the thoracic duct, and (variably) the azygos vein.
questions.keyConcept: Aortic hiatus transmits the aorta and thoracic duct

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following statements regarding the mechanics of inspiration are true EXCEPT:
options: The diaphragm is the most important muscle of inspiration
The suprapleural membrane can be raised
The tone of the anterior abdominal wall muscles is diminished
questions.explanation: The suprapleural membrane is a fixed fibrous structure that resists (rather than participates in) the piston-like protrusion of the pleura/lung apex; it is not actively raised during inspiration, unlike the sternum (anterior movement), ribs (elevation), and diaphragm's descent with reduced anterior abdominal wall tone.
questions.keyConcept: Suprapleural membrane resists apical pleural protrusion rather than being actively raised

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The mucosa of the larynx ABOVE the vocal folds is supplied sensory by the:
questions.explanation: The internal laryngeal nerve (branch of the superior laryngeal nerve) supplies sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds, while the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies sensory innervation below the vocal folds.
questions.keyConcept: Internal laryngeal nerve supplies sensation above the vocal folds; recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies below

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a separate, independent bone (not part of the ethmoid)?
questions.explanation: The inferior nasal concha is a separate, independent facial bone, unlike the superior and middle nasal conchae (parts of the ethmoid's lateral mass) and the crista galli (a projection of the ethmoid's cribriform plate); glabella is a landmark on the frontal bone.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior nasal concha is an independent bone; superior/middle conchae are parts of the ethmoid

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following arteries does NOT supply the medial and lateral walls of the nasal cavity?
questions.explanation: The infraorbital artery, a terminal branch of the maxillary artery, distributes to the face via the infraorbital foramen and does not supply the walls of the nasal cavity; the nasal walls are instead supplied by the sphenopalatine, anterior/posterior ethmoidal, and greater palatine arteries (along with the septal branch of the superior labial artery).
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital artery supplies the face, not the walls of the nasal cavity

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following nerves does NOT innervate the nasal mucosa?
questions.explanation: The greater palatine nerve primarily supplies the mucosa of the hard palate, not the nasal cavity; nasal mucosal sensation is instead provided by the nasopalatine, anterior ethmoidal, and posterior ethmoidal nerves (branches ultimately of the trigeminal nerve).
questions.keyConcept: Greater palatine nerve supplies the hard palate, not nasal mucosa

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which paranasal sinus communicates with the nasal cavity in the superior meatus?
questions.explanation: The posterior ethmoidal air cells drain into the superior meatus, distinguishing them from the anterior and middle ethmoidal cells and the maxillary sinus, all of which drain into the middle meatus.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior ethmoidal sinus drains into the superior meatus

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A tumor erodes the floor of the orbit; the surgeon would most likely find the tumor extending into the:
questions.explanation: The floor of the orbit is formed by the roof of the maxillary sinus; a tumor eroding through the orbital floor would most likely be found extending into (or arising from) the maxillary sinus.
questions.keyConcept: Floor of orbit = roof of maxillary sinus

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The piriform fossa (recess) is located in the:
questions.explanation: The piriform fossa (recess) is a mucosa-lined depression on either side of the laryngeal inlet within the laryngopharynx, a common site for lodgement of foreign bodies and fish bones.
questions.keyConcept: Piriform fossa is located within the laryngopharynx

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The laryngeal prominence ('Adam's apple') is formed by the:
options: Fused laminae of the thyroid cartilage
questions.explanation: The laryngeal prominence is formed anteriorly where the two laminae of the thyroid cartilage fuse at an angle (more acute and prominent in males), commonly known as the Adam's apple.
questions.keyConcept: Laryngeal prominence is formed by the fused laminae of the thyroid cartilage

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is NOT innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid muscle is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve (a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve), making it the sole exception among intrinsic laryngeal muscles, all of which are otherwise supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Cricothyroid is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve, not the recurrent laryngeal nerve

questions.text: Respiratory epithelium is..
questions.explanation: The correct choice is “pseudostratified columnar ciliated.” Respiratory epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium in which motile cilia propel particle-laden mucus toward the pharynx. In contrast, “Simple squamous” is incorrect because it belongs to a different cell lineage, wall layer, or respiratory region and lacks the defining feature specified in the stem.
questions.keyConcept: “pseudostratified columnar ciliated” — the key fact tested by: “Respiratory epithelium is”.

questions.text: How many cell types lining the respiratory epithelium?
questions.explanation: The best answer is “Five.” Respiratory epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium in which motile cilia propel particle-laden mucus toward the pharynx. This differs from, “One” is incorrect because it belongs to a different cell lineage, wall layer, or respiratory region and lacks the defining feature specified in the stem.
questions.keyConcept: “Five” — the key fact tested by: “How many cell types lining the respiratory epithelium”.

questions.text: Kulchitsky cells, all true except

dense cored secretory vesicles in their apical parts
They are numerous in fetal life

It should not be confused with, “neuroendocrine cells present throughout epithelium of conducting airway” is incorrect because it belongs to a different cell lineage, wall layer, or respiratory region and lacks the defining feature specified in the stem.

By comparison, “Brush cells (3%): act as chemoreceptors” is incorrect because it belongs to a different cell lineage, wall layer, or respiratory region and lacks the defining feature specified in the stem.
questions.keyConcept: “Serous cells (30%): secrete serous fluid” — the key fact tested by: “Respiratory epithelium, all true except”.

questions.text: All of the following cells share in the respiratory lining epithelium EXCEPT?
questions.explanation: The structure–function match is “Chief.” Respiratory epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium in which motile cilia propel particle-laden mucus toward the pharynx. By contrast, “Goblet” is incorrect because goblet cells secrete mucin but neither beat cilia nor act as the basal progenitor or neuroendocrine cell.
questions.keyConcept: “Chief” — the key fact tested by: “All of the following cells share in the respiratory lining epithelium EXCEPT”.
questions.subject: Histology

questions.text: Which of the following cells of respiratory epithelium are mitotically active?
questions.explanation: The correct choice is “Basal.” Basal cells are the mitotically active reserve population of respiratory epithelium; they contact the basal lamina and divide to replace ciliated and goblet cells. In contrast, “Goblet” is incorrect because goblet cells are terminally differentiated mucin-secreting luminal cells rather than the principal progenitor pool.
questions.keyConcept: “Basal” — the key fact tested by: “Which of the following cells of respiratory epithelium are mitotically active”.
questions.subject: Histology

questions.text: Which of the following cells of respiratory epithelium lie on the basal lamina and don't reach the surface?
questions.explanation: The appropriate selection is “Basal.” Basal cells contact the basal lamina without reaching the lumen and retain mitotic activity, allowing replacement of ciliated and goblet cells. Notably, “Goblet” is incorrect because goblet cells secrete mucin but neither beat cilia nor act as the basal progenitor or neuroendocrine cell.
questions.keyConcept: “Basal” — the key fact tested by: “Which of the following cells of respiratory epithelium lie on the basal lamina and don't reach the surface”.
questions.subject: Histology

questions.text: Which of the following cells of respiratory epithelium act as chemosensory receptor?
questions.explanation: The correct choice is “Brush.” Brush cells have apical microvilli and basal afferent nerve contacts, fitting a chemosensory role rather than a mucus-propelling role. In contrast, “Goblet” is incorrect because goblet cells secrete mucin but neither beat cilia nor act as the basal progenitor or neuroendocrine cell.
questions.keyConcept: “Brush” — the key fact tested by: “Which of the following cells of respiratory epithelium act as chemosensory receptor”.
questions.subject: Histology

questions.text: Which of the following cells of respiratory epithelium are hormone producing cells?
questions.explanation: The best answer is “Kulchitsky.” Kulchitsky cells sit basally, contain basal dense-core granules, and release neuroendocrine mediators such as serotonin and gastrin-releasing peptide rather than contributing to mucociliary transport. This differs from, “Goblet” is incorrect because goblet cells secrete mucin but neither beat cilia nor act as the basal progenitor or neuroendocrine cell.
questions.keyConcept: “Kulchitsky” — the key fact tested by: “Which of the following cells of respiratory epithelium are hormone producing cells”.
questions.subject: Histology

questions.text: Which of the following is a character of 15 the secretory vesicles of DNES cells?
questions.explanation: The microscopic match is “Dense cored.” Kulchitsky cells sit basally, contain basal dense-core granules, and release neuroendocrine mediators such as serotonin and gastrin-releasing peptide rather than contributing to mucociliary transport. It should not be confused with, “Mucinous” is incorrect because it belongs to a different cell lineage, wall layer, or respiratory region and lacks the defining feature specified in the stem.
questions.keyConcept: “Dense cored” — the key fact tested by: “Which of the following is a character of 15 the secretory vesicles of DNES cells”.
questions.subject: Histology

questions.text: A thyroidectomized patient (removal of thyroid gland) is not followed by a profound change in calcium metabolism, which of the following cells is responsible for that?
questions.explanation: The keyed feature is “Kulchitsky.” Kulchitsky cells sit basally, contain basal dense-core granules, and release neuroendocrine mediators such as serotonin and gastrin-releasing peptide rather than contributing to mucociliary transport. By comparison, “Goblet” is incorrect because goblet cells secrete mucin but neither beat cilia nor act as the basal progenitor or neuroendocrine cell.
questions.keyConcept: “Kulchitsky” — the key fact tested by: “A thyroidectomized patient (removal of thyroid gland) is not followed by a profound change in calcium metabolism, which of the following cells is responsible for that”.
questions.subject: Histology

questions.text: Which of the following is a character of 17 the small granule cells
options: Efferent nerve fibers end on their bases.
questions.explanation: The defining finding is “Present singly or In groups.” Respiratory epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium in which motile cilia propel particle-laden mucus toward the pharynx. Conversely, “Ciliated” is incorrect because cilia propel mucus and are absent from alveoli, so they cannot account for the alveolar process described.
questions.keyConcept: “Present singly or In groups” — the key fact tested by: “Which of the following is a character of 17 the small granule cells”.

questions.text: Which of the following is considered a function of ciliated columnar cells of respiratory epithelium?
questions.explanation: The structure–function match is “Expel mucus and dust particles.” Goblet-cell apical mucin granules hydrate into mucus, which traps particles before cilia move the layer toward the pharynx; chronic smoke exposure drives goblet-cell hyperplasia/metaplasia and mucus excess. By contrast, “Secrete mucin” is incorrect because it belongs to a different cell lineage, wall layer, or respiratory region and lacks the defining feature specified in the stem.
questions.keyConcept: “Expel mucus and dust particles” — the key fact tested by: “Which of the following is considered a function of ciliated columnar cells of respiratory epithelium”.
questions.subject: Histology

questions.text: The histological structure of respiratory columnar cells is characterized by, which of the following?
options: Their bases are related to nerve fibers.
questions.explanation: Histologically, the answer is “Apical cilia.” Respiratory epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium in which motile cilia propel particle-laden mucus toward the pharynx. A tempting alternative is, “Apical microvilli” is incorrect because it belongs to a different cell lineage, wall layer, or respiratory region and lacks the defining feature specified in the stem.
questions.keyConcept: “Apical cilia” — the key fact tested by: “The histological structure of respiratory columnar cells is characterized by, which of the following”.
questions.subject: Histology

questions.text: The histological Structure of respiratory goblet cells is characterized by which of the following?
options: Their bases are related to nerve fibers.
questions.explanation: The appropriate selection is “Apical membrane bound granules.” Goblet-cell apical mucin granules hydrate into mucus, which traps particles before cilia move the layer toward the pharynx; chronic smoke exposure drives goblet-cell hyperplasia/metaplasia and mucus excess. Notably, “Apical cilia” is incorrect because cilia propel mucus and are absent from alveoli, so they cannot account for the alveolar process described.
questions.keyConcept: “Apical membrane bound granules” — the key fact tested by: “The histological Structure of respiratory goblet cells is characterized by which of the following”.
questions.subject: Histology

questions.text: Which of the following cells are characterized by the presence of basal secretory vesicles?
questions.explanation: The correct choice is “Kulchitsky.” Kulchitsky cells sit basally, contain basal dense-core granules, and release neuroendocrine mediators such as serotonin and gastrin-releasing peptide rather than contributing to mucociliary transport. In contrast, “Basal” is incorrect because basal cells are epithelial progenitors that do not reach the lumen, so they lack the stated mature surface function.
questions.keyConcept: “Kulchitsky” — the key fact tested by: “Which of the following cells are characterized by the presence of basal secretory vesicles”.
questions.subject: Histology

questions.text: Both of the following cells in the respiratory epithelium lining are characterized by the presence of basal afferent nerve fibers.
questions.explanation: The best answer is “Kulchitsky & brush.” Kulchitsky cells sit basally, contain basal dense-core granules, and release neuroendocrine mediators such as serotonin and gastrin-releasing peptide rather than contributing to mucociliary transport. This differs from, “Basal & Goblet” is incorrect because goblet cells secrete mucin but neither beat cilia nor act as the basal progenitor or neuroendocrine cell.
questions.keyConcept: “Kulchitsky & brush” — the key fact tested by: “Both of the following cells in the respiratory epithelium lining are characterized by the presence of basal afferent nerve fibers”.

questions.text: Both of the following cells in the respiratory epithelial lining are characterized by the presence of apical microvilli.

It should not be confused with, “Basal & Goblet” is incorrect because goblet cells secrete mucin but neither beat cilia nor act as the basal progenitor or neuroendocrine cell.
questions.keyConcept: “Brush & goblet” — the key fact tested by: “Both of the following cells in the respiratory epithelial lining are characterized by the presence of apical microvilli”.

questions.text: Which of the following cells may be found among the respiratory epithelial lining?
questions.explanation: The keyed feature is “Lymphocytes.” Airway MALT consists of unencapsulated lymphoid nodules plus free lymphocytes; when concentrated around bronchial branch points it is termed BALT and supports local immune sampling. By comparison, “Langerhans” is incorrect because it belongs to a different cell lineage, wall layer, or respiratory region and lacks the defining feature specified in the stem.
questions.keyConcept: “Lymphocytes” — the key fact tested by: “Which of the following cells may be found among the respiratory epithelial lining”.
questions.subject: Histology

questions.text: Which of the following is considered a function of intra-epithelial migratory cells among the respiratory epithelium?
questions.explanation: The defining finding is “Immune defense.” Respiratory epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium in which motile cilia propel particle-laden mucus toward the pharynx. Conversely, “Expel mucus and dust particles” is incorrect because it belongs to a different cell lineage, wall layer, or respiratory region and lacks the defining feature specified in the stem.
questions.keyConcept: “Immune defense” — the key fact tested by: “Which of the following is considered a function of intra-epithelial migratory cells among the respiratory epithelium”.
questions.subject: Histology

questions.text: Neuroendocrine cells lining the respiratory epithelium

By contrast, “Act as sensory receptors” is incorrect because it belongs to a different cell lineage, wall layer, or respiratory region and lacks the defining feature specified in the stem.
questions.keyConcept: “Have basal afferent nerve endings” — the key fact tested by: “Neuroendocrine cells lining the respiratory epithelium”.
questions.subject: Histology

questions.text: Which of the following cells of respiratory epithelium can differentiate into another type of cells?
questions.explanation: The keyed feature is “Basal.” Basal cells function as airway epithelial stem/progenitor cells and can differentiate into ciliated columnar and goblet cells during normal turnover or repair. By comparison, “Goblet” is incorrect because a mature goblet cell specializes in apical mucin secretion and does not normally repopulate other epithelial lineages.
questions.keyConcept: “Basal” — the key fact tested by: “Which of the following cells of respiratory epithelium can differentiate into another type of cells”.
questions.subject: Histology

questions.text: Which of the following cells are characterized by the presence of apical membrane bounded granules?
questions.explanation: The appropriate selection is “Goblet.” Goblet-cell apical mucin granules hydrate into mucus, which traps particles before cilia move the layer toward the pharynx; chronic smoke exposure drives goblet-cell hyperplasia/metaplasia and mucus excess. Notably, “Basal” is incorrect because basal cells are epithelial progenitors that do not reach the lumen, so they lack the stated mature surface function.
questions.keyConcept: “Goblet” — the key fact tested by: “Which of the following cells are characterized by the presence of apical membrane bounded granules”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What are the non-respiratory functions of the respiratory system?
questions.modelAnswer:
Just three
- The route for water loss & heat elimination.
- Maintenance of acid-base balance by altering the amount of CO₂ expired.
- Enhancement of venous return and lymph flow (respiratory pump).
- Defense against inhaled foreign matter by the presence of cilia, phagocytes and mucus secretion.
- Enables speech, singing & other vocalization.
- The nose serves as the organ of smell.
- Vascular reservoir functions of the lungs?
- Synthesis of surfactant for local use in the lungs.
- Synthesis of some prostaglandins and histamine that are released into the blood.
- Removal of certain substances from the blood e.g. Serotonin, norepinephrine and some prostaglandins.
- Secretion of angiotensin-converting enzyme
- Synthesis of tissue plasminogen activator.
questions.explanation: A complete response must include the distinct points represented by “Just three” and “The route for water loss & heat elimination.” Keeping both visible prevents one component from being mistaken for the whole of the non-respiratory functions of the respiratory system.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What are the causes of negativity of Intrapleural Pressure (IPP)?
questions.modelAnswer:
- The stretched lungs tend to pull inward, away from the thoracic wall by their elastic tissue, while the expanded chest cage pulls outward on the lungs:
- Causing a slight expansion of the pleural cavity.
- Producing a very small increase in pleural cavity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Why airway resistance is low in the small airways?
questions.modelAnswer: Small airways are individually narrow, but they are extremely numerous and arranged in parallel. Their combined cross-sectional area is therefore very large, so their total resistance is low under normal conditions.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is maximum voluntary ventilation (MVV), and what is its normal range?
questions.modelAnswer:

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What's the significance of the dead space?
questions.modelAnswer:
- It explains why expired-air composition differs from alveolar-air composition.
- It distinguishes minute ventilation from alveolar ventilation: only (tidal volume − dead-space volume) × respiratory rate reaches gas-exchanging alveoli.
- The conducting-airway component warms, humidifies, and filters inspired air and supports phonation and olfaction.
- An increase in physiologic dead space makes ventilation less efficient.
questions.explanation: Two people can have the same minute ventilation but very different effective alveolar ventilation if their dead-space fractions differ, especially with rapid shallow breathing.
questions.keyConcept: Dead space is ventilated volume that does not exchange gas; it reduces the fraction of each breath available for alveolar ventilation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What factors affect the rate of gas diffusion across the alveolar–capillary membrane?
questions.modelAnswer:

- The membrane thickness.
- The gas diffusion coefficient, which increases with solubility and decreases with the square root of molecular weight.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What does the upper flat (plateau) portion of the O₂–hemoglobin dissociation curve represent?
questions.modelAnswer: It represents the PO₂ range of approximately 60–100 mmHg found in pulmonary capillary and arterial blood, where hemoglobin remains highly saturated and oxygen loading is maintained despite moderate PO₂ changes.
questions.explanation: Because the curve is flat above about 60 mmHg, a moderate fall in alveolar or arterial PO₂ produces only a small fall in hemoglobin saturation.
questions.keyConcept: The plateau is the pulmonary loading and safety-margin region of the O₂–hemoglobin curve.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the physiologic significance of the plateau portion of the O₂–hemoglobin dissociation curve?
questions.modelAnswer:
- It provides a safety margin for oxygen loading in the lungs.
- If arterial PO₂ falls from about 100 to 60 mmHg, hemoglobin saturation falls only modestly (roughly from 97% to about 90%), so arterial oxygen content is relatively preserved.
- Raising PO₂ above the normal range adds little hemoglobin-bound oxygen because hemoglobin is already nearly fully saturated; most additional oxygen is dissolved in plasma.
questions.explanation: Its flat shape prevents small or moderate pulmonary PO₂ changes from causing proportionally large drops in hemoglobin saturation.
questions.keyConcept: The plateau stabilizes arterial oxygen loading against moderate reductions in pulmonary PO₂.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention conditions in which defective ventilation, perfusion, or gas exchange decreases arterial PO₂.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Low inspired PO₂, as at high altitude.
- Alveolar hypoventilation.
- Ventilation–perfusion mismatch.
- Diffusion impairment from edema or fibrosis.
- Right-to-left shunting of blood past ventilated alveoli.
questions.explanation: These mechanisms are separated clinically because they respond differently to supplemental oxygen: V/Q mismatch and diffusion impairment usually improve, whereas a large true shunt responds poorly.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoxemia arises when inspired oxygen is low or when ventilation, perfusion matching, diffusion, or shunt physiology prevents normal arterial oxygenation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What does the steep portion of the O₂–hemoglobin dissociation curve represent?
questions.modelAnswer: - It lies in the blood PO₂ range between 0-60 mm Hg that exists at the systemic capillaries (i.e., at tissue level), where O₂ is being released from Hb.
questions.explanation: This shape supports demand matching: metabolically active tissues lower local PO₂ and automatically receive disproportionately more unloaded oxygen.
questions.keyConcept: The steep portion spans tissue PO₂ values below about 60 mmHg, where a small PO₂ fall releases a large amount of oxygen from hemoglobin.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Define the Haldane effect.
questions.modelAnswer: The Haldane effect is the influence of hemoglobin oxygenation on carbon-dioxide transport: deoxygenated hemoglobin binds more CO₂ and H⁺ in tissues, whereas oxygenation in the lungs reduces that binding and promotes CO₂ unloading.

questions.text: What is hypoxic hypoxia?
questions.modelAnswer: - In this type, the oxygen tension (PO₂) in arterial blood is reduced which decreases Hb saturation with O₂ & thus O₂ content is reduced.
questions.explanation: Hypoxic hypoxia lowers PaO₂; anemic hypoxia lowers oxygen content with near-normal PaO₂; stagnant hypoxia reduces flow; histotoxic hypoxia impairs cellular use. Here it is applied specifically to What is hypoxic hypoxia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: List causes of hypoxic hypoxia?
questions.modelAnswer:
- Inadequate oxygenation of the blood.
- Hypoventilation caused by increased airway resistance or decreased pulmonary compliance.
- Diminished respiratory membrane diffusion due to increased thickness of alveolar membrane.
- Abnormal ventilation-perfusion ratio.
- Venous-to-arterial shunts.
questions.explanation: Hypoxic hypoxia lowers PaO₂; anemic hypoxia lowers oxygen content with near-normal PaO₂; stagnant hypoxia reduces flow; histotoxic hypoxia impairs cellular use. Here it is applied specifically to List causes of hypoxic hypoxia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: List causes of anemic hypoxia.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Anemia.
- Abnormal hemoglobin.
- Carbon monoxide poisoning.
questions.explanation: Anemia lowers the amount of hemoglobin; abnormal hemoglobin impairs its function; and carbon monoxide occupies binding sites and increases the affinity of remaining sites, all reducing usable oxygen carriage.
questions.keyConcept: Anemic hypoxia reduces arterial oxygen content because hemoglobin is deficient, abnormal, or unavailable for oxygen binding, while arterial PO₂ may remain normal.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What are the causes of stagnant hypoxia?
questions.modelAnswer:
- Generalized reduction in tissue blood flow, as in circulatory shock or congestive heart failure.
- Localized reduction in blood flow, as in vascular spasm, obstruction, or ischemia.
questions.explanation: Because delivery equals blood flow multiplied by arterial oxygen content, reduced perfusion can cause tissue hypoxia even when the blood is well oxygenated.
questions.keyConcept: Stagnant (circulatory) hypoxia results from inadequate blood flow despite potentially normal arterial PO₂ and oxygen content.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What are the clinical manifestations of hypoxia?
questions.modelAnswer:
- Headache, easy fatigability, and drowsiness.
- Loss of appetite, nausea, and vomiting.
- Tachycardia and tachypnea.
questions.explanation: Neurologic symptoms reflect cerebral oxygen deficiency, while tachycardia and tachypnea are compensatory attempts to increase oxygen delivery.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoxia commonly produces neurologic symptoms, gastrointestinal upset, tachycardia, and tachypnea as tissues and compensatory systems respond to inadequate oxygen availability.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: When does oxygen toxicity occur?
questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen toxicity can occur after prolonged exposure to a high inspired oxygen concentration; the source describes approximately 80–100% oxygen for 8 hours or more, causing respiratory-tract irritation such as nasal congestion, sore throat, and cough.
questions.explanation: High oxygen is a drug exposure, not an inert treatment. Risk rises as inspired concentration, pressure, and duration increase, so the lowest concentration that achieves the target saturation should be used.
questions.keyConcept: Oxygen toxicity depends on both concentration and exposure duration; prolonged hyperoxia generates reactive oxygen species that injure respiratory epithelium and lung tissue.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Discuss the importance of dorsal respiratory group (DRG) neurons in respiration.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Inspiratory neurons send impulses to the motor neurons supplying the inspiratory muscles.
- When the DRG neurons fire, the inspiratory muscles contract and inspiration starts.
- When the DRG neurons cease firing, the inspiratory muscles relax, and expiration begins.
- Expiration ends when the DRG neurons fire again.

questions.text: What is the role of Ventral Respiratory Group (VRG) in control of breathing?
questions.modelAnswer:

- VRG is brought into action when the demands for ventilation are increase.
- Is especially important in active expiration.

questions.explanation: Quiet expiration follows inspiratory-muscle relaxation and elastic recoil; forced expiration recruits abdominal and internal intercostal muscles.

questions.modelAnswer: - Stretching of the lungs at large tidal volume, as in exercise, stimulates the pulmonary stretch receptors located in the bronchi and lung parenchyma. Impulses travel via vagus nerve to the medullary respiratory center, inhibiting the inspiratory neurons.
