questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “The inner mitochondrial membrane contains the respiratory-chain complexes and ATP synthase and is sufficiently impermeable to sustain a proton gradient” to “The matrix contains pyruvate dehydrogenase, nearly all TCA-cycle enzymes, and fatty-acid oxidation enzymes; succinate dehydrogenase is embedded in the inner membrane.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in are mitochondria the main site of cellular respiration.
questions.keyConcept: The components of the ETC are located in compartment enclosed by the inner mitochondrial membrane) contains, however, almost all of the enzymes for the TCA cycle and oxidation of fatty acids.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Define substrate-level phosphorylation.
questions.modelAnswer: Substrate-level phosphorylation is the direct transfer of a phosphate group from a high-energy metabolic intermediate to ADP or GDP, producing ATP or GTP without requiring the respiratory chain.
questions.explanation: The defining point is “Substrate-level phosphorylation is the direct transfer of a phosphate group from a high-energy metabolic intermediate to ADP or GDP, producing ATP or GTP without….” It directly answers substrate-level phosphorylation and marks the boundary between this concept and closely related alternatives.
questions.keyConcept: The process in which ATP are generated when high-energy metabolic intermediates transfer phosphate to ADP in a process termed.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the fate of the end products of aerobic glycolysis?
questions.modelAnswer: Pyruvate enters mitochondria and is converted by pyruvate dehydrogenase to acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle. Cytosolic NADH is reoxidized through the malate-aspartate or glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle so its reducing equivalents can enter the respiratory chain.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Pyruvate enters mitochondria and is converted by pyruvate dehydrogenase to acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle” to “Cytosolic NADH is reoxidized through the malate-aspartate or glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle so its reducing equivalents can enter the respiratory chain.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in the fate of the end products of aerobic glycolysis.
questions.keyConcept: NADH produced from glycolysis is reoxidized via the electron transport chain • The pyruvate is transported into the mitochondria where it is further oxidized to acetyl CoA which is the major fuel of the TCA cycle.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What happens to NADH and pyruvate during anaerobic glycolysis?
questions.modelAnswer: Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate while oxidizing NADH to NAD+. Regeneration of NAD+ allows glycolysis to continue when mitochondrial oxidation is unavailable or oxygen delivery is inadequate.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate while oxidizing NADH to NAD+” to “Regeneration of NAD+ allows glycolysis to continue when mitochondrial oxidation is unavailable or oxygen delivery is inadequate.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in What happens to NADH and pyruvate during anaerobic glycolysis.
questions.keyConcept: NADH is reoxidized by conversion of pyruvate to lactate, which enters the blood.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Why do some tissues rely on anaerobic glycolysis?
questions.modelAnswer: Mature erythrocytes rely on anaerobic glycolysis because they lack mitochondria. Tissues with limited oxygen delivery, such as intensely exercising skeletal muscle or the relatively hypoxic renal medulla, also use anaerobic glycolysis to maintain ATP production.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Mature erythrocytes rely on anaerobic glycolysis because they lack mitochondria” to “Tissues with limited oxygen delivery, such as intensely exercising skeletal muscle or the relatively hypoxic renal medulla, also use anaerobic glycolysis to maintain ATP….” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in do some tissues rely on anaerobic glycolysis.
questions.keyConcept: Tissues that lack of mitochondria (e.g., R.B.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How do cytosolic NADH reducing equivalents enter mitochondria through the malate-aspartate shuttle?
questions.modelAnswer: Cytosolic malate dehydrogenase uses NADH to reduce oxaloacetate to malate. Malate crosses the inner mitochondrial membrane through a transporter and is reoxidized to oxaloacetate in the matrix, generating mitochondrial NADH; transamination through aspartate completes the shuttle.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Cytosolic malate dehydrogenase uses NADH to reduce oxaloacetate to malate” to “Malate crosses the inner mitochondrial membrane through a transporter and is reoxidized to oxaloacetate in the matrix, generating mitochondrial NADH.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in do cytosolic NADH reducing equivalents enter mitochondria through the malate-aspartate shuttle.
questions.keyConcept: The cytosolic malate dehydrogenase transfers electrons from NADH to cytosolic oxaloacetate to form malate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: List the enzymes involved in the malate-aspartate shuttle.
questions.modelAnswer: The key enzymes are cytosolic and mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase and cytosolic and mitochondrial aspartate aminotransferase. Specific malate-alpha-ketoglutarate and glutamate-aspartate carriers move the intermediates across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
questions.explanation: Oxaloacetate itself does not cross the inner membrane, so reversible reduction to malate permits transport of its reducing equivalents. Reoxidation in the matrix forms NADH at Complex I, preserving the higher ATP yield of cytosolic NADH.
questions.keyConcept: Cytosolic malate dehydrogenase • Mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase • AST.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How do cytosolic NADH reducing equivalents enter the respiratory chain through the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle?
questions.modelAnswer: Cytosolic glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase transfers electrons from NADH to dihydroxyacetone phosphate, forming glycerol-3-phosphate. Mitochondrial glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase then transfers those electrons to FAD and coenzyme Q, bypassing Complex I.
questions.explanation: This shuttle couples cytosolic NADH oxidation to an FAD-dependent mitochondrial enzyme. Because electrons enter at coenzyme Q and bypass Complex I, fewer protons are pumped than with the malate-aspartate shuttle.
questions.keyConcept: Cytoplasmic glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase transfers electrons from NADH to DHAP to form glycerol 3-phosphate • Glycerol 3-phosphate then diffuses to the the electrons are donated to FAD forming FADH2.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Name the three enzymes of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
questions.modelAnswer: The three enzyme components are E1 pyruvate dehydrogenase, E2 dihydrolipoyl transacetylase, and E3 dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase.
questions.explanation: The multienzyme architecture channels reactive intermediates from decarboxylation to acetyl transfer and cofactor regeneration. E1 uses TPP, E2 uses lipoamide and CoA, and E3 reoxidizes lipoamide through FAD and NAD+.
questions.keyConcept: Pyruvate dehydrogenase • Dihyrolipoyl transacetylase • Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the five coenzymes of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?
questions.modelAnswer: The five coenzymes are thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoamide, coenzyme A, FAD, and NAD+.
questions.explanation: TPP and lipoamide handle decarboxylation and acyl transfer, CoA accepts the acetyl group, and FAD/NAD+ reoxidize the complex. Biotin is a key distractor because it carries CO2 in carboxylases rather than in oxidative decarboxylation.
questions.keyConcept: Thiamin pyrophosphate (TPP) • Lipoic acid • FAD • NAD+.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Name the products of oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate.
questions.modelAnswer: Pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate, coenzyme A, and NAD+ to acetyl-CoA, carbon dioxide, NADH, and H+.
questions.explanation: Pyruvate loses one carbon as CO2 while the remaining two-carbon unit is transferred to CoA. Simultaneous reduction of NAD+ makes the reaction oxidative as well as decarboxylating.
questions.keyConcept: CO2 • NADH • H+.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Explain covalent regulation of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
questions.modelAnswer: Pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase phosphorylates E1 and inactivates the complex. Pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase removes the phosphate and activates it; kinase activity rises with ATP, NADH, and acetyl-CoA, whereas phosphatase activity rises with Ca2+ and, in adipose tissue, insulin.
questions.explanation: Phosphorylation switches E1 off, preventing pyruvate oxidation when ATP, NADH, or acetyl-CoA is abundant. Dephosphorylation restores activity when Ca2+ signals muscle work or insulin signals nutrient availability.
questions.keyConcept: PDC activity is controlled principally through accumulation is accompanied by lowering • Phosphorylation by pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase, which inhibits the enzyme.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How does increased cardiac activity affect the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?
questions.modelAnswer: Increased cardiac contraction raises mitochondrial Ca2+. Ca2+ activates pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase, increasing the dephosphorylated active complex and accelerating acetyl-CoA production for the TCA cycle.
questions.explanation: Contraction raises matrix Ca2+, linking workload directly to activation of pyruvate oxidation. This supplies acetyl-CoA and NADH at the same time that cardiac ATP demand increases.
questions.keyConcept: In the heart, increased intramitochondrial Ca2+ during rapid contraction activates the phosphatase, thereby increasing the amount of active, non- phosphorylated PDC.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How do insulin and glucagon affect regulation of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?
questions.modelAnswer: Insulin promotes the active, dephosphorylated pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, especially in adipose tissue, by stimulating the phosphatase. Glucagon favors fuel conservation and pyruvate diversion toward gluconeogenesis in liver, indirectly favoring the inactive phosphorylated complex.
questions.explanation: Insulin favors glucose oxidation by promoting dephosphorylated active pyruvate dehydrogenase. Glucagon favors hepatic glucose conservation and gluconeogenesis, so pyruvate is spared from irreversible conversion to acetyl-CoA.
questions.keyConcept: Insulin favor the active, dephosphorylated form • Glucagon favors the phosphorylated, inactive form.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Describe allosteric regulation of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
questions.modelAnswer: Acetyl-CoA and NADH inhibit the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex as products and also activate pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase. ATP favors kinase-mediated inactivation, whereas ADP and pyruvate inhibit the kinase and preserve active pyruvate dehydrogenase.
questions.explanation: High NADH and acetyl-CoA report that downstream oxidation is saturated and suppress further pyruvate entry. ADP and pyruvate oppose kinase-mediated inhibition when energy demand or substrate availability is high.
questions.keyConcept: PDC is inhibited by its products, acetyl CoA and NADH.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Name three causes of impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase complex activity.
questions.modelAnswer: Causes include congenital deficiency of a pyruvate dehydrogenase component, thiamine deficiency, and arsenite exposure, which inhibits the lipoamide cofactor. Chronic alcohol use can contribute through nutritional thiamine deficiency.
questions.explanation: All listed causes converge on failure of oxidative decarboxylation: genetic defects remove enzyme activity, thiamine deficiency limits TPP, and arsenite disables lipoamide. Pyruvate then accumulates and is increasingly reduced to lactate.
questions.keyConcept: Congenital deficiency of the enzyme • Dietary deficiency of thiamin pyrophosphate in populations that use white polished rice as a main source of carbohydrates • Alcohol addiction • Arsenite.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is lactic acidosis in the context of pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency?
questions.modelAnswer: When pyruvate dehydrogenase activity is impaired, pyruvate is diverted to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase. Accumulating lactate lowers blood pH and produces a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
questions.explanation: Blocking pyruvate dehydrogenase prevents pyruvate carbon from entering acetyl-CoA. Lactate dehydrogenase disposes of excess pyruvate while regenerating NAD+, but proton and lactate accumulation lower blood pH.
questions.keyConcept: Abnormalities in the PDC lead to accumulation of lactate, blood lactate of the pH of the blood.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Name four enzymes of the TCA cycle.
questions.modelAnswer: TCA-cycle enzymes include citrate synthase, aconitase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, succinyl-CoA synthetase, succinate dehydrogenase, fumarase, and malate dehydrogenase.
questions.explanation: Two steps are oxidative decarboxylations (isocitrate DH and alpha-KG DH) that release CO2 and generate NADH; succinate dehydrogenase is unique because it sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane and doubles as Complex II of the electron transport chain, directly linking the cycle to oxidative phosphorylation.
questions.keyConcept: 8 TCA enzymes in cycle order: citrate synthase -> aconitase -> isocitrate DH -> alpha-KG DH -> succinyl-CoA synthetase -> succinate DH -> fumarase -> malate DH.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What reaction is catalyzed by citrate synthase?
questions.modelAnswer: Citrate synthase condenses acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate and hydrolyzes the thioester bond to form citrate and free coenzyme A.
questions.explanation: The defining point is “Citrate synthase condenses acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate and hydrolyzes the thioester bond to form citrate and free coenzyme A.” It directly answers What reaction is catalyzed by citrate synthase and marks the boundary between this concept and closely related alternatives.
questions.keyConcept: Condensation of acetyl CoA and oxaloacetate leading to the formation of citrate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Name the three enzyme components of the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex.
questions.modelAnswer: The components are E1 alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, E2 dihydrolipoyl transsuccinylase, and E3 dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase.
questions.explanation: The defining point is “The components are E1 alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, E2 dihydrolipoyl transsuccinylase, and E3 dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase.” It directly answers the three enzyme components of the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex and marks the boundary between this concept and closely related alternatives.
questions.keyConcept: a-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase • Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What coenzymes are required by the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex?
questions.modelAnswer: The complex requires thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoamide, coenzyme A, FAD, and NAD+.
questions.explanation: The defining point is “The complex requires thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoamide, coenzyme A, FAD, and NAD+.” It directly answers What coenzymes are required by the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex and marks the boundary between this concept and closely related alternatives.
questions.keyConcept: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) • Coenzyme A • Lipoic acid • FAD • NAD oxidation of one molecule of glucose.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Define substrate-level phosphorylation in the TCA cycle.
questions.modelAnswer: Succinyl-CoA synthetase couples cleavage of the high-energy succinyl-CoA thioester to phosphorylation of GDP to GTP. This is the TCA cycle’s substrate-level phosphorylation step and does not directly require oxygen or the respiratory chain.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Succinyl-CoA synthetase couples cleavage of the high-energy succinyl-CoA thioester to phosphorylation of GDP to GTP” to “This is the TCA cycle’s substrate-level phosphorylation step and does not directly require oxygen or the respiratory chain.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in substrate-level phosphorylation in the TCA cycle.
questions.keyConcept: It is the formation of a high- energy phosphate bond where none previously existed without the use of molecular O2 or the ETC • Oxidative decarboxylation of 2 B.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How does malate dehydrogenase close the TCA cycle?
questions.modelAnswer: Malate dehydrogenase oxidizes malate to oxaloacetate while reducing NAD+ to NADH. Regeneration of oxaloacetate permits another acetyl-CoA molecule to enter the cycle.
questions.explanation: Oxaloacetate is consumed by citrate synthase at the start of each turn and must be regenerated. Although malate oxidation is unfavorable in isolation, rapid citrate formation pulls it forward in the intact cycle.
questions.keyConcept: It catalyzes the reaction that converts malate to oxaloacetate, to complete the cycle.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the products of oxidation of one acetyl-CoA molecule in the TCA cycle?
questions.modelAnswer: One acetyl-CoA yields two CO2, three NADH, one FADH2, and one GTP while oxaloacetate is regenerated. Using modern P/O ratios, the reducing equivalents and GTP correspond to about 10 ATP equivalents.
questions.explanation: The two acetyl carbons are ultimately released as CO2 while four reduced carriers and one GTP conserve energy. Modern accounting assigns about 10 ATP equivalents, not the obsolete 12-ATP convention.
questions.keyConcept: Two molecules of CO2 • 3 molecules of NADH • One molecule of FADH • One molecule of GTP.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which TCA-cycle enzymes catalyze reactions that produce NADH?
questions.modelAnswer: Isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase each reduce NAD+ to NADH during one turn of the cycle.
questions.explanation: Each enzyme transfers a hydride to NAD+ at a distinct oxidation step. Succinate dehydrogenase is the key contrast because it reduces FAD instead of NAD+.
questions.keyConcept: Isocitrate dehydrogenase • a-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex • Malate dehydrogenase enzyme.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which two TCA-cycle enzymes catalyze oxidative decarboxylation and release CO2?
questions.modelAnswer: Isocitrate dehydrogenase releases CO2 while converting isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate. Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase releases the second CO2 while forming succinyl-CoA.
questions.explanation: These are the two oxidative decarboxylations of the cycle. Both release carbon dioxide and reduce NAD+, whereas citrate synthase and succinate dehydrogenase do neither.
questions.keyConcept: Isocitrate dehydrogenase • a-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Name the B-complex vitamins whose coenzymes participate in the TCA cycle.
questions.modelAnswer: Niacin supplies NAD+, riboflavin supplies FAD, thiamine supplies thiamine pyrophosphate, and pantothenic acid is a component of coenzyme A.
questions.explanation: The vitamin-derived coenzymes carry electrons, acyl groups, or decarboxylation intermediates. Their distinct chemical roles explain why deficiency of any one can slow oxidative metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Niacin in the form of NAD* • Thiamin (vitamin B1) in the form of TPP.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What provides coarse control of the TCA cycle?
questions.modelAnswer: ADP availability and the capacity to reoxidize NADH through the oxygen-dependent respiratory chain provide coarse control. ATP demand raises ADP, accelerates oxidative phosphorylation, lowers NADH, and permits the TCA cycle to run faster.
questions.explanation: ADP reflects ATP demand, while oxygen permits NADH reoxidation at the respiratory chain. If either is limiting, NADH accumulates and inhibits TCA-cycle dehydrogenases.
questions.keyConcept: Availability of oxygen and the concentration of ADP in the cell constitute the coarse control of the cycle.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Describe mechanisms of fine control of the TCA cycle.
questions.modelAnswer: Low-energy signals such as ADP and Ca2+ activate key control enzymes, including isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. High ATP, NADH, citrate, succinyl-CoA, and long-chain acyl-CoA slow the cycle through product and allosteric inhibition.
questions.explanation: Allosteric effectors tune irreversible steps to cellular energy state and workload. ADP and Ca2+ accelerate flux, whereas ATP, NADH, citrate, and succinyl-CoA signal that further oxidation is unnecessary.
questions.keyConcept: The Citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, a-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are all activated by Ca2+ which is released during muscle contraction.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the allosteric inhibitors of citrate synthase?
questions.modelAnswer: Major inhibitors are ATP, NADH, citrate, succinyl-CoA, and long-chain fatty acyl-CoA. These signals indicate a high-energy state or adequate biosynthetic carbon and therefore reduce citrate formation.
questions.explanation: A complete response must include the distinct points represented by “Major inhibitors are ATP, NADH, citrate, succinyl-CoA, and long-chain fatty acyl-CoA” and “These signals indicate a high-energy state or adequate biosynthetic carbon and therefore reduce citrate formation.” Keeping both visible prevents one component from being mistaken for the whole of the allosteric inhibitors of citrate synthase.
questions.keyConcept: High concentration of ATP • Long chain fatty acyl CoA • Citrate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Give examples of the anabolic roles of TCA-cycle intermediates.
questions.modelAnswer: Citrate can leave mitochondria and supply cytosolic acetyl-CoA for fatty-acid synthesis. Oxaloacetate and alpha-ketoglutarate form aspartate and glutamate by transamination, succinyl-CoA supports heme synthesis, and malate can support gluconeogenesis.
questions.explanation: Withdrawal of cycle intermediates supplies carbon for lipids, amino acids, heme, and glucose. Anaplerotic reactions must replace the withdrawn intermediates so oxidative flux can continue.
questions.keyConcept: After a high carbohydrate meal, citrate efflux and cleavage to acetyl CoA provides acetyl units for cytosolic fatty acid synthesis (lipogenesis).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Why is the TCA cycle described as amphibolic?
questions.modelAnswer: Yes. The cycle is catabolic because it oxidizes acetyl-CoA and captures energy, but it is also anabolic because its intermediates supply carbon for amino acids, heme, glucose, and lipids.
questions.explanation: Oxidation of acetyl-CoA is the catabolic role, whereas export or conversion of intermediates supports biosynthesis. The same cycle therefore integrates energy production with precursor supply.
questions.keyConcept: Yes • It means that TCA cycle has a catabolic nature and anabolic nature too.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Give two examples of TCA-cycle intermediates used to synthesize nonessential amino acids.
questions.modelAnswer: Alpha-ketoglutarate is transaminated to glutamate, and oxaloacetate is transaminated to aspartate.
questions.explanation: Transamination transfers amino groups onto TCA alpha-ketoacids without destroying the basic carbon skeleton relationship. Alpha-ketoglutarate/glutamate and oxaloacetate/aspartate are the principal paired examples.
questions.keyConcept: Oxaloacetate is converted to aspartate Important notes in TCA cycle:.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are anaplerotic reactions?
questions.modelAnswer: Anaplerotic reactions replenish TCA-cycle intermediates removed for biosynthesis. The major example is pyruvate carboxylase converting pyruvate to oxaloacetate.
questions.explanation: Biosynthesis removes TCA intermediates and would otherwise slow acetyl-CoA oxidation. Anaplerosis restores the pool, especially through biotin-dependent pyruvate carboxylase formation of oxaloacetate.
questions.keyConcept: Pathways or reactions that replenish the.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What reaction is catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase?
questions.modelAnswer: Pyruvate carboxylase uses ATP and biotin to add carbon dioxide to pyruvate, forming oxaloacetate. Acetyl-CoA allosterically activates the enzyme.
questions.explanation: Biotin carries activated carbon dioxide and ATP supplies the energy for carbon-carbon bond formation. Acetyl-CoA activation ensures oxaloacetate is replenished when acetyl units need to enter the cycle.
questions.keyConcept: It catalyzes the addition of CO2 to pyruvate to form oxaloacetate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the common molecular cause of cystic fibrosis?
questions.modelAnswer: The most common cystic-fibrosis mutation is a three-nucleotide deletion that removes phenylalanine at position 508 of CFTR. Other pathogenic CFTR variants can also cause the disease.
questions.explanation: F508 deletion disrupts CFTR folding and trafficking, reducing chloride and bicarbonate transport at epithelial surfaces. Water then fails to follow into secretions, producing dehydrated mucus rather than a primary defect in mucus protein synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: It is due to deletion of the codon of phenylalanine in the gene of CFTR protein (Tri-nucleotide deletion).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the function of CFTR, and what results from its loss?
questions.modelAnswer: CFTR is an ATP-gated chloride and bicarbonate channel in epithelial cells. Loss of CFTR decreases salt and water movement, producing dehydrated viscous secretions in the airways, pancreas, and other exocrine organs.
questions.explanation: CFTR coordinates epithelial anion and water movement. Its loss dehydrates luminal secretions, distinguishing cystic fibrosis from disorders caused by excessive elastase activity.
questions.keyConcept: Cystic fibrosis trans-membrane regulator acts as a chloride channel in epithelial cells • Its loss results in the production of thick, sticky secretions in the lungs and pancreas.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How does alpha-1 antitrypsin protect lung elastin, and what happens in its deficiency?
questions.modelAnswer: Alpha-1 antitrypsin inhibits neutrophil elastase and protects pulmonary elastin from proteolysis. Deficiency permits excessive elastase activity, destroys alveolar walls, and predisposes to panacinar emphysema.
questions.explanation: Alpha-1 antitrypsin neutralizes neutrophil elastase before it digests alveolar elastin. Deficiency shifts the protease-antiprotease balance toward matrix destruction and emphysema.
questions.keyConcept: Elastin is protected from degradation by alpha-1 anti-trypsin which inactivate elastase • If there is an anti-trypsin deficiency, increases elastase activity, increase degradation of elastin which leads to lung emphysema.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How does smoking worsen alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency?
questions.modelAnswer: Cigarette oxidants modify the critical methionine in alpha-1 antitrypsin and reduce its ability to inhibit elastase. Smoking also recruits neutrophils, increasing the elastase burden and accelerating emphysema.
questions.explanation: Smoke both oxidatively inactivates the antiprotease and increases neutrophil recruitment. The combined fall in protection and rise in elastase activity accelerates alveolar-wall loss.
questions.keyConcept: Increased the severity of the disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the difference between oxidation and reduction?
questions.modelAnswer: Oxidation is loss of electrons, often accompanied by loss of hydrogen or gain of oxygen. Reduction is gain of electrons, often accompanied by gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen.
questions.explanation: Electron loss and gain must occur as a coupled redox pair. Oxygen addition or hydrogen removal are common biochemical signs of oxidation, but electron transfer is the defining criterion.
questions.keyConcept: Oxidation is the addition of oxygen, removal of hydrogen and removal of electrons.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Give examples of oxidoreductase classes and describe their actions.
questions.modelAnswer: Dehydrogenases transfer electrons or hydrogen to carriers such as NAD+ or FAD. Oxidases reduce oxygen without incorporating it into the substrate, oxygenases incorporate oxygen into substrates, and hydroperoxidases such as catalase remove peroxides.
questions.explanation: The classes differ by the fate of electrons and oxygen: dehydrogenases use carriers, oxidases reduce oxygen, oxygenases insert oxygen, and hydroperoxidases remove peroxides. Cytochrome oxidase is therefore not an oxygenase because it makes water instead of oxygenating a substrate.
questions.keyConcept: Oxidases: These are enzymes concerned with removal of hydrogen, using oxygen as a hydrogen acceptor.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the difference between monooxygenases and dioxygenases?
questions.modelAnswer: Dioxygenases incorporate both atoms of molecular oxygen into a substrate. Monooxygenases incorporate one oxygen atom into the substrate and reduce the other to water, usually using NADPH.
questions.explanation: The distinction is whether one or both oxygen atoms enter the substrate. Monooxygenases need reducing equivalents for the second oxygen atom to become water, whereas dioxygenases incorporate both atoms.
questions.keyConcept: Di-oxygenases: they incorporate both atoms of oxygen molecule into the substrate (in amino acid metabolism).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is required for ATP generation by oxidative phosphorylation?
questions.modelAnswer: Oxidative phosphorylation requires an electron donor such as NADH or FADH2, oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor, an intact proton-impermeable inner mitochondrial membrane, the respiratory-chain complexes, ADP, inorganic phosphate, and ATP synthase.
questions.explanation: Electron donors and oxygen provide the redox energy, but an intact membrane is needed to conserve it as a proton gradient. ADP, Pi, and ATP synthase are then required to convert that gradient into ATP.
questions.keyConcept: Electron donor (NADH or FADH2) • Electron acceptor (O2) an intact inner • All the components of the electron transport chain.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the only nonprotein member of the electron transport chain?
questions.modelAnswer: Coenzyme Q, or ubiquinone, is the only nonprotein electron carrier in the chain. It is lipid soluble and diffuses within the inner mitochondrial membrane.
questions.explanation: The hydrophobic isoprenoid tail lets coenzyme Q diffuse within the membrane and collect electrons from several dehydrogenases. Cytochrome c is also mobile but is a protein on the membrane surface.
questions.keyConcept: Coenzyme Q (CoQ).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: List the four respiratory-chain complexes.
questions.modelAnswer: The four electron-transfer complexes are Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase), Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase), Complex III (cytochrome bc1), and Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase). ATP synthase is often called Complex V but is not an electron-transfer complex.
questions.explanation: Complexes I and II feed electrons into coenzyme Q, Complex III passes them to cytochrome c, and Complex IV reduces oxygen. Only I, III, and IV pump protons; ATP synthase uses rather than generates the gradient.
questions.keyConcept: NADH dehydrogenase (Complex 1) • Succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) • The cytochrome b-c1 complex (Complex III).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Trace electron movement through Complex I.
questions.modelAnswer: NADH transfers a hydride to FMN in Complex I. Electrons then pass through iron-sulfur centers to coenzyme Q, while the released energy drives proton pumping from the matrix.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “NADH transfers a hydride to FMN in Complex I” to “Electrons then pass through iron-sulfur centers to coenzyme Q, while the released energy drives proton pumping from the matrix.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in electron movement through Complex I.
questions.keyConcept: Electrons move from NADH to FMN to the iron of the iron-sulfur centers and then to coenzyme Q.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Describe electron transfer through Complex II.
questions.modelAnswer: Complex II oxidizes succinate to fumarate and reduces enzyme-bound FAD to FADH2. Electrons pass through iron-sulfur centers to coenzyme Q; Complex II does not pump protons.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Complex II oxidizes succinate to fumarate and reduces enzyme-bound FAD to FADH2” to “Electrons pass through iron-sulfur centers to coenzyme Q.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in electron transfer through Complex II.
questions.keyConcept: Succinate dehydrogenase catalyzes the oxidation of succinate to fumarate and the reduction of the coenzyme, FAD to FADH2 • Then, hydrogen atoms are moved from FADH2 to an iron-sulfur protein, and then to coenzyme Q.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Why does Complex II not pump protons?
questions.modelAnswer: The redox-potential difference between succinate/FADH2 and coenzyme Q is too small to release enough free energy for proton translocation. Complex II therefore transfers electrons to Q without contributing directly to the proton gradient.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “The redox-potential difference between succinate/FADH2 and coenzyme Q is too small to release enough free energy for proton translocation” to “Complex II therefore transfers electrons to Q without contributing directly to the proton gradient.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in does Complex II not pump protons.
questions.keyConcept: No energy is released in complex II, and, therefore, no protons are pumped.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Why is coenzyme Q called ubiquinone?
questions.modelAnswer: Coenzyme Q is called ubiquinone because it is widely distributed in biological membranes. Its quinone ring accepts two electrons and two protons, and its isoprenoid tail permits membrane diffusion.
questions.explanation: Its ubiquity reflects its role as a shared membrane electron pool for Complexes I, II, and other flavoproteins. The lipid tail distinguishes it from soluble cytochrome c.
questions.keyConcept: Because it is ubiquitous ring biologic systems.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Why is little usable energy released when Complex II transfers electrons to coenzyme Q?
questions.modelAnswer: FADH2 bound to succinate dehydrogenase and coenzyme Q have relatively similar redox energy levels. Their electron transfer releases too little free energy to power proton pumping, unlike the larger drops across Complexes I, III, and IV.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “FADH2 bound to succinate dehydrogenase and coenzyme Q have relatively similar redox energy levels” to “Their electron transfer releases too little free energy to power proton pumping, unlike the larger drops across Complexes I, III, and IV.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in is little usable energy released when Complex II transfers electrons to coenzyme Q.
questions.keyConcept: Because the FADH2 in succinate heme iron has an available coordination dehydrogenase is at roughly the same energy level as CoQ, and there is no energy released as they transfer electrons to CoQ.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How does cytochrome heme iron differ functionally from hemoglobin heme iron?
questions.modelAnswer: Cytochrome heme iron reversibly cycles between Fe2+ and Fe3+ to carry one electron at a time. Hemoglobin heme iron normally remains Fe2+ while reversibly binding oxygen; oxidation to Fe3+ produces methemoglobin, which cannot bind oxygen effectively.
questions.explanation: Cytochrome heme is designed for reversible one-electron redox cycling. Hemoglobin instead requires ferrous iron for reversible oxygen binding, so ferric methemoglobin is functionally impaired.
questions.keyConcept: Unlike the iron of the heme groups of hemoglobin, the cytochrome iron is reversibly converted from its ferric (Fe3+) to its ferrous (Fe2+) form • The chemiosmotic hypothesis (also known.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Trace electron movement through Complex III.
questions.modelAnswer: Reduced coenzyme Q transfers electrons through the Q cycle to the Rieske iron-sulfur protein, cytochrome c1, and soluble cytochrome c. Cytochrome c then carries one electron at a time to Complex IV.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Reduced coenzyme Q transfers electrons through the Q cycle to the Rieske iron-sulfur protein, cytochrome c1, and soluble cytochrome c” to “Cytochrome c then carries one electron at a time to Complex IV.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in electron movement through Complex III.
questions.keyConcept: Electrons move from cytochrome b to the iron-sulfur centers then to cytochrome c1 then to cytochrome c and then to cytochromes a + a3 (Complex IV).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Why is electron transfer through Complexes III and IV coupled to proton pumping?
questions.modelAnswer: Electron transfer through Complexes III and IV proceeds down favorable redox-potential gradients. The released free energy is coupled to vectorial proton translocation, increasing both the membrane potential and the pH gradient.
questions.explanation: Favorable electron transfer supplies the work needed to move protons against their electrochemical gradient. The stored gradient, not electron flow itself, directly drives ATP synthase.
questions.keyConcept: The cytochromes of the b-c1 complex across the inner mitochondrial have a higher energy level than those of cytochrome oxidase (a+a3).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which respiratory-chain complexes pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
questions.modelAnswer: Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space. Complex II transfers electrons to coenzyme Q but does not pump protons.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space” to “Complex II transfers electrons to coenzyme Q but does not pump protons.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in respiratory-chain complexes pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
questions.keyConcept: Complexes I • Complexes III • Complexes IV.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the structural domains of ATP synthase?
questions.modelAnswer: The Fo domain is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and forms the proton-conducting rotor. The F1 domain projects into the matrix and contains catalytic beta subunits that synthesize ATP.
questions.explanation: Fo provides a membrane proton path and rotary motor, whereas F1 contains the catalytic nucleotide-binding sites. Oligomycin targets Fo, distinguishing proton conduction from ATP chemistry in F1.
questions.keyConcept: (Fo) domain that spans the inner mitochondrial without going through the ATP synthase, • Extra-membranous domain (F1) that appears as a sphere that protrudes into the mitochondrial matrix membrane.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How does ATP synthase use the electrical and pH gradients to phosphorylate ADP?
questions.modelAnswer: Protons flow down the electrochemical gradient through Fo and rotate the c-ring and gamma shaft. Rotation changes F1 beta-subunit conformations, driving ADP and Pi binding, ATP formation, and ATP release.
questions.explanation: Both membrane potential and pH difference favor proton return through Fo. Rotary conformational coupling in F1 converts this ion flow into ATP synthesis rather than allowing the energy to dissipate as heat.
questions.keyConcept: Proton flow through the Fo channel rotates the c-ring and γ shaft, driving F1 β-subunits through conformations that bind ADP + Pi, synthesize ATP, and release it.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What experimental observations support the chemiosmotic theory?
questions.modelAnswer: Artificially imposing a proton gradient across an intact inner mitochondrial membrane can drive ATP synthesis even without respiratory electron flow. Conversely, disrupting or solubilizing the membrane abolishes oxidative phosphorylation because the proton gradient cannot be maintained.
questions.explanation: A proton gradient is sufficient to drive ATP synthesis only when the membrane is intact. Loss of the permeability barrier abolishes coupling even if respiratory enzymes remain present.
questions.keyConcept: Addition of protons (acid) to the external medium of intact mitochondria stimulates • Act on the three sites that produce the the formation of ATP.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Why is ADP a major controller of respiratory-chain activity?
questions.modelAnswer: ATP-consuming work raises ADP concentration, allowing ATP synthase to conduct protons and lowering the proton backpressure on the respiratory chain. Electron transport and oxygen consumption therefore accelerate when ADP is available, a phenomenon called respiratory or acceptor control.
questions.explanation: ADP availability controls proton flow through ATP synthase and therefore the backpressure exerted by the gradient. Low ADP slows electron transport despite available substrate and oxygen, whereas rising ADP accelerates respiration.
questions.keyConcept: ADP constitutes the main controlling factor, because when doing work, ATP is converted to ADPi This allows more respiration (oxidation reactions) to occur • This drug binds to the Fo domain of ATP.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Classify the main inhibitors of oxidative phosphorylation.
questions.modelAnswer: Respiratory-chain inhibitors block electron transfer at a specific complex, ATP synthase inhibitors such as oligomycin block proton-driven phosphorylation, and uncouplers dissipate the proton gradient. These classes have different effects on oxygen consumption and ATP production.
questions.explanation: Blocking a respiratory complex stops downstream electron flow, oligomycin blocks proton re-entry, and uncouplers erase the gradient. Oxygen consumption therefore falls with chain or ATP-synthase inhibition but can rise with uncoupling.
questions.keyConcept: Uncouplers • Oligomycin phosphorylation of ADP to ATP.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Define uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation.
questions.modelAnswer: Uncoupling occurs when protons return to the matrix without passing through ATP synthase. The proton gradient is dissipated, so electron transport and oxygen consumption continue or increase while ATP production falls and energy appears as heat.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Uncoupling occurs when protons return to the matrix without passing through ATP synthase” to “The proton gradient is dissipated, so electron transport and oxygen consumption continue or increase while ATP production falls and energy appears as heat.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation.
questions.keyConcept: It's when protons leak back into the matrix they dissipate the electrochemical gradient across the membrane without generating ATP.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Give examples of physiological and chemical uncouplers.
questions.modelAnswer: Thermogenin (UCP1) is a physiological uncoupler in brown adipose tissue. 2,4-Dinitrophenol is a chemical protonophore that uncouples oxidative phosphorylation.
questions.explanation: UCP1 creates a regulated proton conductance for neonatal thermogenesis, whereas 2,4-dinitrophenol carries protons chemically across the membrane. Both bypass ATP synthase but only UCP1 is physiologically controlled.
questions.keyConcept: Thermogenin (UCP1) • 2,4-dinitrophenol.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: List respiratory-chain inhibitor sites and an example acting at each site.
questions.modelAnswer: Complex I is inhibited by rotenone and barbiturates; Complex III is inhibited by antimycin A; and Complex IV is inhibited by cyanide, carbon monoxide, hydrogen sulfide, and azide. Oligomycin acts separately at the Fo proton channel of ATP synthase.
questions.explanation: Inhibitors are localized by where electron carriers remain reduced upstream and oxidized downstream. Cyanide and carbon monoxide act at oxygen reduction in Complex IV, unlike rotenone at Complex I or antimycin A at Complex III.
questions.keyConcept: Complex IV is inhibited by H,S, carbon monoxide (CO) and cyanide (CN).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Complete the statements about glycerophospholipid synthesis, signaling, degradation, and pulmonary surfactant.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Glycerol-3-phosphate is acylated twice to form phosphatidic acid, the precursor of many glycerophospholipids.
- Phosphatidylserine can form by head-group exchange and can be decarboxylated to phosphatidylethanolamine; phosphatidylethanolamine can be methylated with S-adenosylmethionine to form phosphatidylcholine.
- Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate can be cleaved by phospholipase C to diacylglycerol and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate.
- CDP-diacylglycerol participates in phosphatidylglycerol, cardiolipin, and phosphatidylinositol synthesis.
- Pulmonary surfactant is rich in dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine, and deficiency in premature newborns causes respiratory distress syndrome.
- Fetal lung maturity is assessed using surfactant phospholipids, including the lecithin-to-sphingomyelin ratio.
questions.explanation: Phosphatidic acid and diacylglycerol are branch-point intermediates, while CTP activates either head groups or the phosphatidyl moiety. Surfactant DPPC is a specialized phosphatidylcholine whose saturated chains pack tightly and lower alveolar surface tension.
questions.keyConcept: Glycerol 3-phosphate reacts with fatty acyl CoA to form phosphatidic acid.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Name at least three glycerophospholipids.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylinositol, phosphatidylglycerol, and cardiolipin.
questions.explanation: All members share a glycerol backbone, two acyl chains, phosphate, and a polar head group. Cardiolipin is structurally unusual but remains a glycerophospholipid concentrated in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
questions.keyConcept: Phosphatidylcholine • Phosphatidylethanolamine • Phosphatidylserine • Cardiolipin • Phosphatidylglycerol.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the two main steps in the pathway that adds an activated head group to diacylglycerol?
questions.modelAnswer: Phosphatidic acid is first dephosphorylated to diacylglycerol. Diacylglycerol then accepts an activated head group, such as CDP-choline or CDP-ethanolamine.
questions.explanation: Removing phosphate from phosphatidic acid creates diacylglycerol, which can accept phosphocholine or phosphoethanolamine from a CDP-activated donor. This differs from the CDP-diacylglycerol route, in which the lipid rather than the head group is activated.
questions.keyConcept: Phosphatidic acid is cleaved by a phosphatase to form diacylglycerol (DAG).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How is the choline head group activated during phosphatidylcholine synthesis?
questions.modelAnswer: Choline is phosphorylated and then activated with CTP to form CDP-choline. Phosphocholine is transferred from CDP-choline to diacylglycerol, releasing CMP and forming phosphatidylcholine.
questions.explanation: CTP activation creates the high-energy CDP-choline donor. Transfer to diacylglycerol releases CMP and makes the phosphodiester bond of phosphatidylcholine.
questions.keyConcept: The head group choline is activated by combining with CTP to form CDP-choline.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the two main steps in the CDP-diacylglycerol pathway for adding a head group?
questions.modelAnswer: Phosphatidic acid reacts with CTP to form CDP-diacylglycerol. The activated phosphatidyl group is then transferred to inositol or, through phosphatidylglycerol intermediates, used to form cardiolipin.
questions.explanation: CTP converts phosphatidic acid into an activated phosphatidyl donor. Nucleophilic head groups then displace CMP, driving formation of phosphatidylinositol or phosphatidylglycerol-derived lipids.
questions.keyConcept: Phosphatidic acid reacts with CTP to form CDP-diacylglycerol.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the role of phospholipase D in phospholipid degradation?
questions.modelAnswer: Phospholipase D cleaves the phosphodiester bond between phosphate and the polar head group. The products are phosphatidic acid and the free head-group alcohol.
questions.explanation: The cleavage site leaves phosphate attached to diacylglycerol, so phosphatidic acid is produced. Phospholipase C is the key contrast because it leaves phosphate on the released head group and produces diacylglycerol.
questions.keyConcept: Phospholipase D cleaves the bond between the phosphate and the head group, producing phosphatidic acid and the free alcohol of the head group.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is phospholipidosis?
questions.modelAnswer: Phospholipidosis is excessive intracellular phospholipid accumulation, commonly within lysosomes of organs such as liver, kidney, and lung. It may result from inherited defects or be acquired after drug exposure.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Phospholipidosis is excessive intracellular phospholipid accumulation, commonly within lysosomes of organs such as liver, kidney, and lung” to “It may result from inherited defects or be acquired after drug exposure.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in phospholipidosis.
questions.keyConcept: It is a lysosomal storage disorder characterized by the excess accumulation of phospholipids in tissues (Kidney, lung, liver).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What causes acquired phospholipidosis?
questions.modelAnswer: Cationic amphiphilic drugs can bind phospholipids and inhibit their degradation by lysosomal phospholipases. Poorly degraded drug-phospholipid complexes then accumulate in lysosomes.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Cationic amphiphilic drugs can bind phospholipids and inhibit their degradation by lysosomal phospholipases” to “Poorly degraded drug-phospholipid complexes then accumulate in lysosomes.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in What causes acquired phospholipidosis.
questions.keyConcept: Some drugs bind to phospholipids and inhibit their hydrolysis by lysosomal phospholipases.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the only step in the TCA cycle where FAD is the cofactor for oxidation, and which enzyme catalyzes it?
questions.modelAnswer: Succinate is oxidized to fumarate by succinate dehydrogenase. FAD accepts the two hydrogen equivalents and is reduced to FADH2.
questions.explanation: Oxidizing succinate to fumarate requires removal of two hydrogens across a carbon-carbon single bond, a reaction for which enzyme-bound FAD is suited. The other TCA dehydrogenases transfer hydride to NAD+, whereas succinate dehydrogenase passes FADH2 electrons through Complex II to coenzyme Q.
questions.keyConcept: Succinate is oxidized to fumarate by succinate dehydrogenase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Complete the statements about alpha-1 antitrypsin.
questions.modelAnswer: Alpha-1 antitrypsin is synthesized by the liver, alveolar monocytes, and macrophages. Methionine 358 is required for binding of alpha-1 antitrypsin to its target protease, elastase.
questions.explanation: Hepatic production supplies most circulating alpha-1 antitrypsin, while pulmonary mononuclear phagocytes contribute locally. Methionine 358 is part of the elastase-binding reactive center, so oxidation of this residue weakens antiprotease protection of alveolar elastin.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha-1 antitrypsin is synthesized by the liver, alveolar monocytes, and macrophages.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the composition of coenzyme Q (CoQ)?
questions.modelAnswer: Coenzyme Q is a quinone derivative with a long hydrophobic isoprenoid tail. The tail keeps it mobile within the lipid core of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
questions.explanation: The quinone head group reversibly accepts two electrons and two protons, allowing coenzyme Q to connect two-electron donors with downstream one-electron carriers. Its long isoprenoid tail keeps it lipid soluble and mobile within the inner mitochondrial membrane rather than the aqueous intermembrane space.
questions.keyConcept: Coenzyme Q is a quinone derivative with a long hydrophobic isoprenoid tail.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Why is cytochrome c a mobile electron carrier?
questions.modelAnswer: Cytochrome c is a small soluble protein in the intermembrane space that is loosely associated with the outer surface of the inner mitochondrial membrane. It diffuses between Complex III and Complex IV to transfer electrons.
questions.explanation: Cytochrome c is small, soluble, and only loosely associated with the outer face of the inner mitochondrial membrane. This location permits diffusion from Complex III to Complex IV, unlike the integral membrane cytochromes that remain fixed within their complexes.
questions.keyConcept: Cytochrome c is a small soluble protein in the intermembrane space that is loosely associated with the outer surface of the inner mitochondrial membrane.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the goal of phase 1 of cellular respiration?
questions.modelAnswer: Oxidation of major fuels, including glucose, fatty acids, and amino acids, converges on the production of acetyl-CoA.
questions.explanation: This convergence is precisely why the TCA cycle and electron transport chain can act as one shared final oxidative pathway for chemically very different fuels, instead of the cell needing separate energy-extraction machinery for each fuel type.
questions.keyConcept: Metabolic convergence: carbohydrate, fat, and most amino-acid catabolism all funnel into acetyl-CoA before entering the TCA cycle.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Why is the TCA cycle central to energy generation during cellular respiration?
questions.modelAnswer: Pathways that oxidize fatty acids, glucose, amino acids, acetate, and ketone bodies converge on acetyl-CoA. Acetyl-CoA is then oxidized in the TCA cycle, which captures reducing equivalents for oxidative phosphorylation.
questions.explanation: Many fuel pathways converge on acetyl-CoA, and the TCA cycle captures its oxidation energy mainly as NADH and FADH2. Those carriers feed oxidative phosphorylation, while cycle intermediates also connect energy production to amino-acid, heme, glucose, and lipid metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Pathways that oxidize fatty acids, glucose, amino acids, acetate, and ketone bodies converge on acetyl-CoA.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Why is cytochrome a + a3 (Complex IV) called cytochrome oxidase?
questions.modelAnswer: Complex IV contains the electron-transfer centers that react with molecular oxygen. Its heme a3-CuB center binds oxygen and reduces it to water.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Complex IV contains the electron-transfer centers that react with molecular oxygen” to “Its heme a3-CuB center binds oxygen and reduces it to water.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in is cytochrome a + a3 (Complex IV) called cytochrome oxidase.
questions.keyConcept: Complex IV contains the electron-transfer centers that react with molecular oxygen.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What does the chemiosmotic hypothesis explain?
questions.modelAnswer: The chemiosmotic, or Mitchell, hypothesis explains how electron transport generates a proton-motive force across the inner mitochondrial membrane. ATP synthase uses this gradient to phosphorylate ADP with inorganic phosphate.
questions.explanation: Electron transport does not phosphorylate ADP by direct chemical transfer; it pumps protons and stores energy as membrane potential plus a pH gradient. ATP synthase then couples downhill proton return to ATP formation, explaining why an intact inner membrane is essential.
questions.keyConcept: The chemiosmotic, or Mitchell, hypothesis explains how electron transport generates a proton-motive force across the inner mitochondrial membrane.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the two functional components of the chemiosmotic mechanism?
questions.modelAnswer: The first component is the proton-pumping electron transport chain, which creates the electrochemical gradient. The second is ATP synthase, which allows proton return and couples it to ATP formation.
questions.explanation: The respiratory chain creates the proton-motive force by coupling favorable electron transfer to proton pumping. ATP synthase provides the controlled proton-return pathway and converts rotary motion into catalytic ATP formation.
questions.keyConcept: The first component is the proton-pumping electron transport chain, which creates the electrochemical gradient.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the results of uncoupling, and why do they occur?
questions.modelAnswer: Uncoupling increases oxygen consumption and heat production while decreasing ATP synthesis. Proton leak dissipates the gradient, so electron transport and proton pumping accelerate in an attempt to restore it.
questions.explanation: A complete response must include the distinct points represented by “Uncoupling increases oxygen consumption and heat production while decreasing ATP synthesis” and “Proton leak dissipates the gradient, so electron transport and proton pumping accelerate in an attempt to restore it.” Keeping both visible prevents one component from being mistaken for the whole of the results of uncoupling, and why do they occur.
questions.keyConcept: Uncoupling increases oxygen consumption and heat production while decreasing ATP synthesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the effect of oligomycin on phosphorylation of ADP to ATP?
questions.modelAnswer: Oligomycin binds the Fo domain of ATP synthase and blocks its proton channel. Protons cannot re-enter the matrix through ATP synthase, so phosphorylation of ADP stops and the accumulated gradient secondarily slows electron transport.
questions.explanation: Oligomycin occludes the Fo proton channel, so proton return and ATP-synthase rotation stop. The rising proton gradient then creates backpressure that secondarily slows electron transport and oxygen consumption, unlike an uncoupler that accelerates respiration.
questions.keyConcept: Oligomycin binds the Fo domain of ATP synthase and blocks its proton channel.

questions.text: Amyloidosis is NOT a complication of:
questions.explanation: Chronic suppurative disorders such as bronchiectasis, lung abscess, and empyema can sustain serum amyloid A production and cause secondary AA amyloidosis. Emphysema is destructive enlargement of airspaces without chronic pus formation, so it is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Suppurative lung disease Exam focus: Amyloidosis is NOT a complication of.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Suppurative lung diseases include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis, lung abscess, and empyema are neutrophil-rich pyogenic processes that produce pus and tissue destruction. Bronchial asthma is an eosinophilic obstructive airway disease rather than a suppurative infection.
questions.keyConcept: Suppurative lung disease Exam focus: Suppurative lung diseases include all EXCEPT.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: The histologic features of bronchiectasis include all EXCEPT:
options: Dilation of the bronchi and bronchioles
The bronchial lumen is filled with pus
The bronchial wall is infiltrated by many eosinophils
The intervening lung tissue shows fibrosis
questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis shows permanent airway dilation, wall destruction, purulent luminal material, and fibrosis of adjacent lung. A predominance of eosinophils instead points toward asthma or an allergic process, making that feature the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Bronchiectasis
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Emphysema is mainly due to:
questions.explanation: Emphysema results from protease-mediated destruction of alveolar walls with loss of elastic recoil, which promotes expiratory airway collapse and air trapping. Fibrosis causes restrictive physiology rather than the enlarged distal airspaces of emphysema.
questions.keyConcept: Emphysema
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Acute respiratory distress syndrome is NOT characterized by:
questions.explanation: ARDS causes diffuse alveolar damage with severe hypoxemia, protein-rich edema, surfactant loss, and hyaline membranes. Pulmonary emphysema is a chronic destructive airspace disorder and is not a defining feature of acute diffuse alveolar injury.
questions.keyConcept: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: A child has fever, purulent sputum, and bilateral basal lung lesions with destruction of lung tissue. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis produces chronically dilated, infected bronchi, often in both lower lobes, with purulent sputum and destruction of airway walls and surrounding lung. Septic bronchopneumonia can also be bilateral and purulent, so the wording is somewhat overlapping, but the printed key emphasizes chronic destructive bronchial disease.
questions.keyConcept: Distinguish bronchiectasis (chronic, often bilateral, irreversible bronchial dilation with recurrent purulent sputum) from an acute focal lung abscess or pneumonia.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Inflammation in bronchopneumonia is:
questions.explanation: Bronchopneumonia is a patchy bacterial infection centered on bronchioles and adjacent alveoli, where neutrophils create a suppurative exudate. Catarrhal inflammation is mucus-dominant and does not capture the pus-filled alveolar pattern.
questions.keyConcept: “Suppurative” — the key fact tested by: “Inflammation in bronchopneumonia is”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: The lung tissue has a liver-like consistency in:
questions.explanation: During hepatization in lobar pneumonia, alveoli become packed with fibrin, neutrophils, and red cells, making the affected lobe firm and liver-like. Bronchopneumonia instead creates scattered patchy consolidations rather than uniform lobar hepatization.
questions.keyConcept: “Lobar pneumonia” — the key fact tested by: “The lung tissue has a liver-like consistency in”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Inflammation in lobar pneumonia is:
questions.explanation: Lobar pneumonia characteristically fills alveoli with a fibrin-rich inflammatory exudate, particularly during red and gray hepatization. Suppurative inflammation is more typical of bronchopneumonia, abscess, or empyema.
questions.keyConcept: “Fibrinous” — the key fact tested by: “Inflammation in lobar pneumonia is”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: In viral pneumonia, the inflammatory infiltrate occurs in:
questions.explanation: Viral pneumonia primarily injures the alveolar septa and interstitium, producing mononuclear inflammation with relatively little intra-alveolar exudate. 'Alveolar wall' is anatomically part of the interstitium and is a plausible overlapping distractor, but the printed key selects interstitial tissue.
questions.keyConcept: Viral pneumonia
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Aspiration of gastric contents by a comatose patient leads to:
questions.explanation: Aspiration in an unconscious patient carries gastric contents and oral organisms into dependent lung, where necrosis may evolve into an aspiration abscess. Chemical pneumonitis is also a recognized early consequence but is not offered, so lung abscess is the keyed choice and the stem remains context-sensitive.
questions.keyConcept: Aspiration in the unconscious/supine patient preferentially seeds the right lower lobe (wider, more vertical right main bronchus) and can progress from pneumonitis to a localized abscess.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Aspiration of infected material during anesthesia may lead to:
questions.explanation: Aspiration of infected material during anesthesia introduces anaerobic oral flora into dependent segments and can cause localized liquefactive necrosis with cavitation: a lung abscess. Bronchopneumonia is a plausible earlier pattern, but a necrotizing aspiration complication is better captured by abscess.
questions.keyConcept: Anaerobic oral flora + a dependent lung segment + tissue necrosis is the classic triad behind aspiration-related lung abscess, distinct from diffuse bronchopneumonia.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: A coal miner develops heart failure after many years of exposure. The most likely cause is:
questions.explanation: Long-term coal-dust exposure can cause pneumoconiosis and progressive massive fibrosis, raising pulmonary vascular resistance. The resulting pulmonary hypertension leads to cor pulmonale, unlike systemic hypertension or coronary spasm.
questions.keyConcept: Pneumoconiosis Exam focus: A coal miner develops heart failure after many years of exposure. The most likely cause is.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: The commonest tumor of the lung is:
questions.explanation: The printed key identifies bronchogenic carcinoma, meaning a primary epithelial malignancy arising from bronchial or pulmonary epithelium. Metastases to lung are very common and may outnumber primary tumors in some series, so the unqualified wording 'commonest tumor' is potentially ambiguous.
questions.keyConcept: “Bronchogenic carcinoma” — the key fact tested by: “The commonest tumor of the lung is”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: The most important risk factor for bronchogenic carcinoma is:
questions.explanation: Cigarette smoking is the dominant preventable risk factor for bronchogenic carcinoma and is especially strongly linked to squamous and small-cell carcinoma. Asbestos and radon also increase risk, but their population contribution is smaller.
questions.keyConcept: “Smoking” — the key fact tested by: “The most important risk factor for bronchogenic carcinoma is”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: The most aggressive type of bronchogenic carcinoma is:
questions.explanation: Small-cell carcinoma has a very high proliferative rate, early widespread metastasis, and frequent paraneoplastic syndromes, making it the most aggressive listed subtype. Squamous carcinoma usually grows and spreads less rapidly.
questions.keyConcept: “Small cell carcinoma” — the key fact tested by: “The most aggressive type of bronchogenic carcinoma is”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: The following is NOT true for bronchogenic squamous cell carcinoma:
questions.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma is usually central, strongly smoking-related, and often locally invasive, but small-cell carcinoma is the most aggressive histologic type. Therefore describing squamous carcinoma as the most aggressive is the false statement.
questions.keyConcept: “The most aggressive histologic type” — the key fact tested by: “The following is NOT true for bronchogenic squamous cell carcinoma”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: The following is NOT true for usual pulmonary adenocarcinoma:
questions.explanation: Pulmonary adenocarcinoma is now one of the most common primary lung cancers, often peripheral and relatively less tightly linked to smoking than squamous carcinoma. Calling it rare is therefore the incorrect statement.
questions.keyConcept: “Rare tumor” — the key fact tested by: “The following is NOT true for usual pulmonary adenocarcinoma”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Pulmonary adenocarcinoma in situ was formerly called:
questions.explanation: The former term bronchioloalveolar carcinoma included tumors with lepidic growth; the noninvasive form is now classified as adenocarcinoma in situ. Small-cell and large-cell carcinomas have different morphology and biology.
questions.keyConcept: “Bronchiolo-alveolar carcinoma” — the key fact tested by: “Pulmonary adenocarcinoma in situ was formerly called”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Neurosecretory granules are seen in:
questions.explanation: Small-cell carcinoma is a high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma and contains dense-core neurosecretory granules on ultrastructural examination. Squamous and ordinary adenocarcinomas lack this defining neuroendocrine differentiation.
questions.keyConcept: “Small cell carcinoma” — the key fact tested by: “Neurosecretory granules are seen in”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: The following tumor shows neuroendocrine differentiation:
questions.explanation: Small-cell carcinoma expresses neuroendocrine differentiation, often with synaptophysin, chromogranin, or INSM1 positivity. Mesothelioma is mesothelial rather than neuroendocrine, while conventional squamous and adenocarcinomas do not show this phenotype.
questions.keyConcept: “Small cell carcinoma” — the key fact tested by: “The following tumor shows neuroendocrine differentiation”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Pulmonary small cell carcinoma is characterized by all EXCEPT:
options: It is the most aggressive type
questions.explanation: Small-cell carcinoma is usually central, strongly smoking-associated, highly aggressive, and widely metastatic at diagnosis. Because disease is commonly disseminated and radiosensitive, treatment is primarily systemic therapy rather than surgical cure.
questions.keyConcept: “Curable by surgery” — the key fact tested by: “Pulmonary small cell carcinoma is characterized by all EXCEPT”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Smoking may cause all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Smoking is a major cause of emphysema and carcinomas of lung, larynx, and oral cavity. Typical bronchial carcinoids are neuroendocrine tumors without the strong smoking association seen in small-cell carcinoma.
questions.keyConcept: “Bronchial carcinoid” — the key fact tested by: “Smoking may cause all EXCEPT”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: The commonest site of metastasis from bronchogenic carcinoma is:
questions.explanation: The source key selects the adrenal gland, a classic hematogenous destination for bronchogenic carcinoma. Bone, liver, and brain are also frequent sites, and modern series vary in which site is most common, so the absolute superlative should be interpreted as source-specific.
questions.keyConcept: “Adrenal gland” — the key fact tested by: “The commonest site of metastasis from bronchogenic carcinoma is”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Bronchial carcinoid is characterized by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Bronchial carcinoids are neuroendocrine tumors that may be silent, contain neurosecretory granules, occasionally cause carcinoid syndrome, and can metastasize hematogenously. Unlike small-cell carcinoma, typical carcinoid is not strongly related to smoking.
questions.keyConcept: Bronchial carcinoid
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Pancoast's tumor is a:
options: Lung cancer not related to smoking
questions.explanation: A Pancoast tumor is a bronchogenic carcinoma arising at the lung apex and may invade the brachial plexus or sympathetic chain. A basal tumor would not produce the classic superior sulcus syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: “Apical lung cancer” — the key fact tested by: “Pancoast's tumor is a”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Cannon-ball metastases in the lung arise from:
questions.explanation: Large rounded 'cannon-ball' pulmonary metastases classically arise through hematogenous spread from renal cell carcinoma and some other highly vascular tumors. Prostate and gastric cancers more often show different metastatic patterns.
questions.keyConcept: Metastatic lung tumors Exam focus: Cannon-ball metastases in the lung arise from.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: After tonsillectomy, a child develops fever, productive cough, and a lower-lobe cavity filled with necrotic tissue. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: A cavity containing necrotic material after aspiration-prone surgery is characteristic of a lung abscess, with liquefactive necrosis and purulent exudate. Bronchiectasis causes chronically dilated airways rather than a newly formed solitary necrotic cavity.
questions.keyConcept: Post-tonsillectomy aspiration risk plus a cavitary lesion with necrotic debris points to a localized lung abscess, not bronchiectasis (which is chronic and diffuse, not acute and cavitary).
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: A ceramic-factory worker develops dyspnea, dry cough, and later chronic heart failure. The most likely cause of heart failure is:
questions.explanation: Ceramic work can expose a person to silica, causing nodular pulmonary fibrosis and increased pulmonary vascular resistance. Chronic pulmonary hypertension then produces right-sided heart failure rather than primary ischemic disease.
questions.keyConcept: Pneumoconiosis Exam focus: A ceramic-factory worker develops dyspnea, dry cough, and later chronic heart failure. The most likely cause of heart….
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: A 60-year-old with hemoptysis, colicky renal pain, a lung shadow, and renal calcium stones most likely has which lung tumor?
questions.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma may secrete PTH-related peptide, causing hypercalcemia that can contribute to renal calculi and colicky pain. Adenocarcinoma and carcinoid have different characteristic paraneoplastic profiles.
questions.keyConcept: “Squamous cell carcinoma” — the key fact tested by: “A 60-year-old with hemoptysis, colicky renal pain, a lung shadow, and renal calcium stones most likely has which lung tumor”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Empyema is:
questions.explanation: Empyema is a collection of pus in the pleural cavity and therefore represents suppurative pleuritis. It is not a pyemic abscess within lung parenchyma and is not primarily neoplastic or allergic.
questions.keyConcept: Pleural disease Exam focus: Empyema is.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: The adrenal gland is NOT a common site of metastasis from bronchogenic carcinoma.
questions.explanation: The statement is false because the adrenal glands are classic sites of hematogenous metastasis from bronchogenic carcinoma. Their involvement may be clinically silent despite substantial tumor burden.
questions.keyConcept: “False” — the key fact tested by: “The adrenal gland is NOT a common site of metastasis from bronchogenic carcinoma”.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Cannon-ball metastases are metastatic nodules in the lung arising from hepatocellular carcinoma.
questions.explanation: The statement is false because classic cannon-ball lung metastases are especially associated with renal cell carcinoma and certain other hematogenous tumors, not specifically hepatocellular carcinoma. The rounded appearance reflects large, discrete blood-borne deposits.
questions.keyConcept: Metastatic lung tumors Exam focus: Cannon-ball metastases are metastatic nodules in the lung arising from hepatocellular carcinoma.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Empyema means presence of pus in the pleural cavity.
questions.explanation: The statement is true: empyema literally denotes purulent material within the pleural space. This differs from a lung abscess, where pus occupies a cavity in pulmonary parenchyma.
questions.keyConcept: Pleural disease Exam focus: Empyema means presence of pus in the pleural cavity.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: What is the pathogenesis of the common cold?
questions.modelAnswer:
- The virus attaches to cells of the nasal mucous membrane, enters the cell, and replicates.
- Infected cells lose their ciliary action and slough off when they die.
- Release of inflammatory mediators stimulates excess mucus production, sneezing, and localized inflammation.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “The virus attaches to cells of the nasal mucous membrane, enters the cell, and replicates” to “Infected cells lose their ciliary action and slough off when they die.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in the pathogenesis of the common cold.
questions.keyConcept: The virus attaches to cells of the nasal mucous membrane, enters the cell, and replicates.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: What are the Clinical Manifestations of common cold?
questions.modelAnswer:
- Nasal congestion and rhinorrhea Sore throat.
- Malaise and headache.
questions.explanation: A complete response must include the distinct points represented by “Nasal congestion and rhinorrhea Sore throat” and “Malaise and headache.” Keeping both visible prevents one component from being mistaken for the whole of the Clinical Manifestations of common cold.
questions.keyConcept: Nasal congestion and rhinorrhea Sore throat.
