questions.explanation: A dirty gray pseudomembrane over the tonsils/uvula is classic for diphtheria; its exotoxin has a particular affinity for the myocardium, making toxic myocarditis the most feared and probable complication (glomerulonephritis and amyloidosis are not typical diphtheria complications).
questions.keyConcept: Diphtheria exotoxin → toxic myocarditis (most important complication).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 50-year-old male has had difficulty breathing through his nose for several months. A head CT scan reveals a 4-cm mass involving the nasopharynx that erodes adjacent bone. The mass is excised, and microscopically it is composed of large epithelial cells having indistinct cell borders and prominent nuclei with mature lymphocytes scattered through the lesion. Which factor most likely played the greatest role in the development of this lesion?
questions.explanation: Large epithelial (syncytial) cells with indistinct borders admixed with mature lymphocytes describe undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma, which is strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection.
questions.keyConcept: Undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma (syncytial cells + lymphocytes) is EBV-associated.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy had changing in the character of his voice. On examination multiple polypoid masses were seen on the vocal cords extending to the subglottic region. Microscopic examination of the excised masses showed finger-like polypoid tissue covered by orderly arranged stratified squamous epithelium overlying a fibrovascular connective tissue core. Most likely diagnosis:
questions.explanation: Multiple finger-like papillary excrescences with a fibrovascular core covered by orderly stratified squamous epithelium, occurring in a child with multiple lesions extending subglottically, is characteristic of juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis (HPV 6/11 related).
questions.keyConcept: Juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis = multiple finger-like papillomas, fibrovascular core, HPV-related.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An active primary-stage-school teacher, 30 years old, had noticed that his voice had changed for the past 3 years. On examination there were no palpable head & neck masses but there were two tiny hemispherical smooth-surfaced masses about few millimeters in diameter seen on both vocal cords. The teacher was a smoker. Excisional biopsy was done. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Bilateral tiny smooth hemispherical vocal cord masses in a person with chronic vocal strain/smoking (voice teacher) is the classic description of a laryngeal (singer's) nodule, a reactive lesion from chronic vocal cord trauma.
questions.keyConcept: Singer's/vocal cord nodule = bilateral reactive lesion from chronic vocal strain/irritation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An active teacher, 30 years old, had noticed that his voice had changed for the past 3 years. On examination there were no palpable head & neck masses but there were two tiny hemispherical smooth surfaced masses about few millimeters in diameter seen on both vocal cords. Excisional biopsy was done. It would show:
options: Multiple branched connective tissue cores covered by acanthotic squamous epithelium
Irregular shaped masses of malignant squamous epithelial cells with central keratin formation
Polypoid tissue formed of hyalinized stroma covered by squamous epithelium
questions.explanation: Histologically a singer's/vocal nodule is a polypoid lesion with a hyalinized (fibrous) submucosal stromal core covered by intact squamous epithelium — a benign reactive change, not the branched papillomatous architecture of papilloma nor malignant keratinizing epithelium of carcinoma.
questions.keyConcept: Singer's nodule histology = hyalinized stromal polyp covered by squamous epithelium (benign, reactive).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child presented with change in his voice that did not respond to any medical treatment. Laryngoscopic examination revealed multiple small polypoidal lesions that were excised and showed narrow connective tissue cores covered by acanthotic squamous epithelium. The physician will warn the patient about:
questions.explanation: Juvenile/recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (HPV-driven) is notorious for frequent local recurrence after excision, requiring repeated procedures, even though malignant transformation is rare.
questions.keyConcept: Juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis is characteristically highly recurrent after excision.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 70-year-old man complained of persistent hoarseness of voice for the last 6 months. On examination there was an enlarged non-tender anterior cervical lymph node. On laryngoscopy an irregular fungating mass was seen on the vocal cord with infraglottic extension. Laryngeal biopsy followed by laryngectomy was done. Most likely diagnosis:
questions.explanation: A fungating mass arising directly on the vocal cord (glottis) with infraglottic extension and cervical lymphadenopathy in an elderly patient with hoarseness defines glottic (true vocal cord) carcinoma.
questions.keyConcept: Glottic carcinoma arises on the true vocal cords; hoarseness is an early symptom.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 76-year-old male complained of persistent hoarseness of voice for the last 6 months. On laryngoscopy an irregular fungating mass was seen on the epiglottis. Laryngeal biopsy revealed well differentiated squamous cell carcinoma and was followed by partial laryngectomy. No cervical lymph nodal metastases or distant metastases were found. Which finding is considered the most favourable prognostic value?
options: No lymph nodal metastases or distant metastases
A diagnosis of differentiated squamous cell carcinoma
questions.explanation: Absence of lymph nodal and distant metastasis is the single strongest prognostic factor in laryngeal carcinoma, outweighing tumor differentiation grade or the sparse lymphatic supply of the supraglottic/epiglottic region.
questions.keyConcept: Absence of nodal/distant metastasis is the most important favorable prognostic factor in laryngeal carcinoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: All are true regarding glottic carcinoma EXCEPT:
options: It arises at the true vocal fold
It is the most common site of laryngeal carcinoma
The patient presents by early change of voice
questions.explanation: Because the true vocal cords have a sparse lymphatic supply, glottic carcinoma characteristically shows LATE lymphatic spread (not early), which is why early hoarseness allows earlier detection and better prognosis, despite being the commonest laryngeal carcinoma site.
questions.keyConcept: Glottic carcinoma: sparse cord lymphatics → LATE nodal spread; early voice change aids early detection.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 25-year-old man had a blunt trauma to his chest. He was hospitalized. There were contusions on his right chest wall. After 1 hour, he suffered from difficulty in breathing and pain on the right side. Vital signs are normal but breath sounds were not heard on the right side. Which x-ray finding is most likely to be present?
options: Extensive centriacinar emphysema in right lobe
Patchy infiltrates in the right lung
questions.explanation: Blunt chest trauma with rib contusion, absent breath sounds, and acute dyspnea/pain is classic traumatic pneumothorax, typically with an associated rib fracture puncturing the pleura.
questions.keyConcept: Blunt trauma + absent breath sounds unilaterally = traumatic pneumothorax (often with rib fracture).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Ball and valve leak occurs in which type of pneumothorax?
questions.explanation: Tension pneumothorax results from a one-way (ball-and-valve) leak that allows air into the pleural space on inspiration but prevents its escape on expiration, progressively increasing intrapleural pressure and causing mediastinal shift.
questions.keyConcept: Tension pneumothorax = one-way ball-valve air leak → progressive pressure buildup → mediastinal shift.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: 60 years old, had worked in a shipyard for 30 years, exposed to asbestos. He is complaining of stabbing chest pain and difficulty of breathing. CT scan revealed thickening in pleura, thoracocentesis fluid extract contained blood and malignant spindle shaped cells. A specimen of the tumour found could be stained immunohistochemically positive for which of the following?
questions.explanation: Malignant (sarcomatoid) mesothelioma in an asbestos-exposed shipyard worker is immunohistochemically positive for the mesothelial markers calretinin and CK5/6, and typically negative for CEA (which favors metastatic adenocarcinoma instead).
questions.keyConcept: Mesothelioma IHC: calretinin+ and CK5/6+, CEA-negative (helps distinguish from adenocarcinoma).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In ARDS, neutrophils are activated by pro-inflammatory mediators released from:
questions.explanation: In ARDS, alveolar macrophages are activated first by the initial insult and release pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-1, chemokines) that recruit and activate neutrophils, driving the acute lung injury.
questions.keyConcept: ARDS pathogenesis: macrophages release cytokines → neutrophil recruitment/activation → diffuse alveolar damage.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In ARDS, endothelial & alveolar damage occurs by proteolytic enzymes & reactive molecules produced by:
questions.explanation: Activated neutrophils release proteases (elastase) and reactive oxygen species that directly damage the alveolar-capillary endothelium and epithelium, producing the diffuse alveolar damage characteristic of ARDS.
questions.keyConcept: Neutrophil proteases & ROS mediate the endothelial/alveolar damage of ARDS.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A previously healthy 55-year-old man had undergone laryngeal surgery. Two days postoperatively he experienced increasing respiratory difficulty with decreased arterial oxygen saturation (hypoxia). He was afebrile. After he coughed up a large amount of blood clots his condition improved. Which of the following is most likely the cause of his condition?
questions.explanation: Postoperative bronchial obstruction by a blood clot causes resorption (absorption) atelectasis distal to the obstruction; clearing the obstructing clot (by coughing it up) promptly re-expands the lung and relieves hypoxia, consistent with absorption collapse rather than infection (afebrile).
questions.keyConcept: Post-op airway obstruction by clot/mucus → resorption (absorption) collapse; relieved once obstruction clears.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A neonate had difficulty taking breath after labour. X-ray showed ground glass opacity of both lungs. Which of the following may be the predisposing factor for this condition?
questions.explanation: Maternal diabetes causes fetal hyperinsulinemia, which delays surfactant (lecithin) production by type II pneumocytes, predisposing the neonate to respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease), seen radiologically as diffuse ground-glass opacities.
questions.keyConcept: Maternal diabetes → fetal hyperinsulinemia → delayed surfactant maturation → neonatal hyaline membrane disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 70-year-old man was hospitalized for 10 days following hip replacement as treatment for fracture neck femur. He started to complain of fever, cough and expectoration. Chest x-ray revealed multiple bilateral basal small opacities (consolidated patches). Which is the most likely histologic finding?
options: Alveoli are filled with haemosiderin-laden macrophages, red blood cells and oedema fluid
The alveoli are filled with neutrophils, pus cells and fibrin threads
The alveoli and adjacent bronchioles are filled with suppurative exudate
The alveolar walls are thickened by inflammatory cellular infiltrate and oedema fluid
questions.explanation: Post-operative, bedridden elderly patients are prone to hypostatic bronchopneumonia; histologically bronchopneumonia shows patchy suppurative exudate filling both the alveoli AND the adjacent bronchioles (in contrast to lobar pneumonia, which fills alveoli via inter-alveolar spread without bronchiolar involvement).
questions.keyConcept: Bronchopneumonia = patchy suppurative exudate in alveoli AND adjacent bronchioles (bronchiolocentric).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 37-year-old woman presents with acute onset of productive cough, fever, chills and pleuritic chest pain. A chest x-ray reveals consolidation of the entire lower lobe of her right lung. She unexpectedly dies before treatment due to cardiac arrhythmia. Histologic examination of lung tissue at autopsy reveals multiple neutrophil-rich fibrinous exudates filling the alveolar spaces. Most likely diagnosis:
questions.explanation: Entire-lobe consolidation with fibrinosuppurative (neutrophil-rich, fibrinous) exudate filling alveolar spaces uniformly throughout a lobe is the definition of lobar pneumonia, classically due to Streptococcus pneumoniae.
questions.keyConcept: Lobar pneumonia = fibrinosuppurative exudate filling an entire lobe uniformly via inter-alveolar (Cohn) pores.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A previously healthy 45-year-old patient underwent urgent operation under general anesthesia. One day later he developed progressive fever and signs of chest infection. The fever was not responding to broad-spectrum antibiotics for one week; lab investigations showed markedly elevated total white cell count. Follow-up chest x-ray showed an opaque shadow of the right lung with air-fluid level. Diagnosis:
options: Bronchogenic carcinoma complicated by chest infection
questions.explanation: General anesthesia predisposes to aspiration of oropharyngeal contents (especially into the right lung, which has a wider, more vertical main bronchus); an air-fluid level on x-ray with unremitting fever/leukocytosis is the classic sign of a resulting lung abscess.
questions.keyConcept: Anesthesia → aspiration → lung abscess (air-fluid level on x-ray); right lung favored due to bronchial anatomy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 6-year-old girl had cough, headache, fever and respiratory difficulty for 5 days. Respiratory syncytial virus was isolated from the sputum sample. Which chest x-ray finding is most likely to be present?
questions.explanation: Viral pneumonias (including RSV) characteristically produce an interstitial inflammatory pattern (inflammation confined mainly to alveolar septal walls) rather than the airspace-filling lobar or patchy consolidation seen with bacterial pneumonia.
questions.keyConcept: Viral pneumonia = interstitial infiltrate pattern (septal wall inflammation), unlike bacterial alveolar consolidation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Occult bronchogenic carcinoma means the patient presents by:
options: A very small lesion with persistent cough & haemoptysis
Widespread systemic metastatic disease with no pulmonary symptoms
Both metastatic manifestations and pulmonary symptoms
Paraneoplastic syndrome and associated pulmonary symptoms
questions.explanation: 'Occult' bronchogenic carcinoma refers to a tumor that is clinically silent at its primary pulmonary site (no respiratory symptoms) but has already produced overt, widespread systemic metastases at presentation.
questions.keyConcept: Occult bronchogenic carcinoma = systemic metastases present with NO pulmonary symptoms from the primary.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 55-year-old male, heavy smoker for more than 25 years, complained of cough that became associated with haemoptysis. Chest x-ray revealed an irregular large hilar lung mass with central cavitation. Bronchoscopic biopsy showed lymphocyte-like cells; electron microscopy showed dense-core membrane-bound neurosecretory granules. Diagnosis:
questions.explanation: Small, lymphocyte-like tumor cells with dense-core neurosecretory granules on electron microscopy in a heavy smoker with a large hilar mass are characteristic of small cell (neuroendocrine) lung carcinoma.
questions.keyConcept: Small cell lung carcinoma: small lymphocyte-like cells, dense-core neurosecretory granules, strongly smoking-related, central/hilar.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Large cell carcinoma of the lung
questions.text: Which of the following statements is NOT true for large cell carcinoma of the lung?
options: Giant cells and spindle cells can be seen
Frequent mitoses with abnormal ones are seen
Large tall cells grow along the alveolar septa and project into alveolar spaces
It may show features of squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma on electron microscopy
questions.explanation: Growth of tall cells along intact alveolar septa (lepidic growth) without stromal invasion describes atypical adenomatous hyperplasia/adenocarcinoma in situ, not large cell carcinoma, which is a highly undifferentiated, aggressively invasive tumor.
questions.keyConcept: Lepidic (septal) growth pattern belongs to AAH/adenocarcinoma-in-situ, NOT large cell carcinoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Adenocarcinoma in situ / atypical adenomatous hyperplasia
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true for atypical adenomatous hyperplasia & adenocarcinoma in situ of the lung?
options: Giant cells and spindle cells can be seen
Frequent mitoses with abnormal ones are seen
Large tall cells grow along the alveolar septa and project into alveolar spaces
It may show features of squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma on electron microscopy
questions.explanation: Adenocarcinoma in situ/atypical adenomatous hyperplasia is defined by a purely lepidic growth pattern: atypical tall cuboidal-to-columnar cells proliferating along, but not invading, pre-existing alveolar septa.
questions.keyConcept: AAH/AIS = lepidic growth (tall cells lining intact alveolar septa) without stromal invasion.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is true for small cell carcinoma of the lung?
options: May secrete either corticotrophin and/or antidiuretic hormone
Generally amenable to surgery at time of diagnosis
Usually arises peripherally rather than centrally
Has a less clear relation to smoking
questions.explanation: Small cell lung carcinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor classically associated with ectopic ACTH secretion (Cushing syndrome) and/or ADH secretion (SIADH); PTH-like hormone (hypercalcemia) is instead typical of squamous cell carcinoma.
questions.keyConcept: Small cell carcinoma paraneoplastic syndromes: ectopic ACTH (Cushing) and/or ADH (SIADH).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding adenocarcinoma in situ?
options: It invades the lung parenchyma and brachial plexus
It arises from the main bronchial branches
It grows on alveolar septa with no stromal invasion
It metastasizes early to regional hilar lymph nodes
questions.explanation: By definition, adenocarcinoma in situ is a pre-invasive lesion confined to growth along existing alveolar septal walls (lepidic pattern) without invading the underlying stroma, vessels, or pleura, and therefore does not metastasize.
questions.keyConcept: Adenocarcinoma in situ = pre-invasive lepidic growth on septa, NO stromal invasion, NO metastasis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Routine chest x-ray of a 22-year-old man reveals a solitary, subpleural, well-circumscribed 2cm coin-like opacity. He has no complaints; but he has to do the x-ray before travelling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An asymptomatic, well-circumscribed, coin-lesion (solitary pulmonary nodule) in a young adult is the classic presentation of a pulmonary hamartoma, a benign tumor-like malformation of mature lung tissue elements (cartilage, fat, connective tissue).
questions.keyConcept: Asymptomatic well-circumscribed 'coin lesion' in a young adult = pulmonary hamartoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung (paraneoplastic)
questions.text: A 53-year-old male smoker had a history of progressive cough and weight loss. X-ray showed a hilar mass 4 cm in diameter, with hypercalcemia. The most probable diagnosis:
questions.explanation: A central/hilar mass in a smoker with hypercalcemia points to squamous cell carcinoma, which classically causes hypercalcemia via secretion of a PTH-related peptide (PTHrP), unlike small cell carcinoma's ACTH/ADH pattern.
questions.keyConcept: Squamous cell lung carcinoma: central/hilar, smoking-related, PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung (metastasis)
questions.text: PET/CT for the previous case (hilar squamous cell carcinoma), the most probable site of blood-borne metastasis will be:
questions.explanation: The adrenal gland is the single most common site of blood-borne metastasis from bronchogenic (including squamous cell) carcinoma, followed by liver, brain, and bone.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenal gland is the commonest metastatic site from bronchogenic carcinoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 45-year-old female had progressive cough; x-ray showed a pneumonia-like shadow of 2 cm diameter. The most probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: A small (2 cm), localized pneumonia-like (ground-glass/consolidative) shadow without systemic toxicity is the typical radiologic appearance of adenocarcinoma in situ/bronchioloalveolar pattern lesions, which grow along alveolar septa mimicking consolidation.
questions.keyConcept: Small localized pneumonia-like opacity without systemic toxicity suggests adenocarcinoma in situ (lepidic growth mimics consolidation).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: While recovering in bed 1 week after an abdominal hysterectomy, a 42-year-old woman develops acute shortness of breath with haemoptysis. Physical examination finds the patient afebrile with moderate respiratory distress and calf tenderness. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Post-operative immobilization, calf tenderness (suggesting deep vein thrombosis), and acute dyspnea with haemoptysis in an afebrile patient is the classic triad pointing to pulmonary embolism arising from a DVT.
questions.keyConcept: Post-op immobilization + calf tenderness (DVT) + acute dyspnea/haemoptysis = pulmonary embolism.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 54-year-old non-smoker man has had no major medical problems prior to the past year, when he noted increasing malaise along with a 6 kg weight loss. He currently has no fever, cough, dyspnea or respiratory difficulties. On examination he has non-tender supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. A chest x-ray shows multiple solid nodules ranging from 1-3 cm scattered throughout all lung fields. Which pathological process is most likely to account for these findings?
questions.explanation: Multiple, well-defined nodules scattered bilaterally throughout all lung fields ('cannonball' pattern) with systemic constitutional symptoms and lymphadenopathy, but no respiratory symptoms, is the classic picture of metastatic carcinoma to the lung.
questions.keyConcept: Multiple bilateral 'cannonball' lung nodules = metastatic carcinoma (not a primary lung process).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 44-year-old non-smoker woman has had fever and cough for one month. A chest x-ray reveals a 3 cm peripheral mass in the right upper lobe. Which neoplasm is most likely to be present in this woman?
questions.explanation: A peripheral lung mass in a non-smoking woman is the classic epidemiologic and anatomic profile of pulmonary adenocarcinoma, which (unlike squamous or small cell carcinoma) is less strongly linked to smoking and typically arises peripherally.
questions.keyConcept: Adenocarcinoma: peripheral location, most common lung cancer in non-smokers/women.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The most characteristic feature in pulmonary arterioles of primary pulmonary hypertension is:
questions.explanation: Primary (idiopathic) pulmonary hypertension is histologically defined by plexiform lesions — focal proliferations of endothelial and myofibroblastic cells that form glomeruloid, plexiform channels within and around dilated small pulmonary arterioles.
questions.keyConcept: Primary pulmonary hypertension hallmark = plexiform (endothelial) lesions in small pulmonary arterioles.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man complained of fever and cough with haemoptysis for 2 weeks. Chest x-ray revealed an area of consolidation in the right upper lobe. After antibiotic therapy his fever improved but the cough and haemoptysis did not improve. Repeated chest x-ray revealed right upper lobe collapse. Bronchoscopic examination revealed an obstructing well-circumscribed mass arising from the main bronchus. Which tumor is most likely?
questions.explanation: A well-circumscribed, centrally located endobronchial mass causing obstructive pneumonia followed by lobar collapse, with recurrent haemoptysis, is the classic presentation of a bronchial carcinoid tumor arising from a main bronchus.
questions.keyConcept: Bronchial carcinoid: well-circumscribed endobronchial mass → obstruction → recurrent pneumonia/haemoptysis/collapse.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The commonest cause of epistaxis in young age is:
questions.explanation: In young patients, epistaxis is most commonly due to a localized congenital vascular anomaly (telangiectasia) of the nasal mucosa (e.g. Little's area), rather than systemic causes like hypertension which predominate in older adults.
questions.keyConcept: Epistaxis in the young is most often due to congenital telangiectasia of nasal mucosa; hypertension is the typical cause in older adults.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Allergic nasal polyp is:
questions.explanation: Allergic (inflammatory) nasal polyps are edematous, eosinophil-rich inflammatory outgrowths of nasal/sinus mucosa, not true neoplasms.
questions.keyConcept: Nasal polyps are inflammatory (allergic, eosinophil-rich) lesions, not neoplasms.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Quinzy means:
questions.explanation: Quinsy is the clinical term for a peritonsillar abscess, a suppurative complication of acute tonsillitis.
questions.keyConcept: Quinsy = peritonsillar abscess (suppurative complication of tonsillitis).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The most important complication of tonsillitis is:
questions.explanation: While otitis media and quinsy are common local complications, rheumatic fever is the most important complication of streptococcal tonsillitis because of its potential for serious, chronic cardiac (valvular) damage.
questions.keyConcept: Rheumatic fever is the most important complication of streptococcal tonsillitis due to long-term cardiac sequelae.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Diphtheria is an example of:
questions.explanation: Diphtheria produces a characteristic tough, adherent grey pseudomembrane composed of fibrin, necrotic epithelium, and bacteria over the tonsils/pharynx — the defining feature of membranous (pseudomembranous) inflammation.
questions.keyConcept: Diphtheria = membranous (pseudomembranous) inflammation: adherent fibrino-necrotic membrane.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The general complications of diphtheria are due to:
questions.explanation: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is non-invasive; its systemic complications (myocarditis, neuropathy) result from a powerful exotoxin absorbed into the bloodstream, not from bacteremia or endotoxin.
questions.keyConcept: Diphtheria's systemic complications are exotoxin-mediated, not due to bacterial invasion.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Zenker's necrosis does NOT affect:
questions.explanation: Zenker's (waxy) degeneration/necrosis in diphtheritic toxic myositis characteristically affects the diaphragm, intercostals, thigh, and shoulder (limb girdle) muscles, but classically spares the back muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Diphtheritic (Zenker's) myonecrosis spares back muscles; affects diaphragm, intercostal, thigh, shoulder muscles.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The following is NOT a feature of diphtheria:
options: It is characterised by formation of a pseudomembrane
questions.explanation: Diphtheria is a membranous (fibrino-necrotic), not suppurative, inflammation; there is no pus formation, distinguishing it from bacterial tonsillitis.
questions.keyConcept: Diphtheria is membranous, NOT suppurative inflammation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Suffocation may occur in diphtheric patients due to:
questions.explanation: Diphtheric suffocation can result from multiple mechanisms acting together: systemic toxaemia weakening respiratory muscles, sudden airway obstruction by a separated/dislodged pseudomembrane, and laryngeal muscle spasm.
questions.keyConcept: Diphtheric suffocation is multifactorial: toxaemia, membrane separation, and respiratory muscle spasm all contribute.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Laryngoscleroma is a:
questions.explanation: Laryngoscleroma, like rhinoscleroma, is a chronic granulomatous infection (Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis) of the larynx, not a true neoplasm.
questions.keyConcept: Laryngoscleroma = chronic granulomatous lesion, same aetiology as rhinoscleroma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Singer's nodule of the larynx is:
questions.explanation: A singer's (vocal cord) nodule is a reactive, non-specific inflammatory/degenerative lesion from chronic vocal strain, not a true neoplasm or granuloma.
questions.keyConcept: Singer's nodule = non-specific reactive inflammatory lesion of the vocal cord (not a true tumor).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The following lesion is precancerous:
questions.explanation: Laryngeal squamous cell papilloma (particularly in adults, and with dysplastic change) carries premalignant potential, unlike the purely reactive/inflammatory laryngeal nodule or the granulomatous laryngoscleroma.
questions.keyConcept: Squamous cell papilloma of the larynx is the precancerous option among these choices.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the vocal cords is characterised by all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Glottic (vocal cord) squamous cell carcinoma spreads late and predominantly by lymphatics due to the sparse cord lymphatic supply, but it is not restricted to lymphatic spread ONLY — it can also spread by direct extension; other features (slow growth, well-differentiated, good prognosis, late metastasis) are characteristic.
questions.keyConcept: Vocal cord SCC: slow-growing, well-differentiated, late spread, good prognosis — spread is not exclusively lymphatic.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The inflammatory cellular infiltrate in bronchial asthma consists mainly of:
questions.explanation: The hallmark inflammatory cell in bronchial asthma airway inflammation is the eosinophil, recruited by Th2 cytokines (IL-5) during the late-phase allergic response.
questions.keyConcept: Bronchial asthma airway infiltrate is predominantly eosinophilic.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Complete bronchial obstruction leads to:
questions.explanation: Complete obstruction of a bronchus prevents any air entry distally; trapped air is absorbed and the affected segment collapses (resorption atelectasis).
questions.keyConcept: Complete bronchial obstruction → resorption (absorption) atelectasis/collapse.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Partial bronchial obstruction leads to:
questions.explanation: Partial (ball-valve type) obstruction allows air in during inspiration but traps it on expiration, leading to progressive distal air trapping and emphysema-like overdistension.
questions.keyConcept: Partial (ball-valve) bronchial obstruction → air trapping → emphysema.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The causative organism of pneumonia can be:
questions.explanation: Pneumonia is a syndrome of alveolar/interstitial inflammation that can be caused by any class of microorganism — viruses, bacteria, fungi, or parasites.
questions.keyConcept: Pneumonia can be caused by viruses, bacteria, fungi, or parasites.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Kartagener's syndrome is characterised by:
questions.explanation: Kartagener syndrome (a primary ciliary dyskinesia) is the triad of bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis, and situs inversus/dextrocardia, resulting from defective ciliary motility.
questions.keyConcept: Kartagener syndrome = bronchiectasis + sinusitis + dextrocardia (primary ciliary dyskinesia).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency plays a role in the pathogenesis of:
questions.explanation: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency removes the main protective antiprotease, allowing unchecked neutrophil elastase activity to destroy alveolar walls, causing panacinar emphysema.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency → unopposed elastase activity → panacinar emphysema.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Hyaline membrane disease is NOT characterised by:
options: Pink fibrinous material lining the alveoli
questions.explanation: Hyaline membrane disease (neonatal RDS) shows enlarged, fleshy, airless lungs that sink in water, with collapsed alveoli lined by pink fibrinous hyaline membranes — pulmonary emphysema (permanent airspace enlargement) is not a feature.
questions.keyConcept: Hyaline membrane disease: collapsed alveoli + hyaline membranes; lungs sink in water; NOT emphysematous.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Pulmonary scars may predispose to:
questions.explanation: Adenocarcinoma is the lung cancer subtype most classically associated with arising in areas of pre-existing pulmonary scarring ('scar carcinoma'), often peripherally located.
questions.keyConcept: 'Scar carcinoma' arising in pulmonary scars is typically adenocarcinoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The following is NOT true for the usual pulmonary adenocarcinoma:
options: Equal frequency in males and females
questions.explanation: Unlike the other listed features which correctly describe adenocarcinoma (peripheral, seen in both sexes, less strongly smoking-related, slower growing), adenocarcinoma classically IS related to pulmonary scarring ('scar carcinoma'), making 'NOT related to scarring' the false/incorrect statement.
questions.keyConcept: Adenocarcinoma IS classically associated with pulmonary scarring ('scar carcinoma') — this option is false.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The pulmonary tumor which appears as pneumonia-like consolidation is:
questions.explanation: Bronchioloalveolar carcinoma grows along intact alveolar septa (lepidic growth), producing a diffuse, patchy radiologic appearance that mimics pneumonia consolidation rather than forming a discrete mass.
questions.keyConcept: Bronchioloalveolar carcinoma's lepidic growth pattern mimics pneumonia-like consolidation radiologically.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Chromogranin is a histologic marker of:
questions.explanation: Chromogranin is a neuroendocrine granule marker, positive in small cell carcinoma (a high-grade neuroendocrine tumor) and carcinoid tumors, but not in squamous, adeno-, large cell, or giant cell carcinoma.
questions.keyConcept: Chromogranin = neuroendocrine marker, positive in small cell carcinoma (and carcinoid).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Pulmonary small cell carcinoma is characterised by all EXCEPT:
options: It is the most aggressive type
questions.explanation: Small cell carcinoma is well known for paraneoplastic ectopic hormone production (ACTH causing Cushing syndrome, ADH causing SIADH) — the statement that it is 'NOT associated with hormone production' is the false one (the EXCEPT).
questions.keyConcept: Small cell carcinoma IS classically associated with ectopic hormone production (ACTH, ADH) — contradicts this option.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Oat cell carcinoma is a subtype of:
questions.explanation: 'Oat cell carcinoma' is the classic descriptive name for the most common subtype of small cell lung carcinoma, so named for the oat-grain-like appearance of the small, hyperchromatic tumor cells.
questions.keyConcept: Oat cell carcinoma = classic morphologic subtype/synonym of small cell carcinoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Giant cell carcinoma is a subtype of:
questions.explanation: Giant cell carcinoma is classified as a rare, highly undifferentiated variant of large cell carcinoma of the lung.
questions.keyConcept: Giant cell carcinoma is a variant/subtype of large cell carcinoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Bronchial carcinoid may spread by blood to:
questions.explanation: When bronchial carcinoid tumors do metastasize haematogenously (uncommon, as they are typically low-grade), the liver is the characteristic and most frequently cited site.
questions.keyConcept: Bronchial carcinoid haematogenous spread, when it occurs, characteristically goes to the liver.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Cannon-ball metastases arise from:
questions.explanation: Classic 'cannonball' (large, round, well-circumscribed) pulmonary metastases are most characteristically associated with renal cell carcinoma (and also choriocarcinoma), more so than hepatocellular or prostatic carcinoma.
questions.keyConcept: 'Cannonball' lung metastases are the classic pattern for renal cell carcinoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Malignant mesothelioma is predisposed to by:
questions.explanation: Malignant mesothelioma has a strong, well-established causal association with asbestos exposure (asbestosis); silicosis and anthracosis are not established risk factors for mesothelioma.
questions.keyConcept: Asbestos exposure (asbestosis) is the established risk factor for malignant mesothelioma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Malignant pleural mesothelioma is characterised by all EXCEPT:
options: It is related to heavy exposure to asbestos
It appears as diffuse thickening of the pleura
It is NOT associated with pleural effusion
It may be of the sarcomatoid or epithelial type
It arises from visceral or parietal pleura
questions.explanation: Malignant mesothelioma is very commonly associated with a large, often haemorrhagic pleural effusion — the statement that it is 'NOT associated with pleural effusion' is false and is therefore the EXCEPT answer.
questions.keyConcept: Malignant mesothelioma IS classically associated with pleural effusion (often haemorrhagic) — contradicts this option.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Mesothelioma does NOT arise from:
questions.explanation: Mesothelioma arises from mesothelial-lined serosal surfaces — pleura, peritoneum, and tunica vaginalis testis — but the mesentery itself (a fold of peritoneum, not a distinct mesothelial cavity lining site typically listed) is not a classic primary site in this context; pleura is overwhelmingly the commonest site.
questions.keyConcept: Mesothelioma arises from serosal (mesothelial) surfaces: pleura (commonest), peritoneum, tunica vaginalis — not the mesentery.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Asbestos-related pleural thickening most typically progresses to:
questions.explanation: Heavy asbestos exposure causing diffuse pleural thickening is a recognised precursor/associated finding with malignant mesothelioma, the feared long-term consequence of asbestos exposure.
questions.keyConcept: Diffuse asbestos-related pleural thickening is associated with the development of malignant mesothelioma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Cannonball metastases in the lung are characteristically:
options: Multiple, round, well-circumscribed nodules of the above
questions.explanation: Cannonball metastases are classically described as multiple, large, round, well-circumscribed nodules scattered through both lungs, typical of haematogenous spread from renal cell carcinoma or choriocarcinoma.
questions.keyConcept: Cannonball metastases = multiple round well-circumscribed pulmonary nodules.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child with fever and haematuria following a preceding tonsillitis most probably has:
questions.explanation: Haematuria and fever developing 1-3 weeks after streptococcal tonsillitis/pharyngitis is the classic presentation of acute post-streptococcal (diffuse proliferative) glomerulonephritis, an immune-complex-mediated complication.
questions.keyConcept: Post-tonsillitis fever + haematuria = acute post-streptococcal diffuse glomerulonephritis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Bronchiectasis is characterised by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis characteristically involves the lower lobes / basal segments predominantly (due to gravity-dependent pooling of secretions), not the apices — apical predominance is instead typical of reactivation tuberculosis.
questions.keyConcept: Bronchiectasis is lower-lobe/basal predominant, NOT apical (apical predominance suggests TB instead).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Chronic rhinitis is always of the catarrhal type.
questions.explanation: Chronic rhinitis can be catarrhal, hypertrophic, or atrophic in type, not exclusively catarrhal.
questions.keyConcept: False: Chronic rhinitis is always of the catarrhal type.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Rhinoscleroma is a granulomatous tumor-like lesion.
questions.explanation: Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granulomatous infection that clinically forms a firm, tumor-like nasal mass, though it is inflammatory rather than neoplastic in nature.
questions.keyConcept: True: Rhinoscleroma is a granulomatous tumor-like lesion.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Angiofibroma is the least common benign tumor of the nose.
questions.explanation: Nasopharyngeal (juvenile) angiofibroma, while a distinctive and clinically important vascular tumor, is not the LEAST common benign nasal/nasopharyngeal tumor; nasal polyps and papillomas are more relevant comparators, and angiofibroma is a well-recognised, not rare-of-the-rare, entity in this context.
questions.keyConcept: False: Angiofibroma is the least common benign tumor of the nose.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Epistaxis means severe haemorrhage from the nose.
questions.explanation: Epistaxis simply means bleeding/haemorrhage from the nose of any severity, not specifically severe haemorrhage.
questions.keyConcept: False: Epistaxis means severe haemorrhage from the nose.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Quinsy is a benign tumor of the tonsil.
questions.explanation: Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) is a suppurative inflammatory complication of tonsillitis, not a neoplasm.
questions.keyConcept: False: Quinsy is a benign tumor of the tonsil.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Diphtheria is a suppurative disease of the upper respiratory tract.
questions.explanation: Diphtheria produces a membranous (fibrino-necrotic pseudomembrane), not suppurative, inflammation.
questions.keyConcept: False: Diphtheria is a suppurative disease of the upper respiratory tract.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The systemic complications of diphtheria are due to circulation of the organism in the blood.
questions.explanation: Diphtheria's systemic complications (myocarditis, neuropathy) are due to absorbed exotoxin circulating in the blood, not bacteraemia, since C. diphtheriae remains localized to the pseudomembrane.
questions.keyConcept: False: The systemic complications of diphtheria are due to circulation of the organism in the blood.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Laryngoscleroma and rhinoscleroma have the same aetiology and histology.
questions.explanation: Both are caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis and show identical granulomatous histology (Mikulicz cells, Russell bodies), differing only in anatomic site.
questions.keyConcept: True: Laryngoscleroma and rhinoscleroma have the same aetiology and histology.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Singer's nodule is a neoplastic lesion of the larynx.
questions.explanation: Singer's (vocal cord) nodule is a reactive/degenerative lesion from chronic vocal strain, not a true neoplasm.
questions.keyConcept: False: Singer's nodule is a neoplastic lesion of the larynx.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Vocal cord carcinoma shows late metastases due to minimal blood supply.
questions.explanation: Vocal cord (glottic) carcinoma spreads late because of the sparse LYMPHATIC supply of the true vocal cords, not because of minimal blood supply.
questions.keyConcept: False: Vocal cord carcinoma shows late metastases due to minimal blood supply.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Intrinsic and extrinsic laryngeal carcinomas differ in histology and prognosis.
questions.explanation: Intrinsic (glottic) laryngeal carcinoma differs from extrinsic (supraglottic/hypopharyngeal) carcinoma in behaviour: intrinsic tumors spread late (better prognosis) due to sparse cord lymphatics, while extrinsic tumors metastasize early (worse prognosis) via a richer lymphatic network.
questions.keyConcept: True: Intrinsic and extrinsic laryngeal carcinomas differ in histology and prognosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Intrinsic and extrinsic bronchial asthma have the same aetiology.
questions.explanation: Intrinsic (non-atopic) asthma is triggered by non-allergic factors (infection, irritants, cold air) whereas extrinsic (atopic) asthma is IgE-mediated allergic hypersensitivity — they have different aetiologies despite a shared final inflammatory pathway.
questions.keyConcept: False: Intrinsic and extrinsic bronchial asthma have the same aetiology.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Chronic bronchitis is NOT a suppurative disease.
questions.explanation: Chronic bronchitis is defined by mucus hypersecretion and goblet cell/gland hyperplasia with chronic inflammation, not pus formation; it is non-suppurative (unlike bronchiectasis or lung abscess).
questions.keyConcept: True: Chronic bronchitis is NOT a suppurative disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Infection and partial bronchial obstruction are the two main factors in the pathogenesis of bronchiectasis.
questions.explanation: The classic 'vicious cycle' of bronchiectasis pathogenesis requires both recurrent/persistent infection and impaired drainage from bronchial obstruction, acting together to destroy and dilate the bronchial wall.
questions.keyConcept: True: Infection and partial bronchial obstruction are the two main factors in the pathogenesis of bronchiectasis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Bronchiectasis is NOT a suppurative disease.
questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis is a classic suppurative lung disease, with pus-filled, dilated, destroyed bronchi and copious purulent sputum.
questions.keyConcept: False: Bronchiectasis is NOT a suppurative disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Bronchopneumonia gives the lung a liver-like consistency.
questions.explanation: Diffuse 'hepatization' (liver-like consistency) is characteristic of LOBAR pneumonia (uniform lobar consolidation); bronchopneumonia instead produces patchy, discrete, gray-yellow consolidated foci, not diffuse hepatization.
questions.keyConcept: False: Bronchopneumonia gives the lung a liver-like consistency.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The inflammatory infiltrate in viral pneumonia is mainly interstitial.
questions.explanation: Viral pneumonia characteristically produces interstitial (septal wall) inflammation rather than alveolar space (luminal) exudate seen in bacterial pneumonia.
questions.keyConcept: True: The inflammatory infiltrate in viral pneumonia is mainly interstitial.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Aspiration lung abscess is more common in the right lung due to its wider bronchus.
questions.explanation: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertically oriented than the left, making aspirated material (and resultant abscesses) more likely to lodge in the right lung.
questions.keyConcept: True: Aspiration lung abscess is more common in the right lung due to its wider bronchus.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Pyaemic lung abscesses arise from disseminated infected thrombi.
questions.explanation: Pyaemic (embolic) abscesses result from septic emboli originating from infected thrombi elsewhere in the body, seeding the lung haematogenously and forming multiple abscesses.
questions.keyConcept: True: Pyaemic lung abscesses arise from disseminated infected thrombi.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Lung gangrene is NOT a suppurative condition.
questions.explanation: Lung gangrene arises as a severe necrotizing complication typically superimposed on suppurative infection (e.g. abscess or pneumonia) with putrefactive organisms, and is associated with suppuration.
questions.keyConcept: False: Lung gangrene is NOT a suppurative condition.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Putrefactive organisms causing lung gangrene originate from the intestine.
questions.explanation: Anaerobic putrefactive organisms responsible for lung gangrene are typically derived from the gastrointestinal (intestinal) flora, reaching the lung via aspiration.
questions.keyConcept: True: Putrefactive organisms causing lung gangrene originate from the intestine.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Lung gangrene is always of the moist type.
questions.explanation: Pulmonary gangrene, occurring in a moist, oxygen-poor, richly vascular organ with ongoing suppurative infection, is always of the moist (wet) type, unlike the dry gangrene seen in ischaemic limbs.
questions.keyConcept: True: Lung gangrene is always of the moist type.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Bronchial asthma shows permanent dilation of the terminal air spaces.
questions.explanation: Permanent dilation of air spaces distal to the terminal bronchiole (with alveolar wall destruction) defines emphysema, not asthma, which causes reversible bronchospasm and airway remodeling without permanent airspace enlargement.
questions.keyConcept: False: Bronchial asthma shows permanent dilation of the terminal air spaces.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Emphysema shows permanent dilation of the terminal air passages.
questions.explanation: Emphysema is defined by permanent, abnormal enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole, accompanied by destruction of their walls.
questions.keyConcept: True: Emphysema shows permanent dilation of the terminal air passages.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency plays a role in the pathogenesis of pulmonary collapse.
questions.explanation: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes panacinar EMPHYSEMA via unopposed neutrophil elastase activity; it is not implicated in the pathogenesis of pulmonary collapse (atelectasis), which results from airway obstruction, compression, or loss of surfactant.
questions.keyConcept: False: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency plays a role in the pathogenesis of pulmonary collapse.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In hyaline membrane disease, the lungs float in water.
questions.explanation: In hyaline membrane disease, the airless, collapsed, fluid/fibrin-filled lungs SINK in water (unlike aerated normal lungs which float), a classic autopsy finding.
questions.keyConcept: False: In hyaline membrane disease, the lungs float in water.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In hyaline membrane disease, the alveoli are mostly collapsed.
questions.explanation: Deficient surfactant in hyaline membrane disease leads to widespread alveolar collapse (atelectasis), with the remaining dilated ducts lined by hyaline membranes.
questions.keyConcept: True: In hyaline membrane disease, the alveoli are mostly collapsed.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The brain is the commonest site of metastasis from bronchogenic carcinoma.
questions.explanation: The adrenal gland, not the brain, is the commonest site of haematogenous metastasis from bronchogenic carcinoma, although brain metastasis is also common and clinically important.
questions.keyConcept: False: The brain is the commonest site of metastasis from bronchogenic carcinoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Pancoast's tumor is an apical cancer infiltrating the cervical sympathetic plexus.
questions.explanation: Pancoast tumor arises at the lung apex (superior sulcus) and characteristically invades the cervical sympathetic chain and brachial plexus, producing Horner syndrome and arm/shoulder pain.
questions.keyConcept: True: Pancoast's tumor is an apical cancer infiltrating the cervical sympathetic plexus.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Chromogranin is a marker of all neuroendocrine tumors.
questions.explanation: Chromogranin A is a general marker for neuroendocrine differentiation, positive across the spectrum of neuroendocrine tumors including carcinoid and small cell carcinoma.
questions.keyConcept: True: Chromogranin is a marker of all neuroendocrine tumors.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Bronchial carcinoid never spreads by lymphatics.
questions.explanation: Bronchial carcinoid tumors, although generally low-grade, CAN spread via lymphatics to regional (hilar/mediastinal) lymph nodes, especially atypical variants.
questions.keyConcept: False: Bronchial carcinoid never spreads by lymphatics.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Bronchial carcinoid never spreads by blood.
questions.explanation: Although uncommon given its typically low-grade behaviour, bronchial carcinoid CAN metastasize haematogenously, particularly to the liver.
questions.keyConcept: False: Bronchial carcinoid never spreads by blood.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The liver is a metastatic site of carcinoid tumors.
questions.explanation: The liver is the characteristic site of haematogenous metastasis from carcinoid tumors when spread occurs.
questions.keyConcept: True: The liver is a metastatic site of carcinoid tumors.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Cannon-ball metastases arise from hepatocellular carcinoma.
questions.explanation: Classic cannonball lung metastases are most characteristically associated with renal cell carcinoma (and choriocarcinoma), not hepatocellular carcinoma.
questions.keyConcept: False: Cannon-ball metastases arise from hepatocellular carcinoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Mesothelioma is predisposed to by silicosis.
questions.explanation: Malignant mesothelioma's established occupational risk factor is asbestos exposure (asbestosis), not silicosis.
questions.keyConcept: False: Mesothelioma is predisposed to by silicosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Empyema means pus in the pleural cavity.
questions.explanation: Empyema is defined as the accumulation of pus within the pleural cavity, typically as a complication of pneumonia, lung abscess, or bronchiectasis.
questions.keyConcept: True: Empyema means pus in the pleural cavity.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Secondary pleural tumors are less common than primary pleural tumors.
questions.explanation: Secondary (metastatic) pleural tumors, which seed the pleura from other primary sites (lung, breast, etc.), are far more common than primary pleural tumors such as mesothelioma.
questions.keyConcept: False: Secondary pleural tumors are less common than primary pleural tumors.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Malignant mesothelioma is always of the papillary type.
questions.explanation: Malignant mesothelioma has multiple histologic patterns (epithelial/papillary-tubular, sarcomatoid, and biphasic/mixed) — it is not always papillary.
questions.keyConcept: False: Malignant mesothelioma is always of the papillary type.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Match each type of inflammation with its classic respiratory example.
questions.explanation: This set links inflammation types (catarrhal, membranous, granulomatous, suppurative, fibrinous) to their classic respiratory-tract examples: membranous = diphtheria, granulomatous = rhinoscleroma, suppurative = bronchopneumonia, fibrinous = lobar pneumonia, based on the answer key pattern Bc, Cd, Da, Eb.
questions.keyConcept: Match each premise by the specific relationship tested in “Match each type of inflammation with its classic respiratory example”; do not apply one rule to every pair.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Match each laryngeal/nasal lesion with its correct classification.
questions.explanation: This links laryngeal/nasal lesions to their classification: singer's nodule = non-specific inflammatory, squamous papilloma = precancerous, quinsy = suppurative, rhinoscleroma = granulomatous, angiofibroma = hamartomatous/vascular tumor-like lesion, per answer key Ab, Ba, Cd, De.
questions.keyConcept: Match each premise by the specific relationship tested in “Match each laryngeal/nasal lesion with its correct classification”; do not apply one rule to every pair.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Match each pathologic process with its mechanism.
questions.explanation: This links pathologic pulmonary processes to their causative mechanisms: bronchiectasis = infection+obstruction, gangrene = necrosis+putrefaction, collapse = complete obstruction, emphysema = partial (ball-valve) obstruction, per answer key Ac, Bd, Ca, Db.
questions.keyConcept: Match each premise by the specific relationship tested in “Match each pathologic process with its mechanism”; do not apply one rule to every pair.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Match each lung tumor with its characteristic feature.
questions.explanation: This links major bronchogenic tumor types to their hallmark features, per answer key Ab, Bc, Ca, Dd (as adapted to available options).
questions.keyConcept: Match each premise by the specific relationship tested in “Match each lung tumor with its characteristic feature”; do not apply one rule to every pair.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Match each pleural condition with its description.

pairs.target: Serous fluid in the pleural cavity

questions.explanation: This links pleural fluid collections to their contents: empyema = pus, haemothorax = blood, chylothorax = lymph, hydrothorax = serous fluid, per answer key Ac, Ba, Cd, Db (as adapted to available options).
questions.keyConcept: Match each premise by the specific relationship tested in “Match each pleural condition with its description”; do not apply one rule to every pair.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Match each pneumonia type with its characteristic pattern.

pairs.target: Fibrinosuppurative exudate filling an entire lobe
Necrotizing infection, often right-sided, from aspirated material

questions.explanation: This links pneumonia types to their characteristic distribution/histologic pattern, per answer key Ad, Bc, Ca, Db (as adapted to available options).
questions.keyConcept: Match each premise by the specific relationship tested in “Match each pneumonia type with its characteristic pattern”; do not apply one rule to every pair.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Match each occupational lung disease with its exposure.
questions.explanation: This links pneumoconioses to their causative occupational dust exposures: silicosis-silica, asbestosis-asbestos, anthracosis-coal dust, berylliosis-beryllium, per answer key Ab, Bc, Cd, Da (as adapted to available options).
questions.keyConcept: Match each premise by the specific relationship tested in “Match each occupational lung disease with its exposure”; do not apply one rule to every pair.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Match each interstitial lung disease with its defining histologic feature.

pairs.target: Temporally uniform cellular or fibrosing pattern
Intra-alveolar Masson bodies (organizing connective tissue plugs)

questions.explanation: This links the major idiopathic interstitial pneumonias/granulomatous disease to their defining histology: UIP = temporal heterogeneity/honeycombing, NSIP = uniform pattern, COP = Masson bodies, sarcoidosis = non-caseating granulomas, per answer key Ac, Bb, Ca, Dd (as adapted to available options).
questions.keyConcept: Match each premise by the specific relationship tested in “Match each interstitial lung disease with its defining histologic feature”; do not apply one rule to every pair.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Mention the pathological features of the common cold.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Gross: the nasal mucosa is red, edematous, and thickened.
- Microscopic: there is dense infiltration with numerous neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and some eosinophils.
questions.keyConcept: The common cold produces a nonspecific acute inflammatory reaction (edema plus a mixed neutrophil/lymphocyte/plasma cell/eosinophil infiltrate) rather than any single pathognomonic histologic pattern.
questions.explanation: Because the gross and microscopic findings are nonspecific, diagnosis of the common cold remains clinical; pathology here mainly explains the mechanism behind nasal congestion and discharge.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Enumerate causes of suppurative pleuritis (empyema).
questions.modelAnswer:
- Spread from pyogenic infection in the lung (parapneumonic empyema).
- Direct extension from a subdiaphragmatic or liver abscess.
- Spread by the hematogenous or lymphatic route.
questions.keyConcept: Empyema most often results from direct spread of a pyogenic lung infection into the pleural space, making it a common complication of untreated or inadequately treated pneumonia.
questions.explanation: Recognizing pneumonia as the leading antecedent is why persistent fever or pleuritic pain during pneumonia treatment should prompt evaluation for a developing empyema.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Define chylothorax.
questions.modelAnswer: It is the accumulation of milky lymphatic fluid containing microscopic fat globules in the pleural cavity, most often caused by malignancy within the thoracic cavity (distant cancers metastasizing via lymphatics into the thoracic duct) or by trauma/obstruction of the thoracic duct.
questions.keyConcept: Chylothorax is defined by its lipid-rich, milky lymphatic fluid, distinguishing it from the serous transudate of hydrothorax and the pus-laden exudate of empyema.
questions.explanation: The milky, fat-rich character of the fluid is what triggers a workup for thoracic duct injury or lymphatic obstruction by malignancy, rather than heart, liver, or renal failure.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What are the pathological features of emphysema?
questions.modelAnswer:
- Gross: in panacinar emphysema, the lung is pale and voluminous, mostly affecting the lower lobes; in centriacinar emphysema, the lung is less pale and less voluminous than the panacinar type, present mostly in the upper two-thirds.
- Microscopic: destruction of the alveolar walls without fibrosis, leading to enlarged air spaces; the number of alveolar capillaries is diminished.
questions.keyConcept: Emphysema is defined microscopically by alveolar wall destruction without fibrosis, which is what distinguishes it from fibrotic restrictive lung diseases that also enlarge or distort air spaces.
questions.explanation: The absence of fibrosis alongside loss of alveolar surface area and capillaries explains why emphysema causes irreversible airflow limitation with impaired gas exchange, rather than a restrictive pattern.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Mention the cause of mediastinal (interstitial) emphysema.
questions.modelAnswer: It is caused by entry of air into the interstitium of the lung, or entry into the mediastinum and the subcutaneous connective tissue, along the lobular septa and margins of lobules.
questions.keyConcept: Mediastinal (interstitial) emphysema results from air tracking along tissue planes rather than from alveolar wall destruction, making it mechanistically distinct from true emphysema despite the shared name.
questions.explanation: Understanding this air-tracking mechanism explains why interstitial emphysema can follow barotrauma or chest trauma and present with subcutaneous crepitus far from the original site of air leak.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Define chronic bronchitis.
questions.modelAnswer: It is a clinical diagnosis defined by persistent cough with sputum production for at least 3 months in at least 2 consecutive years, in the absence of any other identifiable cause; the underlying cause is often unknown and it may be associated with scarring and spontaneous pneumothorax.
questions.keyConcept: Chronic bronchitis is defined purely clinically (a time-based cough/sputum criterion), not histologically, which is why the diagnosis can be made before any biopsy or imaging is performed.
questions.explanation: Because the definition is symptom/time-based rather than pathological, it is possible to clinically diagnose chronic bronchitis in a patient who has not yet developed the gland hyperplasia seen on microscopy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What are the complications of asbestos exposure?
questions.modelAnswer:
- Pleural effusion.
- Localized fibrous plaque or diffuse pleural fibrosis.
- Mesothelioma.
- Progressive massive fibrosis: interstitial fibrosis in the lower lobes and subpleural areas that coalesces to form large areas; contraction of the fibrous tissue distorts the normal architecture, creating enlarged air spaces enclosed by fibrosis (honeycomb appearance).
- Bronchogenic carcinoma.
- Laryngeal carcinoma.
questions.keyConcept: Asbestos exposure produces both benign pleural disease (plaques, effusion) and malignant disease (mesothelioma, bronchogenic and laryngeal carcinoma), so pleural plaques on imaging should prompt screening for the malignant complications, not just reassurance.
questions.explanation: Because mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma can occur decades after exposure, recognizing this latency is essential for long-term surveillance of asbestos-exposed workers.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Mention the types of silicosis.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Acute silicosis.
- Chronic silicosis: fibrotic nodules of concentrically arranged hyaline collagen fibers, which is quite distinctive; examination of these nodules under polarized light reveals birefringent silica particles.
questions.keyConcept: Chronic silicosis is histologically distinctive because of its concentrically arranged hyaline collagen nodules and birefringent silica particles visible under polarized light, unlike the less specific fibrosis of other pneumoconioses.
questions.explanation: This distinctive birefringent-particle appearance under polarized light is the practical way pathologists confirm silica as the causative dust rather than another inhaled mineral.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What are the characteristic features of large cell carcinoma of the lung?
questions.modelAnswer: Cancer cells are large, with abundant cytoplasm, large nuclei, and conspicuous nucleoli.
questions.keyConcept: Large cell carcinoma is essentially a diagnosis of exclusion among non-small-cell lung cancers, defined by large undifferentiated cells that lack the specific glandular or squamous features seen in adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma.
questions.explanation: Because it lacks distinguishing glandular or squamous differentiation, large cell carcinoma is diagnosed only after adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma have been excluded on morphology and immunohistochemistry.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Mention 4 suppurative lung diseases.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Bacterial pneumonia.
- Lung abscess.
- Empyema.
- Bronchiectasis (and lung gangrene in severe necrotizing infection).
questions.keyConcept: Suppurative lung diseases share a common thread of bacterial infection producing pus/necrosis, but differ by location and chronicity: pneumonia is parenchymal, abscess is a localized cavity, empyema is pleural, and bronchiectasis is a chronic airway process.
questions.explanation: Distinguishing these by location (parenchyma vs. pleura vs. airway) explains why they need different management, ranging from antibiotics alone to surgical drainage.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Select the fastest-acting inhaled bronchodilator used in asthma
questions.explanation: Inhaled salbutamol is a short-acting beta2 agonist with rapid bronchodilator onset. Salmeterol and tiotropium are maintenance drugs, while ipratropium acts more slowly.
questions.keyConcept: Inhaled salbutamol is a short-acting beta2 agonist with rapid bronchodilator onset

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The safest drug to relieve an acute attack of asthma in a cardiac patient is
questions.explanation: Ipratropium produces bronchodilation with little direct beta1 cardiac stimulation. Beta agonists, epinephrine, and theophylline more readily provoke tachycardia or arrhythmia.
questions.keyConcept: Ipratropium produces bronchodilation with little direct beta1 cardiac stimulation

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All of the following inhibit mast-cell degranulation except
questions.explanation: Penicillin is an antibacterial drug and can itself trigger IgE-mediated allergy rather than stabilize mast cells. Cromolyn and nedocromil are mast-cell stabilizers, and beta2 agonists can reduce mediator release.
questions.keyConcept: Penicillin is an antibacterial drug and can itself trigger IgE-mediated allergy rather than stabilize mast cells

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All of the following are long-term controllers used in asthma except
questions.explanation: Salbutamol is a rapid reliever and does not control chronic airway inflammation. Budesonide, montelukast, and cromolyn are controller therapies.
questions.keyConcept: Salbutamol is a rapid reliever and does not control chronic airway inflammation

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is not a side effect of beta2 agonists
questions.explanation: Beta2 agonists drive potassium into cells and may cause hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia. Tremor, anxiety, tachycardia, and reduced responsiveness with overuse can occur.
questions.keyConcept: Beta2 agonists drive potassium into cells and may cause hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Compared with inhaled beta2 agonists, inhaled anticholinergics
options: Are more effective in bronchial asthma
Are better suited for an acute asthma attack
Produce a slower response in bronchial asthma
questions.explanation: Inhaled antimuscarinics generally bronchodilate more slowly than short-acting beta2 agonists in asthma. They are particularly useful in COPD and as adjuncts in severe exacerbations.
questions.keyConcept: Inhaled antimuscarinics generally bronchodilate more slowly than short-acting beta2 agonists in asthma

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All statements regarding theophylline are true except
options: It inhibits phosphodiesterase and increases cyclic AMP
questions.explanation: Erythromycin inhibits theophylline metabolism and can raise, not lower, serum concentrations. Smoking induces metabolism and may lower theophylline exposure.
questions.keyConcept: Erythromycin inhibits theophylline metabolism and can raise, not lower, serum concentrations

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Selecting a theophylline dose depends on all the following except
options: Congestive heart failure or cor pulmonale
questions.explanation: Theophylline is chiefly cleared by hepatic metabolism, so smoking, liver disease, and heart failure materially alter dosing. Isolated renal insufficiency usually has much less effect on parent-drug clearance.
questions.keyConcept: Theophylline is chiefly cleared by hepatic metabolism, so smoking, liver disease, and heart failure materially alter dosing

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Theophylline toxicities include all the following except
questions.explanation: Theophylline toxicity causes gastrointestinal upset, insomnia, tachyarrhythmias, and seizures. It does not characteristically cause hyperkalemia.
questions.keyConcept: Theophylline toxicity causes gastrointestinal upset, insomnia, tachyarrhythmias, and seizures

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Theophylline is not first-line therapy in asthma for all reasons except
questions.explanation: Theophylline can be administered orally. Its narrow therapeutic index, interactions, and need for monitoring limit routine use.
questions.keyConcept: Theophylline can be administered orally

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All the following dilate bronchi during an acute asthmatic attack except
questions.explanation: Nedocromil is a prophylactic anti-inflammatory mast-cell stabilizer and is not an acute bronchodilator. Salbutamol and ipratropium provide bronchodilation, while theophylline has bronchodilator activity but is rarely preferred acutely.
questions.keyConcept: Nedocromil is a prophylactic anti-inflammatory mast-cell stabilizer and is not an acute bronchodilator

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A drug used in asthma that induces hoarseness and candidiasis is
questions.explanation: Inhaled fluticasone can cause dysphonia and oropharyngeal candidiasis from local glucocorticoid deposition. Rinsing the mouth and using a spacer reduce these effects.
questions.keyConcept: Inhaled fluticasone can cause dysphonia and oropharyngeal candidiasis from local glucocorticoid deposition

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All reduce corticosteroid adverse effects in asthma except
options: Giving oral medication late in the afternoon
Restricting oral therapy to severe uncontrolled cases
questions.explanation: Systemic glucocorticoids are generally timed in the morning to better match circadian cortisol and reduce adrenal suppression. Spacers, mouth rinsing, and limiting systemic exposure reduce toxicity.
questions.keyConcept: Systemic glucocorticoids are generally timed in the morning to better match circadian cortisol and reduce adrenal suppression

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All statements about ciclesonide are true except
options: It is a prodrug activated by airway esterases
High first-pass metabolism and protein binding reduce systemic effects
questions.explanation: Ciclesonide is an inhaled corticosteroid controller, not a bronchodilator. Local activation and high first-pass metabolism help limit systemic and oropharyngeal effects.
questions.keyConcept: Ciclesonide is an inhaled corticosteroid controller, not a bronchodilator

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Therapeutic uses of cromolyn do not include
questions.explanation: Cromolyn is a weak prophylactic agent suitable for mild allergic disease, not severe persistent asthma. It can be used topically for allergic rhinitis and conjunctivitis.
questions.keyConcept: Cromolyn is a weak prophylactic agent suitable for mild allergic disease, not severe persistent asthma

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is not an adverse effect of inhaled cromolyn
questions.explanation: Cromolyn can irritate the airway and cause cough, throat irritation, or bronchospasm. Oral candidiasis is associated with inhaled corticosteroids, not cromolyn.
questions.keyConcept: Cromolyn can irritate the airway and cause cough, throat irritation, or bronchospasm

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Reflex bronchoconstriction is most likely with inhalation therapy using
options: Metered-dose spray of drug in solution
questions.explanation: Dry-powder inhalation may irritate hyperresponsive airways and trigger reflex bronchoconstriction. Aerosol formulation and delivery device influence local airway irritation.
questions.keyConcept: Dry-powder inhalation may irritate hyperresponsive airways and trigger reflex bronchoconstriction

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Advantages of epinephrine in anaphylaxis include all except
options: Wide safety margin with reduced arrhythmia risk
questions.explanation: Epinephrine reverses bronchospasm, mucosal edema, and hypotension through beta2 and alpha1 effects. It does not have a wide safety margin and can cause tachyarrhythmias.
questions.keyConcept: Epinephrine reverses bronchospasm, mucosal edema, and hypotension through beta2 and alpha1 effects

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Salmeterol may be used in a patient on as-needed salbutamol plus inhaled beclomethasone as
options: A replacement for the inhaled corticosteroid
questions.explanation: Salmeterol is a long-acting beta2 agonist used as maintenance add-on therapy to an inhaled corticosteroid. Its slower onset makes it unsuitable as rescue medication.
questions.keyConcept: Salmeterol is a long-acting beta2 agonist used as maintenance add-on therapy to an inhaled corticosteroid

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The drug that should not be given alone and should be combined with an inhaled corticosteroid for asthma control is
questions.explanation: A long-acting beta2 agonist such as salmeterol should not be used as asthma monotherapy because it does not treat airway inflammation. It should be paired with an inhaled corticosteroid.
questions.keyConcept: A long-acting beta2 agonist such as salmeterol should not be used as asthma monotherapy because it does not treat airway inflammation

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Severe acute asthma with acidosis and hypoxia remains refractory to repeated salbutamol and causes dangerous tachycardia; the next useful measure is
questions.explanation: Systemic corticosteroids treat the inflammatory component of a severe exacerbation and reduce relapse, although onset is delayed. More adrenergic agonist may worsen tachycardia, and cromolyn is not a rescue drug.
questions.keyConcept: Systemic corticosteroids treat the inflammatory component of a severe exacerbation and reduce relapse, although onset is delayed

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which is least preferred in status asthmaticus
questions.explanation: Intravenous theophylline has limited added benefit and substantial toxicity in status asthmaticus. Repeated inhaled beta2 agonist, ipratropium, oxygen, and systemic corticosteroid are standard components.
questions.keyConcept: Intravenous theophylline has limited added benefit and substantial toxicity in status asthmaticus

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which statement concerning asthma is wrong
options: Ipratropium is relatively cardiac-safe for acute bronchodilation
Tiotropium is used for long-term COPD management
Theophylline dosing is affected more by hepatic than renal dysfunction
Bambuterol is a prodrug given only by inhalation
