questions.explanation: Urgent management requires diphtheria antitoxin plus antibiotics and airway support; none of the listed single choices provides the required immediate antitoxin treatment.
questions.keyConcept: None of the above — the decisive fact for “The urgent treatment of diphtheria among the listed choices is.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with a tonsillar pseudomembrane has a Gram-stained throat swab. Which finding is expected?
questions.explanation: Corynebacterium diphtheriae appears as pleomorphic club-shaped Gram-positive rods, often in palisades or Chinese-letter arrangements.
questions.keyConcept: Gram-positive club-shaped bacilli — the decisive fact for “A patient with a tonsillar pseudomembrane has a Gram-stained throat swab. Which finding is expected.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A child has perforated otitis media with Gram-positive diplococci and alpha-hemolytic, catalase-negative colonies. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is an alpha-hemolytic, catalase-negative Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococcus and a common cause of acute otitis media.
questions.keyConcept: Streptococcus pneumoniae — the decisive fact for “A child has perforated otitis media with Gram-positive diplococci and alpha-hemolytic, catalase-negative colonies. Which organism is most likely.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A college student has purulent nasal discharge, headache, and facial pain. Which organism is the most likely bacterial cause?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a major bacterial cause of acute sinusitis.
questions.keyConcept: Streptococcus pneumoniae — the decisive fact for “A college student has purulent nasal discharge, headache, and facial pain. Which organism is the most likely bacterial….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An underimmunized child has fever, odynophagia, dysphagia, and pleomorphic Gram-negative bacilli in a good-quality sputum sample. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The specimen is too contaminated by saliva
questions.explanation: Pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli in an inflammatory respiratory specimen are compatible with Haemophilus influenzae.
questions.keyConcept: The appearance suggests Haemophilus influenzae — the decisive fact for “An underimmunized child has fever, odynophagia, dysphagia, and pleomorphic Gram-negative bacilli in a good-quality sputum sample. Which interpretation….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 4-year-old has hoarseness, dyspnea, barking cough, and inspiratory stridor. What is the most probable causative agent?
questions.explanation: Human parainfluenza virus is the classic cause of croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) with barking cough and inspiratory stridor.
questions.keyConcept: Human parainfluenza virus — the decisive fact for “A 4-year-old has hoarseness, dyspnea, barking cough, and inspiratory stridor. What is the most probable causative agent.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A child with barking cough has an etiologic helical virus with a linear RNA genome. Which disease is most commonly associated with this virus?
questions.explanation: Parainfluenza is an enveloped negative-sense RNA virus with helical nucleocapsid and is strongly associated with croup.
questions.keyConcept: Croup — the decisive fact for “A child with barking cough has an etiologic helical virus with a linear RNA genome. Which disease is….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 2-year-old with respiratory difficulty, tachypnea, tachycardia, and stridor undergoes rapid antigen testing. Antibodies should be directed against which parainfluenza antigen?
questions.explanation: Parainfluenza surface HN glycoprotein combines hemagglutinin and neuraminidase activities and is a useful antigenic target.
questions.keyConcept: Hemagglutinin-neuraminidase — the decisive fact for “A 2-year-old with respiratory difficulty, tachypnea, tachycardia, and stridor undergoes rapid antigen testing. Antibodies should be directed against….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which parainfluenza viral protein is responsible for syncytium formation?
questions.explanation: The fusion (F) protein promotes fusion of infected cells and formation of multinucleated syncytia.
questions.keyConcept: F protein — the decisive fact for “parainfluenza viral protein is responsible for syncytium formation.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A child has a progressively worsening paroxysmal cough with posttussive vomiting and marked lymphocytosis. Which feature best characterizes the organism?
options: It produces a toxin that raises cAMP and increases mucus production
It produces a phage-encoded toxin that blocks protein synthesis
questions.explanation: Bordetella pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Gi, increasing cAMP; associated toxins and inflammation increase respiratory secretions and produce lymphocytosis.
questions.keyConcept: It produces a toxin that raises cAMP and increases mucus production — the decisive fact for “A child has a progressively worsening paroxysmal cough with posttussive vomiting and marked lymphocytosis. Which feature best characterizes….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A pernasal swab is collected from a child with whooping cough. What is the best diagnostic approach?
options: Demonstration of bipolarity in methylene-blue stain
questions.explanation: PCR of a nasopharyngeal specimen is a sensitive rapid test for Bordetella pertussis, particularly early in disease.
questions.keyConcept: PCR — the decisive fact for “A pernasal swab is collected from a child with whooping cough. What is the best diagnostic approach.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which virulence factor causes the marked lymphocytosis of pertussis?
questions.explanation: Pertussis toxin inhibits Gi signaling and causes lymphocytosis by impairing lymphocyte trafficking from blood into lymphoid tissue.
questions.keyConcept: Pertussis toxin — the decisive fact for “virulence factor causes the marked lymphocytosis of pertussis.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement about whooping-cough vaccine is correct?
options: Killed whole-cell vaccine is very safe
The acellular vaccine contains capsular polysaccharide
The safest form contains small amounts of four antigens
questions.explanation: Acellular pertussis vaccines contain selected purified antigens and are less reactogenic than killed whole-cell preparations.
questions.keyConcept: The safest form contains small amounts of four antigens — the decisive fact for “statement about whooping-cough vaccine is correct.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A small Gram-negative respiratory rod produces an exotoxin that reduces phagocyte bactericidal activity; its vaccine induces antibodies to four proteins including the exotoxin. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Bordetella pertussis is a small Gram-negative coccobacillus; acellular vaccines include pertussis toxoid and other adhesin antigens.
questions.keyConcept: Bordetella pertussis — the decisive fact for “A small Gram-negative respiratory rod produces an exotoxin that reduces phagocyte bactericidal activity; its vaccine induces antibodies to….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: For which bacterial vaccine are toxic adverse effects an important concern?
questions.explanation: Killed whole-cell pertussis vaccine is substantially more reactogenic than acellular pertussis formulations.
questions.keyConcept: Killed whole-cell Bordetella pertussis vaccine — the decisive fact for “For which bacterial vaccine are toxic adverse effects an important concern.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 2-month-old with fever, persistent cough, wheezing, cyanosis, and radiographic pneumonia most likely has infection with which virus?
questions.explanation: RSV is the leading cause of bronchiolitis and an important cause of pneumonia in young infants.
questions.keyConcept: Respiratory syncytial virus — the decisive fact for “A 2-month-old with fever, persistent cough, wheezing, cyanosis, and radiographic pneumonia most likely has infection with which virus.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A virus is isolated from a 2-month-old treated for bronchiolitis. Which virus could be the etiologic agent?
questions.explanation: RSV is the classic etiologic agent of infant bronchiolitis.
questions.keyConcept: Respiratory syncytial virus — the decisive fact for “A virus is isolated from a 2-month-old treated for bronchiolitis. Which virus could be the etiologic agent.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which RSV protein is responsible for viral attachment?
questions.explanation: The RSV G glycoprotein mediates attachment to respiratory epithelial cells; F protein mediates fusion and syncytia.
questions.keyConcept: G protein — the decisive fact for “RSV protein is responsible for viral attachment.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which RSV antigen is targeted by preventive monoclonal antibodies?
questions.explanation: Palivizumab and newer RSV monoclonal prophylaxis target the fusion (F) protein.
questions.keyConcept: Fusion protein — the decisive fact for “RSV antigen is targeted by preventive monoclonal antibodies.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement concerning RSV is incorrect?
options: It has a single-stranded RNA genome
It causes pneumonia primarily in infants
RT-PCR is the most sensitive diagnostic method
questions.explanation: RSV commonly causes bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants, but the wording that it causes pneumonia primarily in infants is the keyed incorrect statement in this source set.
questions.keyConcept: It causes pneumonia primarily in infants — the decisive fact for “statement concerning RSV is incorrect.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with chronic cough, weight loss, fever, hemoptysis, and acid-fast bacilli has tuberculosis. What is the main virulence feature of the organism?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives within macrophages by resisting phagolysosomal killing, allowing persistent intracellular infection.
questions.keyConcept: Intracellular survival inside phagocytes — the decisive fact for “A patient with chronic cough, weight loss, fever, hemoptysis, and acid-fast bacilli has tuberculosis. What is the main….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which is an important virulence factor of Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: Mycolic acids form the lipid-rich acid-fast cell wall and contribute to resistance against chemicals and host defenses.
questions.keyConcept: Mycolic acid — the decisive fact for “is an important virulence factor of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Why are mycobacteria described as acid-fast?
options: They are rapidly decolorized by acid-alcohol
Once stained, they resist decolorization with acid-alcohol
questions.explanation: The mycolic-acid-rich cell wall retains carbol fuchsin despite acid-alcohol decolorization.
questions.keyConcept: Once stained, they resist decolorization with acid-alcohol — the decisive fact for “are mycobacteria described as acid-fast.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient has granulomas, giant cells, and acid-fast bacilli; a close relative had tuberculosis. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Granulomatous pulmonary disease with acid-fast bacilli is characteristic of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
questions.keyConcept: Mycobacterium tuberculosis — the decisive fact for “A patient has granulomas, giant cells, and acid-fast bacilli; a close relative had tuberculosis. Which organism is most….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis should also be evaluated for which condition?
questions.explanation: HIV testing is essential because impaired cell-mediated immunity greatly increases tuberculosis risk and modifies management.
questions.keyConcept: HIV/AIDS — the decisive fact for “A patient diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis should also be evaluated for which condition.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A sputum acid-fast smear is positive but the tuberculin test is negative. How can definitive diagnosis be obtained?
questions.explanation: Culture on an egg-based medium such as Lowenstein-Jensen confirms viable Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
questions.keyConcept: Culture on egg-containing medium — the decisive fact for “A sputum acid-fast smear is positive but the tuberculin test is negative. How can definitive diagnosis be obtained.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the most rapid method listed for diagnosing active tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: Direct acid-fast staining provides the fastest immediate result among the listed methods, although molecular tests are more sensitive.
questions.keyConcept: Acid-fast stain — the decisive fact for “is the most rapid method listed for diagnosing active tuberculosis.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with an old tuberculosis lesion has household contacts. What is the first screening action listed for family members?
questions.explanation: An interferon-gamma release assay is an accepted test for tuberculosis infection, particularly in BCG-vaccinated contacts.
questions.keyConcept: Interferon-gamma assay — the decisive fact for “A patient with an old tuberculosis lesion has household contacts. What is the first screening action listed for….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which TST result should receive latent-tuberculosis treatment according to the printed key?
questions.explanation: The keyed source applies the 10-mm occupational-risk threshold to microbiology laboratory personnel.
questions.keyConcept: Microbiology laboratory worker with 10 mm — the decisive fact for “TST result should receive latent-tuberculosis treatment according to the printed key.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In pneumococcal pneumonia, which factor releases inflammatory fragments from the organism and promotes lung damage?
questions.explanation: Autolysin releases cell-wall fragments and pneumolysin, amplifying inflammation and lung injury.
questions.keyConcept: Autolysin — the decisive fact for “In pneumococcal pneumonia, which factor releases inflammatory fragments from the organism and promotes lung damage.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which pneumococcal factor directly damages cellular membranes?
questions.explanation: Pneumolysin is a cholesterol-dependent pore-forming toxin that damages host-cell membranes.
questions.keyConcept: Pneumolysin — the decisive fact for “pneumococcal factor directly damages cellular membranes.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the major contribution of the pneumococcal capsule to virulence?
options: Need for anticapsular antibody to permit opsonization
questions.explanation: The capsule resists phagocytosis; type-specific anticapsular antibody enables effective opsonization and clearance.
questions.keyConcept: Need for anticapsular antibody to permit opsonization — the decisive fact for “is the major contribution of the pneumococcal capsule to virulence.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which mechanism is central to pneumococcal pathogenesis?
options: Inhibition of phagocytosis by polysaccharide capsule
questions.explanation: The polysaccharide capsule is antiphagocytic and is the principal determinant of pneumococcal virulence.
questions.keyConcept: Inhibition of phagocytosis by polysaccharide capsule — the decisive fact for “mechanism is central to pneumococcal pathogenesis.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: How can pneumococcus be typed in the laboratory?
questions.explanation: The Quellung reaction demonstrates type-specific capsular swelling with antisera.
questions.keyConcept: Quellung capsular-swelling reaction — the decisive fact for “can pneumococcus be typed in the laboratory.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which intervention prevents invasive pneumococcal disease in an appropriate older or high-risk adult?
questions.explanation: PPSV23 contains purified capsular polysaccharides from 23 pneumococcal serotypes and is used in selected adults.
questions.keyConcept: 23-valent capsular polysaccharide vaccine — the decisive fact for “intervention prevents invasive pneumococcal disease in an appropriate older or high-risk adult.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The pneumococcal conjugate vaccine is recommended to which groups according to the source?
options: High-risk people older than two years
All ages older than two months
Both immunocompromised patients and children younger than five years
questions.explanation: Conjugate vaccines are effective in young children and are important in selected immunocompromised or high-risk groups.
questions.keyConcept: Both immunocompromised patients and children younger than five years — the decisive fact for “The pneumococcal conjugate vaccine is recommended to which groups according to the source.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient hospitalized after smoke inhalation develops ventilator-associated pneumonia. Sputum grows strict-aerobic, oxidase-positive Gram-negative rods. Which organism is responsible?
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an oxidase-positive, nonfermenting aerobic Gram-negative rod and an important ventilator-associated pathogen.
questions.keyConcept: Pseudomonas aeruginosa — the decisive fact for “A patient hospitalized after smoke inhalation develops ventilator-associated pneumonia. Sputum grows strict-aerobic, oxidase-positive Gram-negative rods. Which organism is….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement best describes the airway behavior of Pseudomonas growing on routine media in this setting?
options: It tightly adheres to epithelial cells
It produces pyocyanin that damages epithelium
questions.explanation: Pyocyanin generates oxidative injury, impairs ciliary function, and damages respiratory epithelium; Pseudomonas is not an obligate intracellular organism.
questions.keyConcept: It produces pyocyanin that damages epithelium — the decisive fact for “statement best describes the airway behavior of Pseudomonas growing on routine media in this setting.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A postoperative patient develops pneumonia from a Gram-negative rod that produces green pigment and does not ferment carbohydrates. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a nonfermenter that produces blue-green pigments including pyocyanin.
questions.keyConcept: Pseudomonas aeruginosa — the decisive fact for “A postoperative patient develops pneumonia from a Gram-negative rod that produces green pigment and does not ferment carbohydrates.….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the main characteristic of Pseudomonas aeruginosa among the listed options?
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a highly drug-resistant opportunistic pathogen, especially in hospitalized, burned, neutropenic, and cystic-fibrosis patients.
questions.keyConcept: Opportunistic pathogenicity — the decisive fact for “is the main characteristic of Pseudomonas aeruginosa among the listed options.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which is a characteristic of Pseudomonas aeruginosa?
options: Capsule as its main virulence factor
Can cause septic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation through endotoxin
questions.explanation: As a Gram-negative bacillus, Pseudomonas lipopolysaccharide can trigger septic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
questions.keyConcept: Can cause septic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation through endotoxin — the decisive fact for “is a characteristic of Pseudomonas aeruginosa.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Pathogenicity of Pseudomonas is due to which factors?
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas virulence is multifactorial and includes endotoxin, exotoxin A, biofilm alginate, elastases, and proteases.
questions.keyConcept: All of the above — the decisive fact for “Pathogenicity of Pseudomonas is due to which factors.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which condition predisposes to Pseudomonas pneumonia?
questions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis airways are commonly colonized by mucoid Pseudomonas, causing chronic destructive infection.
questions.keyConcept: Cystic fibrosis — the decisive fact for “condition predisposes to Pseudomonas pneumonia.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the primary function of the structure producing Klebsiella mucoid colonies?
questions.explanation: The thick polysaccharide capsule is antiphagocytic until specific antibody and complement opsonize the organism.
questions.keyConcept: Resists phagocytosis unless opsonized — the decisive fact for “is the primary function of the structure producing Klebsiella mucoid colonies.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with lung cancer develops atypical pneumonia. Sputum Gram stain is unremarkable, but small Gram-negative rods grow on charcoal-yeast-extract agar. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Legionella grows on buffered charcoal yeast extract containing iron and cysteine and often stains poorly with Gram stain.
questions.keyConcept: Legionella pneumophila — the decisive fact for “A patient with lung cancer develops atypical pneumonia. Sputum Gram stain is unremarkable, but small Gram-negative rods grow….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with fever, dry cough, dyspnea, myalgia, and diffuse infiltrate should be rapidly tested for Legionella by which method?
questions.explanation: Urinary antigen testing rapidly detects Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 and is widely used in clinical diagnosis.
questions.keyConcept: Urinary antigen detection — the decisive fact for “A patient with fever, dry cough, dyspnea, myalgia, and diffuse infiltrate should be rapidly tested for Legionella by….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient develops severe atypical pneumonia after exposure to a misty water fountain. Which test most sensitively identifies the suspected organism among these options?
options: Respiratory culture on charcoal-based nutrient agar
questions.explanation: Urinary antigen testing is rapid and sensitive for common Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 infection.
questions.keyConcept: Urinary antigen detection — the decisive fact for “A patient develops severe atypical pneumonia after exposure to a misty water fountain. Which test most sensitively identifies….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which finding would support Legionella pneumophila infection?
options: Direct fluorescent antibody in BAL fluid
Leukocytes with no visible bacteria on Gram stain
questions.explanation: Legionella may be detected by urinary antigen, special culture, or fluorescent methods and often produces inflammatory sputum without visible organisms on Gram stain.
questions.keyConcept: All of the above — the decisive fact for “finding would support Legionella pneumophila infection.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An older smoker has pneumonia; sputum contains neutrophils and the organism grows on buffered charcoal yeast extract but not blood agar. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Legionella requires buffered charcoal yeast extract supplemented with iron and cysteine and does not grow on routine blood agar.
questions.keyConcept: Legionella pneumophila — the decisive fact for “An older smoker has pneumonia; sputum contains neutrophils and the organism grows on buffered charcoal yeast extract but….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement about Legionnaires disease is correct?
options: It is caused by an obligate intracellular bacterium
It results from contaminated milk consumption
It may be associated with renal failure
It is diagnosed by cold agglutinins
questions.explanation: Legionellosis can produce extrapulmonary findings including hyponatremia, gastrointestinal symptoms, elevated liver enzymes, and renal dysfunction.
questions.keyConcept: It may be associated with renal failure — the decisive fact for “statement about Legionnaires disease is correct.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A college student has malaise, low-grade fever, harsh cough, and interstitial pneumonia; the white count is normal. What is most likely?
questions.explanation: Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes walking pneumonia with mild systemic findings despite patchy interstitial infiltrates.
questions.keyConcept: Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection — the decisive fact for “A college student has malaise, low-grade fever, harsh cough, and interstitial pneumonia; the white count is normal. What….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: How can Mycoplasma pneumoniae be confirmed sensitively after routine sputum cultures show normal flora?
options: PCR for an organism lacking a cell wall
questions.explanation: PCR directly detects Mycoplasma nucleic acid and is more specific than nonspecific cold agglutinins.
questions.keyConcept: PCR for an organism lacking a cell wall — the decisive fact for “can Mycoplasma pneumoniae be confirmed sensitively after routine sputum cultures show normal flora.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which bacterium is a frequent cause of outbreaks of community-acquired atypical pneumonia in young adults?
questions.explanation: Mycoplasma pneumoniae commonly causes outbreaks of walking pneumonia in schools, colleges, and military settings.
questions.keyConcept: Mycoplasma pneumoniae — the decisive fact for “bacterium is a frequent cause of outbreaks of community-acquired atypical pneumonia in young adults.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement about Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia is incorrect?
options: Specific IgM or PCR can diagnose it
Chronic infection is common because the organism replicates intracellularly
CARDS toxin promotes inflammation and airway obstruction
It cannot be cultured in vitro because it lacks a cell wall
questions.explanation: Mycoplasma can be cultured on specialized sterol-containing media; lack of a cell wall does not prevent in-vitro growth, though culture is slow and impractical.
questions.keyConcept: It cannot be cultured in vitro because it lacks a cell wall — the decisive fact for “statement about Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia is incorrect.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: If Chlamydia pneumoniae is suspected, which method can detect the organism?
options: Culture of respiratory secretions in tissue-culture cells
questions.explanation: Chlamydiae are obligate intracellular bacteria and can be propagated in susceptible tissue-culture cells.
questions.keyConcept: Culture of respiratory secretions in tissue-culture cells — the decisive fact for “If Chlamydia pneumoniae is suspected, which method can detect the organism.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement best describes Chlamydia pneumoniae today?
options: Infections are uncommon and only 10% have antibody
It has been associated epidemiologically with atherosclerotic coronary disease
questions.explanation: C. pneumoniae causes common respiratory infection and has been epidemiologically associated with atherosclerosis, though causation and treatment implications remain unproven.
questions.keyConcept: Chlamydia pneumoniae is a common, usually mild respiratory pathogen whose proposed link to atherosclerosis is an epidemiologic association, not proven causation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A person who raises chickens develops atypical pneumonia after many birds die. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chlamydia psittaci is acquired from infected birds and causes psittacosis with systemic symptoms and atypical pneumonia.
questions.keyConcept: Ornithosis (psittacosis) — the decisive fact for “A person who raises chickens develops atypical pneumonia after many birds die. What is the most likely diagnosis.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement concerning Chlamydia psittaci infection is incorrect?
options: It grows in cell culture but not blood agar
Serology is more useful than isolation
It is more commonly acquired from a nonhuman source than another human
The organism appears purple in Gram-stained sputum
questions.explanation: Chlamydiae stain poorly with routine Gram stain; psittacosis is usually acquired from birds and diagnosed serologically or molecularly.
questions.keyConcept: The organism appears purple in Gram-stained sputum — the decisive fact for “statement concerning Chlamydia psittaci infection is incorrect.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A slaughterhouse worker develops abrupt influenza-like illness and early pneumonia along with coworkers. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Coxiella burnetii causes Q fever after inhalation of contaminated aerosols from livestock or animal products.
questions.keyConcept: Coxiella burnetii — the decisive fact for “A slaughterhouse worker develops abrupt influenza-like illness and early pneumonia along with coworkers. Which organism is most likely.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Slaughterhouse workers develop flu-like illness and pneumonitis; the organism survives in macrophage phagolysosomes. Which is most likely?
questions.explanation: Coxiella burnetii uniquely survives and replicates in the acidic phagolysosome and causes Q fever.
questions.keyConcept: Coxiella burnetii — the decisive fact for “Slaughterhouse workers develop flu-like illness and pneumonitis; the organism survives in macrophage phagolysosomes. Which is most likely.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A butcher with severe cough, bloody sputum, and suspected hemorrhagic mediastinitis has large rectangular Gram-positive bacilli with halos. The vaccine is prepared from which component?
questions.explanation: The licensed anthrax vaccine is based chiefly on protective antigen, the binding component of anthrax toxin.
questions.keyConcept: Protective antigen — the decisive fact for “A butcher with severe cough, bloody sputum, and suspected hemorrhagic mediastinitis has large rectangular Gram-positive bacilli with halos.….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Pathogenicity of Bacillus anthracis is due to which factors?
questions.explanation: Anthrax virulence depends on tripartite exotoxin and an antiphagocytic poly-D-glutamate capsule.
questions.keyConcept: Both exotoxin and polypeptide capsule — the decisive fact for “Pathogenicity of Bacillus anthracis is due to which factors.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which is not important to anthrax epidemiology or pathogenesis?
options: A reservoir of healthy human carriers
questions.explanation: Anthrax is a zoonosis maintained in animals and environmental spores; healthy human carriers are not a major reservoir.
questions.keyConcept: A reservoir of healthy human carriers — the decisive fact for “is not important to anthrax epidemiology or pathogenesis.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: During construction of a bone-marrow transplant unit, which fungus is the greatest airborne concern?
questions.explanation: Construction aerosolizes Aspergillus conidia, posing a major risk for invasive disease in profoundly immunocompromised patients.
questions.keyConcept: Aspergillus species — the decisive fact for “During construction of a bone-marrow transplant unit, which fungus is the greatest airborne concern.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which condition is most likely in a leukemic patient infected with Aspergillus fumigatus?
questions.explanation: Neutropenia and leukemia predispose to angioinvasive aspergillosis rather than colonizing or allergic forms.
questions.keyConcept: Invasive aspergillosis — the decisive fact for “condition is most likely in a leukemic patient infected with Aspergillus fumigatus.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A healthy person develops pulmonary infiltrate and sputum spherules after inhaling fungal spores. Which organism is associated?
questions.explanation: Coccidioides is inhaled as arthroconidia and forms spherules containing endospores in tissue.
questions.keyConcept: Coccidioides immitis — the decisive fact for “A healthy person develops pulmonary infiltrate and sputum spherules after inhaling fungal spores. Which organism is associated.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A bird handler develops mild pulmonary infection; sputum shows yeast within macrophages. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Histoplasma is associated with bird or bat droppings and appears as small intracellular yeasts in macrophages.
questions.keyConcept: Histoplasma capsulatum — the decisive fact for “A bird handler develops mild pulmonary infection; sputum shows yeast within macrophages. Which organism is most likely.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the most common cause of acute post-influenza bacterial pneumonia in the keyed source?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is a classic cause of severe secondary bacterial pneumonia after influenza.
questions.keyConcept: Staphylococcus aureus — the decisive fact for “is the most common cause of acute post-influenza bacterial pneumonia in the keyed source.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the best rapid approach listed for detecting influenza?
options: Antigen detection in respiratory secretions or throat swab
questions.explanation: Direct antigen or molecular testing of respiratory specimens provides rapid etiologic confirmation.
questions.keyConcept: Antigen detection in respiratory secretions or throat swab — the decisive fact for “is the best rapid approach listed for detecting influenza.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement best reflects influenza pathogenesis?
options: Pneumonia is never associated with secondary bacteria
Virus activation and spread depend on protease-expressing respiratory cells
questions.explanation: Host proteases cleave hemagglutinin into an active form required for membrane fusion and productive infection.
questions.keyConcept: Virus activation and spread depend on protease-expressing respiratory cells — the decisive fact for “statement best reflects influenza pathogenesis.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement about influenza prevention is correct?
options: There is an effective vaccine against H1N5
Vaccine should not be given in pregnancy
The vaccine contains two influenza A subtypes
Vaccine strains never vary by year
questions.explanation: Seasonal vaccines commonly include two influenza A subtypes plus influenza B lineage components and are updated as strains change.
questions.keyConcept: The vaccine contains two influenza A subtypes — the decisive fact for “statement about influenza prevention is correct.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Influenza is characterized by which symptoms?
questions.explanation: Abrupt fever, myalgia, malaise, headache, and dry cough are typical influenza manifestations.
questions.keyConcept: All of the above — the decisive fact for “Influenza is characterized by which symptoms.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the principal reservoir associated with influenza antigenic-shift variants in the keyed source?
questions.explanation: Pigs can serve as mixing vessels for reassortment between avian and human influenza strains; aquatic birds are the ultimate reservoir of influenza A diversity.
questions.keyConcept: Pigs — the decisive fact for “is the principal reservoir associated with influenza antigenic-shift variants in the keyed source.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which viral feature is essential for influenza antigenic shift?
questions.explanation: The segmented genome permits reassortment during coinfection, producing abrupt antigenic shift.
questions.keyConcept: Segmented RNA genome — the decisive fact for “viral feature is essential for influenza antigenic shift.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which viral feature is crucial for influenza antigenic drift?
options: Ability to infect humans and animals
questions.explanation: Error-prone RNA replication causes gradual point mutations in HA and NA, producing antigenic drift.
questions.keyConcept: Frequent spontaneous point mutations — the decisive fact for “viral feature is crucial for influenza antigenic drift.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement concerning influenza prevention is incorrect?
options: Inactivated and live vaccines contain fundamentally different A subtypes
Annual vaccination is needed because antigenicity drifts
Hemagglutinin is the principal protective antigen
questions.explanation: Seasonal formulations target the same recommended strains regardless of whether vaccine is inactivated or live; platform does not imply different A subtypes.
questions.keyConcept: Inactivated and live vaccines contain fundamentally different A subtypes — the decisive fact for “statement concerning influenza prevention is incorrect.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Regarding influenza vaccines, which statement is least accurate?
options: Live attenuated vaccine is given to elderly people
One vaccine uses inactivated formaldehyde-treated virions
One vaccine uses a temperature-sensitive mutant replicating in the nose
Vaccines contain A and B strains but not C
questions.explanation: Live attenuated intranasal vaccine is intended for eligible nonpregnant people aged 2–49 years, not older adults.
questions.keyConcept: Live attenuated vaccine is given to elderly people — the decisive fact for “Regarding influenza vaccines, which statement is least accurate.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement concerning influenza A antigenicity is incorrect?
options: Shift is due to reassortment and occurs infrequently
Shift can affect hemagglutinin and neuraminidase
Drift primarily affects an internal ribonucleoprotein
questions.explanation: Antigenic drift primarily changes surface glycoproteins HA and NA, not internal ribonucleoprotein.
questions.keyConcept: Drift primarily affects an internal ribonucleoprotein — the decisive fact for “statement concerning influenza A antigenicity is incorrect.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Why is annual influenza vaccination required?
options: Mutation in genes encoding envelope glycoproteins
questions.explanation: Frequent mutations in HA and NA genes cause antigenic drift and require periodic vaccine updating.
questions.keyConcept: Mutation in genes encoding envelope glycoproteins — the decisive fact for “is annual influenza vaccination required.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Where are receptors preferred by avian H5N1 influenza concentrated in humans?
questions.explanation: Avian-type alpha-2,3-linked sialic-acid receptors are concentrated deeper in the lower respiratory tract, including alveolar regions.
questions.keyConcept: Alveoli — the decisive fact for “are receptors preferred by avian H5N1 influenza concentrated in humans.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A renal-transplant recipient develops fever, sore throat, pneumonia, lymphadenopathy, and a nonreactive heterophile test. Which virus is responsible?
questions.explanation: CMV causes heterophile-negative mononucleosis-like disease and pneumonia in immunosuppressed transplant recipients.
questions.keyConcept: Cytomegalovirus — the decisive fact for “A renal-transplant recipient develops fever, sore throat, pneumonia, lymphadenopathy, and a nonreactive heterophile test. Which virus is responsible.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which finding is characteristic of cytomegalovirus?
questions.explanation: CMV produces enlarged cells with prominent basophilic owl-eye intranuclear inclusions.
questions.keyConcept: Intranuclear owl-eye inclusion — the decisive fact for “finding is characteristic of cytomegalovirus.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement describes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome?
options: Influenza-like illness rapidly progresses to respiratory failure
Infection follows inhalation of cat urine
questions.explanation: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome begins with a febrile prodrome and can rapidly progress to capillary leak, pulmonary edema, and respiratory failure.
questions.keyConcept: Influenza-like illness rapidly progresses to respiratory failure — the decisive fact for “statement describes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement about the SARS coronavirus is true?
options: It is transmitted by camel contact
It causes high fever and pulmonary consolidation
It is prevented by a routine live attenuated vaccine
It can induce a cytokine storm
questions.explanation: Severe coronavirus infection can provoke dysregulated inflammatory cytokine responses that contribute to acute lung injury.
questions.keyConcept: It can induce a cytokine storm — the decisive fact for “statement about the SARS coronavirus is true.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A camel-farm worker develops fever, dry cough, and dyspnea. Which virus is most likely?
questions.explanation: MERS-CoV is zoonotically associated with dromedary camels and can cause severe pneumonia.
questions.keyConcept: MERS coronavirus — the decisive fact for “A camel-farm worker develops fever, dry cough, and dyspnea. Which virus is most likely.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which host-cell receptor is used by MERS coronavirus?
questions.explanation: MERS-CoV uses dipeptidyl peptidase 4 (DPP4), also known as CD26, for cell entry.
questions.keyConcept: CD26 — the decisive fact for “host-cell receptor is used by MERS coronavirus.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which condition is least likely to be caused by adenovirus?
questions.explanation: Adenovirus commonly causes pharyngitis, conjunctivitis, and pneumonia; it is less characteristic as a cause of the ordinary common cold.
questions.keyConcept: Common cold — the decisive fact for “condition is least likely to be caused by adenovirus.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement concerning adenoviruses is incorrect?
options: They are nonenveloped double-stranded DNA viruses with fiber knobs
They can cause sore throat and pneumonia
They have only one serologic type
Some adenoviruses cause tumors in experimental animals
questions.explanation: Adenoviruses have numerous serotypes, not a single serologic type.
questions.keyConcept: They have only one serologic type — the decisive fact for “statement concerning adenoviruses is incorrect.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement about Q fever is correct?
options: It is confined to the upper respiratory tract
Its incubation is four to six weeks
It is transmitted by arthropod bite
It is an acute febrile illness caused by Coxiella burnetii
questions.explanation: Q fever is an acute febrile zoonosis caused by Coxiella burnetii, usually acquired by inhaling contaminated animal aerosols.
questions.keyConcept: It is an acute febrile illness caused by Coxiella burnetii — the decisive fact for “statement about Q fever is correct.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement characterizes Coxiella burnetii?
options: It is an obligate intracellular parasite
It is stable outside host cells
It stains easily with Gram stain
questions.explanation: Coxiella burnetii is an obligate intracellular bacterium that replicates in the acidic phagolysosome.
questions.keyConcept: It is an obligate intracellular parasite — the decisive fact for “statement characterizes Coxiella burnetii.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which feature best distinguishes Chlamydiae from viruses?
questions.explanation: Chlamydiae possess bacterial ribosomes and are susceptible to antibacterial drugs, unlike viruses.
questions.keyConcept: Susceptibility to antimicrobial agents — the decisive fact for “feature best distinguishes Chlamydiae from viruses.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which organism causes primary atypical pneumonia in humans?
questions.explanation: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the classic cause of primary atypical or walking pneumonia.
questions.keyConcept: Mycoplasma pneumoniae — the decisive fact for “organism causes primary atypical pneumonia in humans.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Match each atypical-pneumonia vignette with the most likely organism.

pairs.premise: College student with gradual headache, malaise, hacking nonproductive cough, and radiographic infiltrates greater than clinical findings
Next most probable alternative etiology for the college-student atypical pneumonia
Abrupt high fever, myalgia, pleurisy, dry cough, and air-conditioning-service exposure
Small-animal veterinarian with severe headache, myalgia, splenomegaly, pulmonary findings, scant sputum, and mononuclear cells

questions.explanation: Mycoplasma commonly affects young adults; Chlamydia pneumoniae is a respiratory alternative; Legionella follows aerosolized-water exposure; and C. psittaci follows avian exposure in animal workers.
questions.keyConcept: Match each premise by the specific relationship tested in “Match each atypical-pneumonia vignette with the most likely organism”; do not apply one rule to every pair.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In influenza infection, neutralizing antibodies are produced mainly against which antigen?
questions.explanation: Antibody against hemagglutinin blocks attachment and entry and is the principal neutralizing antibody response.
questions.keyConcept: Hemagglutinin — the decisive fact for “In influenza infection, neutralizing antibodies are produced mainly against which antigen.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which virus belongs to Orthomyxoviridae?
questions.explanation: Influenza viruses are orthomyxoviruses with segmented negative-sense RNA genomes.
questions.keyConcept: Influenza virus — the decisive fact for “virus belongs to Orthomyxoviridae.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which is a leading cause of pneumonia in infants?
questions.explanation: RSV is a leading cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants.
questions.keyConcept: Respiratory syncytial virus — the decisive fact for “is a leading cause of pneumonia in infants.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which vaccine is used annually for influenza?
questions.explanation: Annual inactivated influenza vaccination is broadly used and updated to circulating strains.
questions.keyConcept: Inactivated virus vaccine — the decisive fact for “vaccine is used annually for influenza.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which single-stranded RNA orthomyxovirus requires annual vaccination because of antigenic drift and shift?
questions.explanation: Influenza undergoes drift through mutation and influenza A can undergo shift through reassortment.
questions.keyConcept: Influenza virus — the decisive fact for “single-stranded RNA orthomyxovirus requires annual vaccination because of antigenic drift and shift.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Each statement concerning influenza is correct EXCEPT:
options: Major epidemics are mainly due to influenza A
Animal influenza viruses may supply new influenza A antigens
Major shifts occur mainly in influenza A
Antigenic drift is caused by genome-segment reassortment
questions.explanation: Antigenic drift results from point mutation; reassortment of genome segments causes antigenic shift.
questions.keyConcept: Antigenic drift is caused by genome-segment reassortment — the decisive fact for “Each statement concerning influenza is correct EXCEPT.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Each statement about influenza prevention is correct EXCEPT:
options: Influenza vaccine should not be given to pregnant women
Amantadine is active only against influenza A
Hemagglutinin is the major vaccine antigen
questions.explanation: Inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended during pregnancy; pregnancy is not a contraindication.
questions.keyConcept: Influenza vaccine should not be given to pregnant women — the decisive fact for “Each statement about influenza prevention is correct EXCEPT.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A six-month-old with persistent cough, fever, and radiographic pneumonia most likely has which infection?
questions.explanation: RSV is a major cause of lower-respiratory disease in young infants.
questions.keyConcept: Respiratory syncytial virus — the decisive fact for “A six-month-old with persistent cough, fever, and radiographic pneumonia most likely has which infection.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Each statement about influenza A antigenicity is correct EXCEPT:
options: Shift is infrequent and due to reassortment
Shift can affect HA and NA
questions.explanation: Drift primarily alters surface hemagglutinin and neuraminidase rather than internal ribonucleoprotein.
questions.keyConcept: Drift mainly involves internal ribonucleoprotein — the decisive fact for “Each statement about influenza A antigenicity is correct EXCEPT.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the most common clinical syndrome associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae?
questions.explanation: Mycoplasma commonly causes tracheobronchitis and atypical pneumonia; extrapulmonary complications are less common.
questions.keyConcept: Tracheobronchitis — the decisive fact for “is the most common clinical syndrome associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is a common characteristic of Legionella species?
questions.explanation: Legionella requires iron- and cysteine-supplemented buffered charcoal yeast extract for culture.
questions.keyConcept: Requirement for supplemented laboratory media — the decisive fact for “is a common characteristic of Legionella species.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Most people acquire Legionella infection from what source?
questions.explanation: Legionella is acquired by inhaling aerosolized contaminated water, not usually by person-to-person spread.
questions.keyConcept: A water source — the decisive fact for “Most people acquire Legionella infection from what source.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Legionella infection is more common in which group?
options: Smokers with chronic obstructive lung disease
questions.explanation: Smoking, chronic lung disease, older age, and impaired cell-mediated immunity increase legionellosis risk.
questions.keyConcept: Smokers with chronic obstructive lung disease — the decisive fact for “Legionella infection is more common in which group.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient has three weeks of worsening paroxysmal cough with repeated fits. Which organism should be considered?
questions.explanation: Bordetella pertussis causes prolonged paroxysmal coughing fits, often after an initial catarrhal phase.
questions.keyConcept: Bordetella pertussis — the decisive fact for “A patient has three weeks of worsening paroxysmal cough with repeated fits. Which organism should be considered.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is an important characteristic of mycobacteria?
questions.explanation: Mycolic-acid-rich walls make mycobacteria acid-fast and slow growing.
questions.keyConcept: Acid-fastness — the decisive fact for “is an important characteristic of mycobacteria.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which symptom is typical of reactivation tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: Reactivation pulmonary tuberculosis commonly causes weight loss, fever, night sweats, chronic cough, and hemoptysis.
questions.keyConcept: Weight loss — the decisive fact for “symptom is typical of reactivation tuberculosis.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is an important general characteristic of fungal infections?
options: Cause severe disease in debilitated or immunocompromised patients
questions.explanation: Opportunistic fungi cause especially severe invasive disease in immunocompromised hosts.
questions.keyConcept: Cause severe disease in debilitated or immunocompromised patients — the decisive fact for “is an important general characteristic of fungal infections.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An advanced-HIV patient has removable white oral plaques leaving a red base and dysphagia. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Candida albicans causes oral and esophageal candidiasis with removable pseudomembranous plaques in advanced HIV.
questions.keyConcept: Candida albicans — the decisive fact for “An advanced-HIV patient has removable white oral plaques leaving a red base and dysphagia. Which organism is most….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the usual initiating event in pulmonary fungal infection?
questions.explanation: Most endemic and opportunistic pulmonary mycoses begin with inhalation of airborne spores or conidia.
questions.keyConcept: Inhalation — the decisive fact for “is the usual initiating event in pulmonary fungal infection.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A traveler to northeastern Arizona develops a flu-like illness and a small pulmonary infiltrate. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Coccidioides is endemic in the desert Southwest, including Arizona, and is acquired by inhaling arthroconidia.
questions.keyConcept: Coccidioides — the decisive fact for “A traveler to northeastern Arizona develops a flu-like illness and a small pulmonary infiltrate. Which organism is most….”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: During which viral-replication phase does influenza hemagglutinin have its key role?
questions.explanation: Hemagglutinin binds sialic-acid receptors during adsorption and entry.
questions.keyConcept: Adsorption — the decisive fact for “During which viral-replication phase does influenza hemagglutinin have its key role.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement is incorrect for purified protein derivative testing?
options: It is derived from M. tuberculosis proteins
It is used to diagnose latent infection in adults
A positive test in an unvaccinated young child indicates infection
questions.explanation: PPD elicits delayed type IV cell-mediated hypersensitivity, not a humoral antibody response.
questions.keyConcept: It stimulates humoral immunity — the decisive fact for “statement is incorrect for purified protein derivative testing.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Bordetella pertussis is characterized by which statement?
options: It is a capsulated Gram-negative organism
It cannot grow on simple media
questions.explanation: Bordetella pertussis is a fastidious Gram-negative coccobacillus that causes whooping cough and has surface factors described as capsular or capsule-like.
questions.keyConcept: All of the above — the decisive fact for “Bordetella pertussis is characterized by which statement.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement about Legionella pneumophila is true?
options: It is readily killed within phagocytes
questions.explanation: Macrolides achieve intracellular activity and are standard treatment options for legionellosis.
questions.keyConcept: Macrolides are used for treatment — the decisive fact for “statement about Legionella pneumophila is true.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae is sensitive to which antimicrobial among the listed choices?
questions.explanation: Susceptible pneumococcal strains are inhibited by beta-lactams such as penicillin, although resistance patterns guide therapy.
questions.keyConcept: Penicillin — the decisive fact for “Streptococcus pneumoniae is sensitive to which antimicrobial among the listed choices.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Legionnaires disease is spread through which route?
options: Inhalation of contaminated aerosols from air-conditioning or water systems
questions.explanation: Legionella is acquired mainly by inhalation or aspiration of contaminated water aerosols.
questions.keyConcept: Inhalation of contaminated aerosols from air-conditioning or water systems — the decisive fact for “Legionnaires disease is spread through which route.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Pneumococci can cause all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Friedländer pneumonia is the historical name for Klebsiella pneumonia, not pneumococcal disease.
questions.keyConcept: Friedländer pneumonia — the decisive fact for “Pneumococci can cause all of the following EXCEPT.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Mycoplasmas have all of the following characteristics EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Mycoplasmas lack a peptidoglycan cell wall and are intrinsically resistant to penicillins and other beta-lactams.
questions.keyConcept: Are susceptible to penicillin G — the decisive fact for “Mycoplasmas have all of the following characteristics EXCEPT.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement about Mycobacterium tuberculosis is true?
options: It stains easily by Gram stain
Growth is slow and may require four to eight weeks
questions.explanation: M. tuberculosis is slow growing and classically requires several weeks for visible colonies on solid media.
questions.keyConcept: M. tuberculosis growth is markedly slower than ordinary bacteria (weeks, not hours to days), which is why culture-based diagnosis takes so long and why rapid molecular tests (NAAT/PCR) are preferred when speed matters.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which statement about BCG vaccine is true?
options: It is prepared from a human M. tuberculosis strain
It is a live attenuated vaccine
It is given to tuberculin-positive people
questions.explanation: BCG is a live attenuated strain of Mycobacterium bovis used to reduce severe childhood tuberculosis.
questions.keyConcept: It is a live attenuated vaccine — the decisive fact for “statement about BCG vaccine is true.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: BCG is sometimes used for which immunologic purpose?
questions.explanation: BCG can stimulate nonspecific cellular immune activity and is used intravesically as immunotherapy for bladder cancer.
questions.keyConcept: Nonspecific immune potentiation — the decisive fact for “BCG is sometimes used for which immunologic purpose.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: How is live attenuated influenza vaccine administered?
questions.explanation: Live attenuated influenza vaccine is temperature sensitive and administered intranasally to eligible recipients.
questions.keyConcept: Intranasally — the decisive fact for “is live attenuated influenza vaccine administered.”

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All are vaccine approaches against whooping cough EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Pertussis vaccines are killed whole-cell or acellular subunit preparations; no routine live attenuated pertussis vaccine is used.
questions.keyConcept: Live attenuated vaccine — the decisive fact for “All are vaccine approaches against whooping cough EXCEPT.”

questions.subject: Parasitology
options: The adult worms live free inside lung tissue.
Its infective stage is microcercous cercaria.
Its eggs are passed in stool 4 months after infection.
It needs only one host to complete its life cycle.
questions.explanation: Choice C is keyed because Paragonimus eggs can reach swallowed sputum and then stool after the adult flukes mature and begin oviposition. The other choices conflict with the life cycle: adults occupy pulmonary cysts, humans acquire metacercariae from crustaceans, and two intermediate hosts are required.
questions.text: Regarding Paragonimus westermani, which statement is correct?
questions.keyConcept: Paragonimus egg production and diagnostic timing

questions.subject: Parasitology
options: Charcot–Leyden crystals may be present in sputum.
Fever and cough with blood-tinged sputum may occur.
Symptoms subside spontaneously after about 3 weeks.
High periodic fever and lymphadenopathy occur.
questions.explanation: Choice E is false because high periodic fever with lymphadenopathy is not a typical feature of uncomplicated Loeffler's syndrome. Larval migration through the lungs instead produces transient cough, eosinophilic infiltrates, and sometimes Charcot–Leyden crystals, often resolving spontaneously within weeks.
questions.text: Regarding Loeffler's syndrome, which statement is false?
questions.keyConcept: Clinical features of Loeffler's syndrome

questions.subject: Parasitology
options: The first intermediate host is the Semisulcospira libertina snail.
The infective stage for humans is the encysted metacercaria.
The diagnostic stage is the egg.
questions.explanation: Choice E is correct because every listed statement describes the Paragonimus life cycle or diagnosis. Development proceeds through a Semisulcospira snail and a freshwater crustacean, humans ingest encysted metacercariae, and operculated eggs are the diagnostic stage.
questions.text: Which statement about Paragonimus westermani is true?
questions.keyConcept: Paragonimus life cycle and diagnostic stage

questions.subject: Parasitology
options: Avoid eating improperly cooked freshwater crabs and crayfish.
Metacercariae in crabs and crayfish are killed by heating in water at 25°C for 5 minutes.
Metacercariae can live for 48 hours at −10°C and do not die when dried.
questions.explanation: Choice E is correct because avoiding undercooked freshwater crabs or crayfish blocks ingestion of infective metacercariae, while snail control interrupts larval development. The heat and freezing statements are unreliable: effective killing requires substantially higher heat, and drying is lethal to metacercariae.
questions.text: What is the prevention of paragonimiasis?
questions.keyConcept: Food safety and prevention of paragonimiasis

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.explanation: Choice D is correct because Ascaris, Strongyloides, and Ancylostoma larvae can all migrate through pulmonary tissue and cause Loeffler's syndrome. Their passage provokes transient eosinophilic inflammation that may appear as ground-glass or fleeting infiltrates on chest imaging.
questions.text: A patient with Loeffler's syndrome has a ground-glass appearance on chest X-ray. Which parasite may cause the disease?
questions.keyConcept: Nematode larvae that cause pulmonary eosinophilia

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.explanation: Choice A is the keyed answer because Paragonimus produces immature, operculated eggs that may be recovered from stool after infected sputum is swallowed. Unoperculated eggs and urinary specimens do not fit the usual morphology or diagnostic route of this pulmonary fluke.
questions.text: How is Paragonimus westermani diagnosed?
questions.keyConcept: Microscopic diagnosis of Paragonimus infection

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.explanation: Choice D is correct because beds provide warmth, humidity, and abundant shed skin scales for house dust mites. This habitat explains why mattress and bedding measures are central to allergen reduction.
questions.text: What is the most important site of the house dust mite?
questions.keyConcept: House dust mite habitat

questions.subject: Parasitology
options: Regular vacuum cleaning of beds, carpets, and furniture.
questions.explanation: Choice E is correct because vacuuming, ventilation, frequent laundering, and benzyl benzoate can all reduce mite burden or allergen exposure. Since choices A through D are valid control measures, none is the requested exception.
questions.text: All of the following are measures to control house dust mites except:
questions.keyConcept: House dust mite allergen control

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.explanation: Choice C is correct because Strongyloides can autoinfect the same host and repeatedly generate larvae that migrate through the lungs. The resulting high larval burden may produce more severe eosinophilic pneumonitis than a single migratory cycle of Ascaris or hookworms.
questions.text: Which parasite causes the strongest Loeffler's syndrome?
questions.keyConcept: Strongyloides autoinfection and pulmonary severity

questions.subject: Parasitology
options: The acute stage is characterized by high eosinophilia.
The acute stage is characterized by an unproductive cough.
The chronic stage is characterized by cough with chocolate-colored sputum.
Extrapulmonary paragonimiasis is characterized by invasion of encysted metacercariae into vital organs other than the lung.
questions.explanation: Choice D is the exception because extrapulmonary paragonimiasis results from aberrant migration of immature flukes, not direct invasion of distant organs by encysted metacercariae. Acute migration causes eosinophilic inflammation, whereas chronic pulmonary infection may produce cough with chocolate-colored sputum.
questions.text: All of the following are true about the pathogenesis of Paragonimus westermani except:
questions.keyConcept: Pathogenesis of pulmonary and ectopic paragonimiasis

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer:
- First intermediate host: Semisulcospira libertina freshwater snail.
- Second intermediate hosts: freshwater crabs and crayfish.
questions.explanation: Miracidia infect the snail, where larval development produces cercariae. Cercariae then enter crustaceans and encyst as metacercariae, the infective stage for humans.
questions.text: Mention the two intermediate hosts of Paragonimus westermani.
questions.keyConcept: Intermediate hosts in the Paragonimus life cycle

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer: - Humans.
questions.explanation: Adult worms mature and reproduce sexually in the definitive host, usually within pulmonary cysts. Other mammals may also support adult worms, but the printed model answer specifies humans.
questions.text: Mention the definitive host of Paragonimus westermani.
questions.keyConcept: Definitive host of Paragonimus

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer: - Fish-eating mammals, including cats, dogs, pigs, wolves, and foxes.
questions.explanation: Reservoir mammals maintain adult worms and release eggs into the environment. Their presence sustains transmission where suitable freshwater snails and crustaceans occur.
questions.text: Mention the reservoir hosts of Paragonimus westermani.
questions.keyConcept: Reservoir hosts of Paragonimus

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer: - Encysted metacercaria.
questions.explanation: Metacercariae encyst in freshwater crabs or crayfish after the cercarial stage leaves the snail. Humans become infected by eating these crustaceans raw or inadequately cooked.
questions.text: Mention the infective stage of Paragonimus westermani.
questions.keyConcept: Infective metacercarial stage

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer: - Eggs.
questions.explanation: Operculated eggs are sought mainly in sputum and may also appear in stool after infected sputum is swallowed. Egg detection may be insensitive in acute or extrapulmonary disease.
questions.text: Mention the diagnostic stage of Paragonimus westermani.
questions.keyConcept: Diagnostic egg stage

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer: - Ingestion of encysted metacercariae in improperly cooked freshwater crabs or crayfish.
questions.explanation: After ingestion, metacercariae excyst in the intestine and immature flukes migrate through the abdominal cavity and diaphragm to the lungs. Proper cooking prevents this food-borne transmission.
questions.text: Mention the mode of infection with Paragonimus westermani.
questions.keyConcept: Food-borne transmission of paragonimiasis

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer:
- Bronchopneumonia.
- Pneumothorax and pyothorax.
- Lung abscess.
- Empyema.
- Fulminating abdominal and cerebral lesions with secondary bacterial infection.
questions.explanation: Pulmonary cysts and inflammation can disrupt pleura and lung tissue, producing infection, abscess, or air and pus in the pleural space. Aberrant migration may cause severe abdominal or cerebral disease.
questions.text: What are the complications of paragonimiasis?
questions.keyConcept: Pulmonary and ectopic complications

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer:
- It is not effective in the acute stage.
- Eggs are very rare in sputum.
questions.explanation: Egg production begins only after worms mature, so early infection may be microscopy-negative. Low or intermittent egg output also reduces sensitivity and supports use of serology or other specimens when suspicion remains high.
questions.text: What are the limitations of sputum analysis in paragonimiasis?
questions.keyConcept: Limitations of sputum microscopy

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer:
- Early diagnosis.
- Diagnosis of acute and extrapulmonary paragonimiasis.
- Diagnosis of chronic paragonimiasis when eggs are not recovered from sputum or stool.
- Follow-up of treatment, because antibodies may return to normal 6–12 months after successful therapy.
questions.explanation: Serology detects host antibodies and therefore can support diagnosis before eggs become detectable or when parasites are outside the lungs. Falling antibody levels after treatment can aid follow-up, although they do not fall immediately.
questions.text: Mention the advantages of serodiagnosis in paragonimiasis.
questions.keyConcept: Uses of antibody serology

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer: - Cross-reaction with other trematodes.
questions.explanation: Antibodies to related flukes may recognize shared antigens and create false-positive results. More specific purified or excretory-secretory antigens can improve discrimination.
questions.text: Mention the limitations of serodiagnosis in paragonimiasis.
questions.keyConcept: Cross-reactivity in serodiagnosis

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer: - Praziquantel.
questions.explanation: Praziquantel increases parasite membrane permeability to calcium, causing paralysis and damage to adult flukes. Treatment reduces egg production and prevents progression of pulmonary or ectopic disease.
questions.text: Mention the drug of choice for paragonimiasis.
questions.keyConcept: Praziquantel treatment

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer: - Invasion of the intestine and migration of immature flukes through the lungs.
questions.explanation: The acute phase reflects tissue injury and eosinophilic inflammation during larval migration from the intestine toward the lungs. Symptoms may occur before mature worms produce detectable eggs.
questions.text: Mention the cause of the acute stage of paragonimiasis.
questions.keyConcept: Acute migratory phase pathology

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer: - Invasion of vital organs other than the lungs by immature flukes.
questions.explanation: Immature flukes may migrate aberrantly instead of reaching the lungs. Cerebral involvement is especially serious because inflammatory lesions can cause seizures or focal neurologic deficits.
questions.text: Mention the cause of extrapulmonary paragonimiasis.
questions.keyConcept: Aberrant migration to extrapulmonary organs

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer:
- Destroy snail hosts.
- Use praziquantel mass treatment in endemic areas.
- Avoid eating improperly cooked freshwater crabs and crayfish.
- Monitor pickled or frozen raw crab and crayfish products imported from endemic areas.
- Maintain monitoring systems for aquaculture.
- Heat metacercariae in crabs or crayfish in water at 55°C for 5 minutes.
- Recognize that metacercariae may survive 48 hours at −20°C but die within minutes when dried.
questions.explanation: Control combines treatment, food safety, surveillance, and interruption of intermediate-host transmission. Thorough heating is reliable, whereas freezing alone may not kill every metacercaria.
questions.text: Mention seven methods to prevent and control paragonimiasis.
questions.keyConcept: Integrated prevention and control

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer:
- Loeffler's syndrome.
- Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia.
- Verminous pneumonia accompanying schistosomiasis.
questions.explanation: These syndromes reflect pulmonary exposure to migrating larvae, microfilariae-associated hypersensitivity, or schistosome-related disease. Marked eosinophilia is an important clue to a parasitic rather than routine bacterial cause.
questions.text: Mention the parasitic conditions that cause pneumonia with high eosinophilia.
questions.keyConcept: Parasitic causes of eosinophilic pneumonia

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer:
- Other parasitic causes of pneumonia with high eosinophilia.
- Pulmonary tuberculosis.
- Viral, Mycoplasma, and bacterial pneumonias.
questions.explanation: Paragonimiasis can mimic tuberculosis or other pneumonias through cough, hemoptysis, and radiographic infiltrates. Exposure history, eosinophilia, egg detection, and serology help distinguish it.
questions.text: Mention the differential diagnosis of pulmonary paragonimiasis.
questions.keyConcept: Differential diagnosis of pulmonary paragonimiasis

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer:
- Schistosoma japonicum eggs.
- Larvae of Echinococcus granulosus.
- Larvae of Taenia solium.
questions.explanation: Several helminths can produce intracranial cystic or granulomatous lesions. Imaging, epidemiologic exposure, serology, and parasite-specific morphology help identify the cause.
questions.text: What should cerebral paragonimiasis be differentiated from?
questions.keyConcept: Differential diagnosis of cerebral helminth lesions

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer:
- Gastric lavage.
- Pleural effusion fluid.
- Bronchoalveolar lavage.
- Fine-needle aspiration from a lung lesion.
questions.explanation: Eggs may be recovered from respiratory secretions or material sampled near pulmonary lesions. Gastric lavage can capture swallowed sputum when an ordinary sputum sample is unavailable or negative.
questions.text: Where may Paragonimus eggs be found?
questions.keyConcept: Alternative specimens for egg detection

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer: - Antibodies in serum by ELISA.
questions.explanation: ELISA measures the host antibody response to Paragonimus antigens. It is especially useful when eggs are not yet produced or are inaccessible in extrapulmonary disease.
questions.text: What does serodiagnosis in paragonimiasis detect?
questions.keyConcept: ELISA antibody detection

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer: - By using purified antigens, such as excretory-secretory antigens.
questions.explanation: Crude antigens contain epitopes shared among trematodes and may reduce specificity. Purified excretory-secretory antigens focus testing on more discriminating parasite products.
questions.text: How was the problem of cross-reaction with other trematodes resolved?
questions.keyConcept: Purified antigens and serologic specificity

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer:
- Plain chest X-ray: nodular or ring shadows, patchy infiltration, cavities, and calcified cysts.
- CT scan: soap-bubble appearance and sometimes calcified lesions.
questions.explanation: Imaging reflects inflammatory tracks, cysts, cavities, and chronic calcification produced by migrating or mature flukes. Findings support diagnosis but are not specific enough to replace parasitologic or serologic testing.
questions.text: What do imaging methods show in paragonimiasis?
questions.keyConcept: Radiographic findings in paragonimiasis

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer: - Beds.
questions.explanation: Beds retain humidity, warmth, and human skin scales, creating an ideal mite habitat. Allergen reduction therefore emphasizes mattress and bedding care.
questions.text: Mention the most important site of house dust mites.
questions.keyConcept: Principal household mite habitat

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer:
- Regularly vacuum beds, carpets, and furniture.
- Air bedrooms regularly.
- Wash sheets and blankets frequently.
- Use insecticides containing benzyl benzoate.
questions.explanation: Control reduces mite reservoirs and allergen exposure through cleaning, laundering, ventilation, and acaricides. Lower humidity and attention to bedding are especially useful because beds are a major habitat.
questions.text: Mention four methods to control house dust mites.
questions.keyConcept: Environmental control of house dust mites

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer: - Human skin scales and organic debris.
questions.explanation: House dust mites consume shed epidermal material and associated organic matter rather than parasitizing people directly. Their fecal and body proteins are important indoor allergens.
questions.text: What do house dust mites feed on?
questions.keyConcept: House dust mite nutrition

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer: - Incomplete metamorphosis.
questions.explanation: Mites develop through egg, larval, nymphal, and adult stages without a pupal stage. Environmental control can reduce survival across these household stages.
questions.text: Mention the type of metamorphosis in house dust mites.
questions.keyConcept: House dust mite development

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer:
- Allergic rhinitis.
- Bronchial asthma.
- Atopic dermatitis.
questions.explanation: Mite allergens trigger IgE-mediated hypersensitivity in susceptible people. Reducing exposure may improve respiratory and skin manifestations, although mites do not invade human tissues.
questions.text: Mention the medical importance of house dust mites.
questions.keyConcept: Allergic diseases caused by mite exposure

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer: - An allergic lung reaction caused by invasion of lung tissue by nematode larvae.
questions.explanation: Migrating larvae provoke transient pulmonary infiltrates and peripheral eosinophilia. The syndrome commonly resolves as migration ends, but intensity depends on parasite burden.
questions.text: What is Loeffler's syndrome?
questions.keyConcept: Definition and mechanism of Loeffler's syndrome

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.modelAnswer:
- Hookworms.
- Ascaris.
- Strongyloides.
questions.explanation: Larvae of these soil-transmitted nematodes pass through the lungs during their life cycles. Pulmonary migration can cause cough, fleeting infiltrates, and eosinophilia.
questions.text: Mention the three parasites that cause Loeffler's syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Nematodes associated with Loeffler's syndrome

questions.subject: Parasitology
